explanation: Ethylene is the gaseous hormone produced by ripening fruit, and it spreads through the air to trigger ripening in nearby fruit. Auxin promotes cell elongation, not ripening. Gibberellins promote germination and stem elongation and do not travel as vapors. Cytokinins promote cell division and are not airborne.

subject: biology-2
question: Researchers interrupt the long night of a **short-day plant** with a brief flash of red light, and the plant does not flower. What explains this result?

options.text: The flash converted phytochrome to the red-absorbing form, which prevents flowering.
The plant is actually a long-day plant, since long-day plants need continuous darkness.
Red light halted photosynthesis, so the plant lacked energy to flower.
Flowering depends on an unbroken dark period, and red light converts phytochrome to the far-red-absorbing form that breaks the signal.

explanation: Short-day plants flower only when the night exceeds a critical length, and a red flash in the middle of the night converts phytochrome to the far-red-absorbing form, interrupting the darkness signal. A names the wrong conversion, red light produces the far-red-absorbing form. B inverts the classification, long-day plants flower when nights are short. C mistakes the effect, a brief flash does not halt photosynthesis.

subject: biology-2
question: A sea anemone shows **radial symmetry**, with body parts repeated around a central axis so that a slice along any plane through that axis yields mirror halves. It also has only two germ layers and is therefore **diploblastic**. To which phylum does this animal belong?

options.text: Cnidaria
Platyhelminthes
Annelida
Porifera

explanation: Cnidarians such as sea anemones and jellyfish are diploblastic and radially symmetric. Flatworms and annelids are triploblastic with bilateral symmetry, so B and C fail. Sponges have no true tissues or organized symmetry at all, which eliminates D.

subject: biology-2
question: A parasitic roundworm has a fluid-filled **body cavity** that lies between the mesoderm and the endoderm, so the cavity is only partially lined by mesoderm. Which term classifies this body plan?

options.text: Acoelomate
Pseudocoelomate
Coelomate
Triploblastic

explanation: Roundworms are pseudocoelomates, with a cavity between mesoderm and endoderm that is not fully lined by mesoderm. Acoelomates have no cavity at all, and coelomates have a true coelom completely lined by mesoderm. Triploblastic describes having three germ layers, not a cavity type, so D fails.

subject: biology-2
question: A free-living **flatworm** is flattened top to bottom, shows bilateral symmetry, has three germ layers, and packs its organs directly in mesoderm with no body cavity. Which two terms describe this body plan?

options.text: Diploblastic and coelomate
Triploblastic and coelomate
Triploblastic and acoelomate
Diploblastic and pseudocoelomate

explanation: Flatworms have three germ layers, making them triploblastic, and they lack any body cavity, making them acoelomate. Cnidarians are the classic diploblasts. Coelomates such as annelids and chordates have a fully lined cavity, and pseudocoelomates such as roundworms have a partially lined one, so A, B, and D fail.

subject: biology-2
question: In **deuterostomes**, the first opening of the embryo becomes the anus and the second opening becomes the mouth, while **protostomes** develop in the opposite order. Which pair of animal groups are deuterostomes?

options.text: Annelids and mollusks
Arthropods and roundworms
Flatworms and cnidarians
Echinoderms and chordates

explanation: Echinoderms and chordates share deuterostome development, in which the first opening becomes the anus. Annelids, mollusks, and arthropods are protostomes, where the first opening becomes the mouth, so A and B fail. Cnidarians are diploblastic and show neither pattern, which eliminates C.

subject: biology-2
question: Insects, crabs, and spiders share a hard **exoskeleton**, jointed appendages, and a **segmented** body divided into repeating units along the head-to-tail axis. Which statement best describes this group?

options.text: They are segmented animals with a hard exoskeleton and jointed legs, placed in phylum **Arthropoda**.
They are unsegmented deuterostomes that use a water vascular system for movement.
They are segmented coelomates with a muscular foot, a mantle, and often a shell.
They are segmented worms with a closed circulatory system and bristles.

explanation: Arthropods are defined by segmentation, a chitinous exoskeleton, and jointed appendages. B describes echinoderms, which are unsegmented deuterostomes with a water vascular system. C describes mollusks, which have a foot and mantle but are not segmented. D describes annelids, which share segmentation but have neither an exoskeleton nor jointed legs.

subject: biology-2
question: A marine animal draws water in through pores, traps food particles, and shows **no true tissues**, nerves, or organs even as an adult. To which phylum does this animal belong?

options.text: Cnidaria
Mollusca
Porifera
Echinodermata

explanation: Sponges, phylum Porifera, are the only animals without true tissues, because their cells work independently as water is drawn through pores. Cnidarians have tissues and a nerve net, mollusks have organs such as a mantle and foot, and echinoderms have tube feet and radial symmetry.

subject: biology-2
question: All chordates show four features at some point in life: a **notochord**, a **dorsal hollow nerve cord**, **pharyngeal slits**, and a **post-anal tail**. Which structure below is NOT one of these four chordate features?

options.text: The dorsal hollow nerve cord
The notochord
The pharyngeal slits
A four-chambered heart

explanation: The four chordate features are the notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, and post-anal tail, so A, B, and C are all true chordate marks. A four-chambered heart evolved much later, only in birds and mammals, and is not used to define the chordate phylum.

subject: biology-2
question: In early human embryos a stiff rod, the **notochord**, runs beneath the developing nerve cord. As the embryo grows, bone forms around the rod and gradually replaces most of it. Which adult structure is the notochord's modified fate?

options.text: The brain
The vertebral column
The digestive tract
The gill arches

explanation: In vertebrates the notochord is replaced by the vertebral column, blocks of bone that enclose and protect the nerve cord. The brain develops from the anterior end of the dorsal hollow nerve cord, the digestive tract forms from the endoderm, and gill-related structures trace to the pharyngeal slits, so A, C, and D fail.

subject: biology-2
question: The **amniotic egg** contains a shell, a food supply, and membranes that protect the embryo and store its wastes. Which major new way of life did this egg make possible for the first time in vertebrates?

options.text: Reproduction on land, away from standing water
Filter feeding in open water
Complete metamorphosis during development
Endothermic regulation of body temperature

explanation: The amniotic egg is a self-contained chamber that keeps the embryo moist, so reptiles, birds, and mammals no longer need water for breeding. Fishes and amphibians still lay eggs in water, metamorphosis is an insect and amphibian life-cycle strategy, and a warm body is unrelated to the egg itself, so B, C, and D fail.

subject: biology-2
question: The earliest vertebrates, such as lampreys, have a round, sucking mouth. Later fishes evolved **jaws**, a paired biting structure that let them grasp prey and that helped power new sensory organs. What is this key evolutionary innovation?

options.text: The amniotic egg
Jaws
Feathers
Milk

explanation: Jaws evolved from modified gill arches in early fishes and allowed them to hunt larger prey. The amniotic egg appears only in reptiles, birds, and mammals, feathers only in birds, and milk only in mammals, so none of the other options predates the fishes.

subject: biology-2
question: A fossil shows a fused wishbone, air-filled bones, and a body covering of **feathers**, keratin structures that evolved from reptilian scales. Which vertebrate class does this fossil belong to?

options.text: Amphibia
Mammalia
Aves
Reptilia

explanation: Feathers, along with the wishbone and air-filled bones that lighten the skeleton, define birds, class Aves. Amphibians have moist skin and never grow feathers, mammals grow hair and produce milk, and reptiles have scales but lack feathers, so A, B, and D fail.

subject: biology-2
question: A warm-blooded animal with hair feeds its newborn a nutrient fluid produced by special glands. Which feature, found in essentially all living mammals, is the defining innovation that separates them from every other vertebrate class?

options.text: A post-anal tail
An amniotic egg
Four limbs
Mammary glands

explanation: Mammary glands and the milk they produce define mammals, and essentially all living mammals nurse their young. A post-anal tail is a chordate feature shared with other classes, the amniotic egg also occurs in reptiles and birds, and four limbs are widespread among tetrapods, so A, B, and C fail.

subject: biology-2
question: A crayfish has an **open circulatory system**, while a human has a **closed circulatory system**. Which statement correctly contrasts these two arrangements?

options.text: In an open system, blood flows only through vessels; in a closed system, hemolymph bathes tissues directly.
In an open system, hemolymph bathes tissues directly; in a closed system, blood stays inside vessels.
Open systems always have a four-chambered heart; closed systems have no heart at all.
Closed systems are found only in insects and arthropods; open systems are found in all vertebrates.

explanation: In an open circulatory system, the fluid called hemolymph leaves the vessels and bathes the organs directly before seeping back, which is typical of arthropods such as crayfish and insects. In a closed circulatory system, blood is confined to vessels and exchanges materials through their walls, as in humans and earthworms. A reverses the two systems, C misstates heart structure, and D assigns the systems to the wrong animal groups.

subject: biology-2
question: A fish heart pumps blood to the gills, where gas exchange occurs, and the blood then continues to the body before returning to the heart. This pattern is best described as which of the following?

options.text: Double circulation, because blood makes two loops from the heart.
Open circulation, because the gills spill blood into the body cavity.
Incomplete double circulation, because the heart lacks a septum.
Single circulation, because blood passes through the heart once for each complete trip around the body.

explanation: In single circulation, blood makes one circuit per trip around the body, passing from heart to gills to body and back to the heart, so the heart is not used between the gills and the body. Double circulation requires separate pulmonary and systemic circuits, which fish lack. The gills do not spill blood into the body cavity, and the missing septum in the fish heart is a structural fact that does not describe the circuit pattern.

subject: biology-2
question: A red blood cell has just returned from the body and is entering the **right atrium** of the heart. Which sequence correctly traces its path until it reaches the lungs?

options.text: Right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs
Right ventricle → right atrium → pulmonary vein → lungs
Left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → lungs
Right atrium → pulmonary vein → right ventricle → lungs

explanation: Blood returning from the body enters the right atrium, passes through a valve into the right ventricle, and is pumped out through the pulmonary artery to the lungs, where it unloads carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen. B reverses the atrium and ventricle and misroutes blood into the pulmonary vein, which actually returns blood from the lungs. C traces the left-side pathway that leaves through the aorta to the body, and D sends blood into the pulmonary vein before the ventricle.

subject: biology-2
question: Which sequence correctly lists the path that inhaled air follows from outside the body to the **alveoli**, the gas exchange surfaces?

options.text: Nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
Nose → trachea → pharynx → larynx → bronchioles → bronchi → alveoli
Mouth → larynx → pharynx → trachea → alveoli → bronchioles → bronchi
Nose → bronchi → bronchioles → trachea → larynx → pharynx → alveoli

explanation: Air enters through the nose or mouth, passes through the pharynx and larynx into the trachea, which branches into the bronchi and then the smaller bronchioles, finally reaching the alveoli where gases are exchanged by diffusion. B, C, and D each place the pharynx, larynx, trachea, or branching airways in the wrong order. Only the alveoli provide the thin, moist, highly branched surface where gas exchange actually occurs.

subject: biology-2
question: Most of the **carbon dioxide** produced by body tissues and carried in human blood is transported in which form?

options.text: Bound to the iron atoms of hemoglobin.
Dissolved directly in the plasma as free gas.
As bicarbonate ions formed inside red blood cells.
Stored as gas bubbles inside red blood cells.

explanation: The enzyme carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells converts carbon dioxide and water into carbonic acid, which splits into hydrogen ions and bicarbonate ions, and roughly 70 percent of the carbon dioxide travels to the lungs in this bicarbonate form. A describes the small fraction of carbon dioxide that binds to hemoglobin, and the binding sites are amino groups rather than iron, which is reserved for oxygen. B covers only about 7 percent of carbon dioxide that dissolves in plasma, and D describes no real transport mechanism.

subject: biology-2
question: When the **diaphragm** contracts during inhalation, what happens to the chest cavity and the air?

options.text: The chest cavity shrinks, raising air pressure inside the lungs and pushing air out.
The chest cavity enlarges, lowering air pressure inside the lungs so that air flows in.
The ribs move downward and inward, compressing the lungs.
The alveoli actively expand by contracting their smooth muscle.

explanation: Inhalation is an active process in which the diaphragm flattens and the rib muscles lift the ribs, enlarging the thoracic cavity and lowering the air pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure so air rushes in. A and C describe exhalation, the passive phase in which the cavity shrinks and the ribs move down and inward. The alveoli have no smooth muscle of their own, so D is anatomically wrong.

subject: biology-2
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes **mechanical digestion** from **chemical digestion** in humans?

options.text: Mechanical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces by chewing and stomach churning, while chemical digestion uses enzymes and acids to break large molecules into smaller ones.
Mechanical digestion begins in the small intestine, while chemical digestion occurs only in the mouth.
Mechanical digestion uses enzymes to break peptide bonds, while chemical digestion is only physical grinding.
Both mechanical and chemical digestion occur only in the stomach.

explanation: Mechanical digestion raises the surface area of food without changing the molecules, using teeth and stomach churning, while chemical digestion breaks the bonds in large molecules using enzymes and stomach acid. B wrongly starts mechanical digestion in the small intestine, where most chemical digestion actually occurs. C swaps the definitions, and D ignores the mouth and the small intestine entirely.

subject: biology-2
question: **Bile** is produced by the liver, stored in the gallbladder, and released into the small intestine. What is the role of bile in digestion?

options.text: Bile digests proteins into amino acids by breaking peptide bonds.
Bile emulsifies fats into small droplets so that lipase enzymes can digest them.
Bile lowers the pH of chyme so that stomach enzymes can keep working.
Bile absorbs glucose directly through the intestinal wall into the blood.

explanation: Bile salts act like detergent, breaking large fat globules into tiny droplets through emulsification and giving the enzyme lipase a much larger surface area to work on. Bile contains no protein-digesting enzymes, so A is wrong, and bile helps raise rather than lower the pH in the small intestine, so C is wrong. Absorption of nutrients is the job of the intestinal wall, not bile, so D is wrong.

subject: biology-2
question: **Villi** and **microvilli** line the inner surface of the small intestine and greatly increase its surface area. What is the main benefit of this arrangement?

options.text: It strengthens peristalsis so that food moves faster through the gut.
It traps bacteria so that harmful microbes cannot reach the colon.
It secretes hydrochloric acid that sterilizes incoming chyme.
It maximizes the area available for absorbing digested nutrients into the blood and lymph.

explanation: Each villus is a fingerlike projection packed with blood capillaries and a lacteal, and microvilli on its surface create a brush border, so the combined surface area is enormous and nutrient absorption is maximized. Peristalsis does not depend on villi, so A is wrong. Villi neither trap bacteria nor secrete hydrochloric acid, so B and C are wrong.

subject: biology-2
question: Which sequence correctly traces the path of fluid through a **nephron** from filtration to the collecting duct?

options.text: Bowman's capsule → glomerulus → distal tubule → loop of Henle → proximal tubule → collecting duct
Collecting duct → distal tubule → loop of Henle → proximal tubule → Bowman's capsule → glomerulus
Glomerulus → Bowman's capsule → proximal tubule → loop of Henle → distal tubule → collecting duct
Glomerulus → loop of Henle → proximal tubule → distal tubule → Bowman's capsule → collecting duct

explanation: Blood pressure pushes filtrate from the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule, after which the fluid travels through the proximal tubule, the loop of Henle, and the distal tubule, finally entering the collecting duct. A places Bowman's capsule before the glomerulus and jumbles the tubule order. B runs the entire pathway backwards, and D places the loop of Henle too early in the sequence.

subject: biology-2
question: Which pairing of an animal group with its main **nitrogenous waste** product is correct?

options.text: Aquatic fish excrete uric acid because it is the least toxic waste.
Terrestrial birds excrete ammonia because it dissolves easily in the blood.
Mammals excrete urea, which is moderately toxic and requires some water but less than ammonia.
Reptiles excrete urea, which can be stored dry inside the egg.

explanation: Mammals convert ammonia to urea in the liver, and because urea is moderately toxic it requires a small amount of water for excretion, more than uric acid needs but less than ammonia. Aquatic fish excrete ammonia directly into the water, so A is wrong. Birds and reptiles excrete uric acid, which is nearly insoluble and can be stored dry in eggs, so B and D are wrong.

subject: biology-2
question: When the body is dehydrated, the pituitary gland releases the hormone **ADH**. What effect does ADH have on the kidneys?

options.text: ADH decreases water reabsorption so that urine volume increases.
ADH increases sodium reabsorption, and water follows into the blood.
ADH raises the glomerular filtration rate so that more urine is produced.
ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed and urine becomes concentrated.

explanation: ADH inserts water channel proteins into the cells of the collecting ducts, allowing water to be reabsorbed back into the blood, which concentrates the urine and conserves body water. A and C describe the opposite of this effect. Sodium reabsorption is controlled mainly by aldosterone, so B describes a different hormone's action.

subject: biology-2
question: A **neuron** gathers incoming signals from many neighboring cells before deciding to fire. Which part of the neuron receives those incoming signals and conducts them toward the cell body?

options.text: The **myelin sheath**, which insulates the axon so signals travel faster.
The **dendrites**, which receive signals from other neurons and carry them toward the cell body.
The **axon**, which carries signals away from the cell body toward the terminals.
The **axon terminals**, which release neurotransmitters onto the next cell.

explanation: The dendrites are the input branches of the neuron, receiving signals and conducting them toward the cell body, which is their defining job. A describes the myelin sheath's insulating role, which speeds conduction but does not collect signals. C and D accurately describe the axon and the axon terminals, but those structures send signals away from the cell body rather than collecting them.

subject: biology-2
question: A neuron at rest keeps its inside about 70 millivolts more negative than the outside, even when no signals are moving. What maintains this **resting membrane potential**?

options.text: The **sodium-potassium pump** exports three sodium ions for every two potassium ions it imports, and potassium leaks out more easily than sodium leaks in, keeping the inside negative.
Sodium ions rush into the resting cell through open channels, keeping the inside slightly positive.
The pump continuously ejects potassium ions while sodium stays balanced, making the interior negative.
The resting membrane blocks all ion movement, so the charge comes only from fixed negative proteins.

explanation: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to export three sodium ions for every two potassium ions it imports, and because the resting membrane leaks potassium more readily than sodium, the inside of the neuron stays about 70 millivolts negative. B gets the direction wrong, since sodium entry is limited at rest and cannot make the inside positive. C wrongly says potassium is pumped out, when the pump actually brings it in. D contradicts the membrane's selective permeability, which is what allows the ion gradients to exist.

subject: biology-2
question: A weak stimulus fades away without effect, but a stronger stimulus that pushes the neuron's membrane potential to about negative 55 millivolts triggers an **action potential**. What happens at the **threshold**?

options.text: Voltage-gated potassium channels open first, sodium channels stay closed, and the cell becomes more negative.
The membrane potential drifts gradually back to rest as the stimulus fades.
Voltage-gated sodium channels open, sodium floods in, and the membrane rapidly depolarizes to a positive peak.
Sodium channels inactivate permanently, and the cell can never fire again.

explanation: At threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open, sodium rushes into the cell, and the membrane rapidly depolarizes toward a positive peak, which is the rising phase of the action potential. A reverses the channel sequence, because sodium channels open before potassium channels. B describes a graded potential fading back to rest, not the all-or-none firing that threshold triggers. D confuses temporary sodium channel inactivation with permanent loss of excitability.

subject: biology-2
question: A neuron fires at the start of its axon, and the signal travels all the way to the axon terminals without fading. Which statement best describes how the **all-or-none** action potential propagates along the axon?

options.text: The signal grows weaker with distance, like a ripple spreading across a pond.
Each segment fires at a smaller amplitude, so only short axons can transmit signals.
The signal stops at the first gap in the myelin sheath unless the stimulus is repeated.
The depolarization of one segment opens sodium channels in the next segment, so the full-strength signal regenerates at every point along the axon.

explanation: An action potential is all-or-none and regenerates, because the depolarization of one membrane region opens sodium channels in the adjacent region, so the impulse travels at full strength. A and B are false because action potentials do not weaken or shrink as they move along an axon. C is false because propagation is self-sustaining once the first action potential has fired.

subject: biology-2
question: After a neuron releases a **neurotransmitter** into the **synaptic cleft**, the receiving cell responds, and then the message must be stopped quickly. Which mechanism ends the signal?

options.text: The neurotransmitter stays in the cleft, keeping the receiving cell stimulated until the next impulse.
The receiving cell absorbs the neurotransmitter and stores it for later use.
The cleft widens so the neurotransmitter becomes too dilute to act.
The neurotransmitter is cleared by **reuptake** into the presynaptic terminal or broken down by enzymes in the cleft.

explanation: Reuptake by the presynaptic terminal and enzymatic degradation in the cleft both clear the neurotransmitter, allowing the receiving cell to return to rest. A would leave receptors continuously stimulated and the signal ongoing. B is wrong because the neurotransmitter is stored in the presynaptic terminal, not absorbed by the receiving cell. C describes no real mechanism for ending a synaptic signal.

subject: biology-2
question: Two neurons release different neurotransmitters onto the same receiving neuron, one opening sodium channels and the other opening chloride channels. Which statement correctly describes the **excitatory** and **inhibitory** effects on the receiving neuron?

options.text: The sodium signal depolarizes the receiving neuron toward threshold, while the chloride signal makes firing harder.
Both signals excite the receiving neuron, and it fires immediately.
The sodium signal makes the neuron more negative, and the chloride signal pushes it toward threshold.
The two signals cancel exactly, so the neuron can never fire.

explanation: Sodium entry depolarizes the receiving membrane toward threshold, which is excitatory, while chloride entry pushes the membrane away from threshold, which is inhibitory. B is wrong because chloride does not excite the cell. C swaps the two effects. D overstates the result, because a neuron integrates many inputs and can still fire if excitation outweighs inhibition.

subject: biology-2
question: You decide to raise your hand, and your heart beats faster when you are excited without you deciding anything. Which statement correctly pairs the **somatic nervous system** and the **autonomic nervous system** with their jobs?

options.text: The autonomic nervous system moves your hand because it controls voluntary muscles.
The somatic nervous system commands skeletal muscles, while the autonomic nervous system regulates the heart and glands without conscious effort.
Both systems control only skeletal muscle, just at different speeds.
The autonomic nervous system controls the brain, and the somatic system controls the spinal cord.

explanation: The somatic nervous system sends motor commands to skeletal muscles under voluntary control, while the autonomic nervous system regulates the heart, glands, and smooth muscle without conscious effort, and both are divisions of the peripheral nervous system. A assigns the voluntary hand movement to the autonomic system, reversing their roles. C is wrong because the autonomic system does not control skeletal muscle. D is wrong because both systems connect through the brain and spinal cord rather than one system owning each.

subject: biology-2
question: One patient cannot coordinate balance and smooth movements, and another patient cannot form new memories. Which statement correctly matches the **cerebellum** and the **hippocampus** to these symptoms?

options.text: The cerebellum stores new memories, and the hippocampus coordinates balance.
The medulla controls voluntary thought, and the cerebellum regulates breathing.
The cerebellum coordinates balance and smooth movement, while the hippocampus is important for forming new memories.
The hypothalamus plans movements, and the medulla forms memories.

explanation: The cerebellum coordinates balance and smooth movement, while the hippocampus is essential for forming new memories. A swaps the two functions, putting memory in the cerebellum and balance in the hippocampus. B confuses the medulla's control of breathing and heart rate with voluntary thought. D assigns the wrong jobs to the hypothalamus and the medulla.

subject: biology-2
question: A **peptide hormone** such as insulin and a **steroid hormone** such as cortisol both carry messages to target cells. How does each class of hormone produce its effect?

options.text: Both hormones cross the membrane and bind receptors in the nucleus.
Steroid hormones bind surface receptors, and peptide hormones enter the nucleus.
Both hormones bind surface receptors, so they act in the same way.
Peptide hormones bind receptors on the cell surface and trigger signaling cascades, while steroid hormones cross the membrane and bind receptors inside the cell.

explanation: Peptide hormones are water soluble and cannot cross the lipid membrane, so they bind surface receptors and trigger signaling cascades, while steroid hormones are lipid soluble, diffuse across the membrane, and bind receptors inside the cell. A and C ignore the solubility difference between the two hormone classes. B swaps the two mechanisms, putting steroid hormones on the surface and peptide hormones inside.

subject: biology-2
question: After a meal, blood glucose rises and the pancreas releases **insulin**, bringing the glucose level back down. Which statement correctly describes this regulatory loop and the opposite role of **glucagon**?

options.text: The loop is negative feedback, because insulin lowers glucose and reverses the rise that triggered its release, while glucagon raises glucose when it falls.
The loop is positive feedback, because insulin amplifies the rise in blood glucose.
The pancreas releases insulin when glucose is low, and insulin raises glucose by breaking down glycogen.
Glucagon lowers blood glucose after meals, and insulin raises it between meals.

explanation: Rising glucose triggers insulin release, and insulin lowers glucose, so the response opposes the original change, which is the definition of negative feedback. Glucagon has the opposite job, raising glucose when it falls too low. B mislabels the loop as positive feedback, C swaps the hormone roles, and D swaps the jobs of insulin and glucagon.

subject: biology-2
question: A virus enters the body for the first time, and **B cells** respond by secreting **antibodies** that neutralize the virus. Which statement best describes the mechanism by which antibodies neutralize the virus?

options.text: Antibodies enter infected cells and destroy the virus's genetic material.
Antibodies bind to the virus surface, blocking it from attaching to host cells and marking it for destruction by other immune cells.
Antibodies raise the body temperature to kill the virus directly.
Antibodies act as enzymes that digest the virus into harmless pieces.

explanation: Antibodies are proteins that bind specific antigens on the virus surface, which blocks the virus from attaching to host cells and marks it for destruction by phagocytes. A and D are wrong because antibodies do not enter cells and are not enzymes that digest pathogens. C is wrong because fever is a general innate defense, not a job of antibodies.

subject: biology-2
question: A person receives a **vaccine** containing a weakened virus and, months later, the live virus enters the body. Why does the vaccinated person stay healthy while an unvaccinated person becomes sick?

options.text: The innate immune system remembers the virus from the vaccine and produces antibodies within minutes.
The weakened virus from the vaccine stays in the blood and digests the live virus on re-entry.
The vaccine triggers the adaptive immune system to form **memory cells**, so a later exposure produces a fast, strong response that clears the virus quickly.
The vaccine permanently raises the body temperature, which destroys the live virus.

explanation: Vaccination presents antigens from a weakened or killed pathogen without causing disease, and the adaptive immune system responds by generating memory cells, including helper **T cells** that recognize antigen presented by **MHC** molecules. On later exposure, memory cells mount a rapid secondary response that produces large amounts of antibody and clears the virus quickly. A is wrong because the innate immune system has no memory and does not produce antibodies. B and D are wrong because the vaccine does not remain in the blood to digest the virus or keep the body warm.

subject: biology-2
question: A population of aphids reproduces entirely by **asexual reproduction** for many generations. Which of the following is the most serious long-term disadvantage of this strategy?

options.text: The population will produce little or no genetic variation, leaving it vulnerable if the environment changes.
Each offspring will have a new combination of genes from two parents, which slows reproduction.
The population will grow so slowly that it cannot replace individuals that die.
Offspring will be genetically identical to both parents at once, which doubles the mutation load.

explanation: Asexual reproduction produces genetically identical offspring with no recombination, so no new gene combinations arise to respond to a changing environment. B describes sexual reproduction, whose genetic novelty is exactly what asexual populations lack. C is false because asexual reproduction is usually fast and produces many offspring. D is wrong because asexual offspring are copies of a single parent, not a fusion of two.

subject: biology-2
question: In some species of bees, unfertilized eggs develop directly into **haploid** males, while fertilized eggs develop into **diploid** females. Which of the following best classifies this mode of reproduction?

options.text: Budding, in which a new individual grows out of the parent's body.
Parthenogenesis, because an egg develops without being fertilized.
Fragmentation, because the body splits into pieces that each grow.
External fertilization, because eggs are released and met by sperm outside the body.

explanation: The scenario is the defining case of parthenogenesis, in which an unfertilized egg develops into a new individual. A and C describe outgrowths of the parent's body or body pieces growing into new individuals, neither of which occurs here. D involves sperm meeting eggs outside the body, which the stem does not describe.

subject: biology-2
question: A marine biologist cuts a sea star into two pieces, and each piece grows into a complete adult. Meanwhile, a hydra grows a small outgrowth on its side that pinches off as a new individual. Which pair of terms correctly names the sea star's mode of **asexual reproduction** first and the hydra's mode second?

options.text: Parthenogenesis and budding
Fragmentation and parthenogenesis
Fragmentation and budding
Budding and fragmentation

explanation: Regrowing a full adult from a cut piece is the definition of fragmentation, and a side outgrowth that detaches is the definition of budding, so C pairs the two correctly. A swaps fragmentation for parthenogenesis, which requires unfertilized eggs. B places parthenogenesis where budding belongs. D reverses the correct order.

subject: biology-2
question: Which of the following statements best contrasts **spermatogenesis** with **oogenesis** in humans?

options.text: Oogenesis produces four functional gametes per meiotic cycle, while spermatogenesis produces one.
Both processes pause in prophase of meiosis I until puberty.
Spermatogenesis begins before birth, while oogenesis continues throughout life.
Spermatogenesis produces four functional sperm from one primary spermatocyte, while oogenesis produces one ovum and polar bodies from one primary oocyte.

explanation: Each primary spermatocyte yields four functional sperm, whereas each primary oocyte yields a single ovum plus polar bodies, preserving the cytoplasm the egg needs. A reverses those numbers, attributing four gametes to oogenesis. B fails because spermatogenesis runs continuously from puberty and does not pause in prophase of meiosis I. C reverses the timing, since oogenesis begins before birth and spermatogenesis begins at puberty.

subject: biology-2
question: Which of the following environmental conditions would most strongly favor the evolution of **external fertilization** over **internal fertilization**?

options.text: A dry desert habitat where gametes quickly dry out.
An aquatic habitat where many males and females release gametes into the water at the same time.
A habitat with few individuals, where encounters between mates are rare.
A habitat with heavy predation on exposed eggs and sperm.

explanation: External fertilization works best in aquatic habitats where many individuals release eggs and sperm into the water together, because water protects the gametes and brings them together. A dry habitat, rare encounters between mates, and heavy predation on exposed gametes would all favor internal fertilization, which protects gametes and eggs inside the body.

subject: biology-2
question: During the **cleavage** stage of early embryonic development, which of the following best describes what happens to the cells?

options.text: The embryo grows larger, because each mitotic division adds more cytoplasm.
Cells begin expressing tissue-specific genes and forming organs.
The zygote undergoes rapid mitotic divisions without overall growth, producing a solid ball called the morula and then a hollow ball called the blastula.
The zygote divides by meiosis to reduce its chromosome number.

explanation: Cleavage is a rapid series of mitotic divisions that subdivide the zygote's cytoplasm into smaller cells without growth of the whole embryo. The solid ball of cells is the morula, and the hollow fluid-filled ball that follows is the blastula. A describes growth that cleavage does not show, B describes gastrulation and later differentiation, and D is wrong because cleavage divisions are mitotic and keep the chromosome number constant.

subject: biology-2
question: During **gastrulation**, three **germ layers** form. Which germ layer gives rise to most of the muscle tissue of the body?

options.text: The mesoderm, which also forms bone and blood.
The ectoderm, which also forms the nervous system.
The endoderm, which also forms the gut lining.
All three layers contribute equally to muscle.

explanation: Muscle, bone, blood, and connective tissue are all mesodermal derivatives, so the mesoderm is the layer that gives rise to most of the body's muscle. B and C name layers whose derivatives are the skin and nervous system or the gut lining. D is false, since muscle forms from the mesoderm alone.

subject: biology-2
question: A researcher traces a group of embryonic cells and finds that they form the brain, spinal cord, and outer layer of skin. From which germ layer did these cells most likely come?

options.text: The mesoderm, which forms muscle and blood.
The endoderm, which forms the gut lining.
The yolk sac, an extraembryonic membrane.
The ectoderm, which forms the nervous system and skin.

explanation: The ectoderm gives rise to the nervous system (the brain and spinal cord) and the outer layer of skin, exactly the derivatives the researcher traced. A and B name layers whose derivatives are muscle and blood or the gut lining. C is an extraembryonic membrane, not a germ layer of the embryo.

subject: biology-2
question: During **neurulation**, the neural plate folds upward and fuses to form the **neural tube**. If the posterior end of this tube fails to close completely, which of the following conditions would most directly result?

options.text: A defect in the development of the spinal cord and the tissue around it.
A failure to form any germ layers.
The complete absence of muscle tissue.
The failure of the amnion to form around the embryo.

explanation: The neural tube develops into the brain and spinal cord, so incomplete closure of its posterior end disrupts spinal cord development. B is wrong because germ layers form earlier, during gastrulation. C is wrong because muscle arises from mesoderm, not the neural tube. D is wrong because the amnion is an extraembryonic membrane unrelated to the neural tube.

subject: biology-2
question: In Spemann and Mangold's classic experiment, tissue from the dorsal lip of the blastopore of one newt embryo was transplanted into a second embryo, and the host cells then formed a second complete neural tube and body axis. This transplanted tissue, known as the **Spemann organizer**, worked by which of the following mechanisms?

options.text: The transplant replaced the host cells with its own differentiated neurons.
The transplanted cells released signals that induced surrounding host cells to change their developmental fate.
The transplant divided by meiosis and doubled the host chromosome number.
The transplant fused with the host gut and redirected its blood flow.

explanation: The dorsal lip of the blastopore is the Spemann organizer, whose cells secrete signaling molecules that induce neighboring cells to form a second body axis, so the second neural tube is built from host cells, not graft cells. A is wrong for exactly that reason. C and D describe effects that do not occur in the experiment and have nothing to do with induction.

subject: biology-2
question: In a developing amniote embryo, which of the following best describes the function of the **amnion**?

options.text: It supplies the embryo with oxygen and nutrients from the mother.
It stores nitrogenous wastes produced by the embryo.
It encloses the embryo in a fluid-filled sac that cushions it and prevents drying out.
It connects the embryo to the yolk sac and later to the placenta.

explanation: The amnion surrounds the embryo with amniotic fluid, cushioning it against shocks and preventing desiccation, which is what allowed amniotes to reproduce on land. A describes the gas exchange of the chorion and the nutrient supply of the placenta. B describes the allantois, which stores nitrogenous wastes. D describes the connecting stalk and umbilical cord, which link the embryo to the yolk sac and placenta.

subject: biology-2
question: In mammals, the **placenta** replaces several roles that extraembryonic membranes play in the shelled egg of a bird. Which combination of functions does the placenta take over?

options.text: Cushioning the embryo and storing nutrients for the hatchling.
Producing the shell and insulating the embryo against temperature change.
Supplying the egg with yolk and storing nitrogenous wastes until hatching.
Exchanging nutrients, gases, and wastes between the mother and the embryo.

explanation: The placenta is the exchange organ between maternal blood and fetal blood, delivering nutrients and oxygen while removing carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes, which replaces the combined roles of the yolk sac, chorion, and allantois in the egg. A misassigns cushioning, which belongs to the amnion, and nutrient storage to the placenta. B describes the shell's protection, which the placenta does not provide. C names roles that stay inside the egg and never reach the embryo.

subject: biology-2
question: A population of large mammals in a well-protected reserve has a **survivorship curve** in which almost every individual survives through early and middle life, with most deaths occurring among old individuals. Which survivorship curve shape best describes this population?

options.text: Type I, where mortality concentrates in old age.
Type II, where mortality is constant at every age.
Type III, where mortality is highest among the very young.
A J-shaped curve, since survival tracks population growth.

explanation: In a Type I survivorship curve, mortality concentrates late in life because adults protect and care for their young. Type II describes constant mortality at every age, and Type III describes heavy death among the very young. A J-shaped curve describes population growth, not survival, so it cannot describe this population.

subject: biology-2
question: A population of algae in a lake grows with **exponential growth** at an intrinsic rate of increase r = 0.5 per day. If the current population size N is 1000 cells, what is the daily growth rate dN/dt?

options.text: 500 cells per day
1000 cells per day
2000 cells per day
250 cells per day

explanation: The exponential growth equation is dN/dt = rN, so multiply the rate r = 0.5 per day by the current size N = 1000 cells. That gives 500 cells per day. Option B reports the population size itself, C doubles it, and D divides instead of multiplying.

subject: biology-2
question: A population of deer grows with **logistic growth** at r = 0.2 per year, with a current population size N = 400 and a **carrying capacity** K = 800. Using the logistic equation dN/dt = rN(1 - N/K), what is the current growth rate?

options.text: 20 deer per year
40 deer per year
80 deer per year
160 deer per year

explanation: The logistic equation dN/dt = rN(1 - N/K) requires multiplying the rate, the current size, and the correction term together. With N/K equal to 0.5, the correction term (1 - N/K) is also 0.5, so 0.2 x 400 x 0.5 equals 40 deer per year. Option C ignores the correction term entirely, D doubles the population before applying the rate, and A applies the correction twice.

subject: biology-2
question: A population of rabbits has hovered near its carrying capacity for several months. Which statement best describes the population during this time?

options.text: Population size hovers near the carrying capacity as birth rates and death rates balance.
The population resumes exponential growth because resources are still abundant.
The population crashes to zero because all resources are exhausted.
The growth rate reaches its maximum because crowding boosts reproduction.

explanation: At carrying capacity, N approaches K so the logistic correction term (1 - N/K) nears zero and growth slows almost to a stop. Birth rates and death rates balance, so the population size fluctuates near K rather than growing without limit. Exponential growth requires abundant resources, crowding does not boost reproduction, and a stable population does not crash to zero.

subject: biology-2
question: Which of the following is a **density-dependent** factor that limits population growth?

options.text: A volcanic eruption that buries a forest.
Competition for nesting sites, which intensifies as crowding increases.
A severe drought that dries up ponds.
A lightning-caused wildfire.

explanation: Density-dependent factors strengthen their effect as population density rises, and competition for limited nesting sites is the classic example. A volcanic eruption, a drought, and a wildfire strike with equal force whether the population is large or small, so they are density-independent.

subject: biology-2
question: Which organism is most likely to be **r-selected**?

options.text: A blue whale that bears one calf every few years.
A redwood tree that lives for centuries and reproduces slowly.
A dandelion that scatters thousands of small seeds each season.
An elephant that raises each calf for many years.

explanation: r-selected species maximize reproduction, producing many small offspring with little or no parental care, and the dandelion is the textbook example. The blue whale, the redwood, and the elephant all invest in few offspring, long lives, or extended care, which are K-selected traits.

subject: biology-2
question: A country's **age structure** diagram is broad at the base and narrow at the top. What does this shape predict about the population's future?

options.text: A stable population size with slow growth.
Rapid population growth in the coming decades as the young reach reproductive age.
A shrinking population because deaths exceed births.
No change, because age structure does not affect future growth.

explanation: A broad base means a large fraction of the population is young and has not yet reproduced. As those individuals mature, they will add more births than deaths, so the population will grow rapidly for decades. A stable population shows roughly equal bars at every age, and a shrinking population has a narrow base.

subject: biology-2
question: Two species of warblers feed in the same forest, with one foraging in the upper canopy and the other in the lower branches. What does this division of the shared resource represent?

options.text: Competitive exclusion, in which the weaker species is eliminated.
Interspecific competition, since both species need the same insects.
Intraspecific competition among members of a single species.
**Resource partitioning**, which lets the two species coexist by dividing the shared resource.

explanation: Feeding in different parts of the canopy divides the shared insect resource, which is resource partitioning, a form of niche partitioning that lets competing species coexist. Competitive exclusion would predict one species being eliminated, which the stem says does not happen. Interspecific competition names the pressure, not the solution, and intraspecific competition occurs within a single species.

subject: biology-2
question: A salamander species can survive in damp forest zones from stream edges to hilltops, but predators confine it to the stream edges. Which term best describes the area the salamander actually occupies?

options.text: **Fundamental niche**, the full range of conditions the species can tolerate.
Fundamental niche, the reduced range that results from predation.
Realized niche, the reduced portion of the potential range actually occupied because of predation.
Realized niche, the complete range the species could occupy if predators were absent.

explanation: The **fundamental niche** is the full range of conditions a species can tolerate, while the **realized niche** is the portion actually occupied after competition and predation shrink it. Predators confine the salamander to the stream edge, so its realized niche is smaller than its fundamental niche. Option A states the definition of the fundamental niche correctly but answers the wrong question, and D calls the full potential range the realized niche.

subject: biology-2
question: A harmless moth species has wing patterns that closely resemble those of a toxic butterfly species. What is this defense called?

options.text: Camouflage, because the moth blends into the tree bark where it rests.
Warning coloration, because bright patterns advertise that the butterfly is toxic.
**Mimicry**, because the harmless moth copies the appearance of a toxic species.
Aggressive mimicry, because the moth lures insect prey by resembling a flower.

explanation: A harmless species resembling a toxic one is mimicry, because the mimic gains protection by copying the warning signal of a dangerous model. Camouflage hides an organism against its background rather than copying another species, and warning coloration is the bright display worn by the toxic animal itself. Aggressive mimicry is a predator's trick for luring prey, and this moth hunts nothing.

subject: biology-2
question: Which pairing is an example of **commensalism**?

options.text: A fungus and an alga forming a lichen, with both partners gaining from the union.
A tapeworm absorbing nutrients from the intestine of its host.
Bees pollinating flowers while gathering nectar from them.
Barnacles attaching to a whale's skin, gaining transport while the whale is unaffected.

explanation: Commensalism is a relationship in which one species benefits while the other is unaffected, and the barnacles gain free transport from the whale. The lichen and the bee example are both mutualisms in which both partners benefit. The tapeworm is a parasite because it harms its host.

subject: biology-2
question: A forest fire burns a mature forest down to bare soil, leaving the soil intact but removing all living plants. What type of **succession** follows, which organisms appear first, and how does the community change over time?

options.text: Primary succession, beginning with lichens breaking down bare rock.
Primary succession, because the fire destroyed every organism in the soil.
Secondary succession, beginning directly with the climax tree species.
Secondary succession, beginning with fast-growing **pioneer species** such as grasses and herbs that are gradually replaced by shrubs and then trees.

explanation: Because the fire leaves the soil intact, the regrowth is secondary succession, not primary succession. Pioneer species such as grasses and herbs colonize first and are gradually replaced by shrubs and then trees as the community develops toward a climax state. Primary succession requires ground with no soil, such as bare rock, and climax species arrive last, not first.

subject: biology-2
question: Ecologists measure the total chemical energy that phytoplankton in a lake capture from sunlight through photosynthesis, and they separately measure the energy that remains after the producers consume energy through respiration for their own maintenance. Which measurement is the **gross primary productivity**, and which is the **net primary productivity**?

options.text: The first is gross primary productivity and the second is net primary productivity.
The first is net primary productivity and the second is gross primary productivity.
Both measurements are gross primary productivity, because autotrophs always produce more than they use.
The first is secondary productivity and the second is gross primary productivity.

explanation: Gross primary productivity is the total energy fixed by photosynthesis, and net primary productivity is what remains after producers spend energy on their own respiration. B swaps the two terms. C ignores the respiration loss, and D confuses producer productivity with consumer productivity.

subject: biology-2
question: A grassland produces 50,000 kcal of new plant biomass in one growing season. If the **10 percent rule** governs energy transfer between **trophic levels** and primary consumers eat the plants, roughly how many kcal are available to tertiary consumers?

options.text: 5,000 kcal, because primary consumers pass most of their energy directly upward.
50 kcal, because each transfer wastes about 90 percent of the energy as heat.
500 kcal, because only one transfer separates producers from tertiary consumers.
50,000 kcal, because energy is recycled within the food web.

explanation: With 10 percent transfer efficiency, the 50,000 kcal of plants becomes 5,000 kcal for primary consumers, then 500 kcal for secondary consumers, then about 50 kcal for tertiary consumers. B is the only option with the correct three-transfer arithmetic. A and C skip one and two transfers, and D ignores the one-way flow of energy.

subject: biology-2
question: In a forest, the standing **biomass** of all the trees greatly exceeds the biomass of all the deer, and the deer in turn outweigh the wolves. What explains this pyramid-shaped pattern?

options.text: Herbivores digest plants so efficiently that little plant matter ever remains.
Producers grow more slowly than consumers reproduce, so consumers accumulate.
Each trophic level loses most of its energy as heat, so less biomass can be supported at each higher level.
Decomposers consume the wolves before they can reproduce.

explanation: Energy flows one way through the ecosystem, and most of it is lost as heat at each transfer, so each higher trophic level can support less biomass. A is wrong because herbivores digest plants poorly, which is exactly why plant biomass stays large. B gets the growth relationship backwards, and D gives decomposers a role they do not play.

subject: biology-2
question: A farmer notices that nitrogen keeps disappearing from the soil even though she applies fertilizer, and a soil scientist explains that some of it returns to the atmosphere as nitrogen gas. Which process in the **nitrogen cycle** is responsible?

options.text: **Nitrogen fixation**, carried out by bacteria living in root nodules.
**Nitrification**, which converts ammonia to nitrate.
**Ammonification**, performed by decomposers.
**Denitrification**, which converts nitrate back into atmospheric nitrogen gas.

explanation: Denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate to nitrogen gas, which returns nitrogen to the atmosphere and completes the cycle. Fixation pulls atmospheric nitrogen into the soil instead of releasing it. Nitrification makes nitrate, and ammonification releases ammonia from dead matter; neither produces nitrogen gas.

subject: biology-2
question: In the **carbon cycle**, which reservoir holds the most carbon at any given moment?

options.text: Sedimentary rocks, such as limestone formed from the shells of marine organisms.
The atmosphere, in the form of carbon dioxide.
Living organisms, in the form of organic compounds.
The deep ocean water column.

explanation: The vast majority of Earth's carbon is locked in sedimentary rocks such as limestone over geological timescales. The ocean is large but holds far less carbon than the rock record. The atmosphere and living organisms are small pools by comparison, even though they exchange carbon rapidly.

subject: biology-2
question: Unlike the carbon cycle and the nitrogen cycle, the **phosphorus cycle** has no significant gaseous phase. Which consequence follows from this difference?

options.text: Phosphorus moves freely through the atmosphere, so it never limits plant growth.
Phosphorus moves mainly through rock, soil, water, and organisms, so its supply is slow and local.
Phosphorus is a rare element that plays no role in living cells.
Plants obtain phosphorus directly from the air like carbon dioxide.

explanation: The phosphorus cycle moves through weathering rock, soil, water, and organisms with no atmospheric step, so fresh phosphorus arrives slowly and often limits productivity. A and D describe an atmospheric phase that does not exist. C is false because phosphorus forms part of ATP, nucleic acids, and cell membranes.

subject: biology-2
question: Solar energy powers the **water cycle**, which moves water between the ocean, atmosphere, and land. Which statement about this cycle is most accurate?

options.text: Evaporation and transpiration both return water vapor to the atmosphere, while precipitation returns water to the surface.
Water moves only from the ocean to the land, and the ocean level never changes.
The cycle runs entirely on gravity, with no energy input from the sun.
Plants take no part in the cycle because their roots only absorb water.

explanation: Evaporation and transpiration send water vapor into the air, and precipitation returns water to oceans and land, a loop driven by solar energy. B denies the return leg of the loop. C ignores the solar energy that drives evaporation, and D ignores transpiration, the water plants release through their leaves.

subject: biology-2
question: A traveler lands in a region with year-round high temperatures, heavy rainfall in every month, and towering trees with dense canopies that allow little light to reach the forest floor. Which **terrestrial biome** is described?

options.text: **Temperate deciduous forest**, where trees drop their leaves each autumn.
**Taiga**, with long cold winters and conifers.
**Savanna**, dominated by scattered trees and seasonal grasses.
**Tropical rainforest**, with high and steady rainfall and warmth.

explanation: Year-round heat and steady rainfall define the tropical rainforest, whose layered canopy keeps the forest floor dark. The temperate deciduous forest drops its leaves seasonally and has colder winters, the taiga is cold with conifers, and the savanna has distinct wet and dry seasons with scattered trees.

subject: biology-2
question: In which biome would you find **permafrost**, a very short growing season, and mostly low vegetation such as mosses, lichens, and dwarf shrubs, with almost no tall trees?

options.text: **Tundra**, which is cold, windy, and underlain by permanently frozen soil.
**Temperate grassland**, which supports deep-rooted grasses on fertile soil.
**Desert**, which receives very little precipitation.
**Tropical rainforest**, which is hot and wet all year.

explanation: Tundra is cold and windy, with permafrost, a short growing season, and low, hardy vegetation. Grasslands have deep fertile soil and no permafrost. Deserts are dry rather than frozen, and rainforests are hot and wet, so neither matches the description.

subject: biology-2
question: At the mouth of a river, freshwater mixes with saltwater in a shallow, nutrient-rich zone that serves as a nursery for many young fish and shellfish. What is this ecosystem called?

options.text: **Abyssal zone**, the deep, dark region of the open ocean.
**Estuary**, where freshwater and saltwater meet and productivity is high.
**Intertidal zone**, the shoreline alternately covered and exposed by the tides.
**Coral reef**, a warm, shallow habitat built by reef-building animals.

explanation: An estuary forms where a river meets the sea, and the nutrients delivered by the river make it highly productive and rich in young fish. The abyssal zone is dark and deep, the intertidal zone is tidal shoreline, and a coral reef is built by reef animals, so none describes a river mouth.

subject: biology-2
question: A lake once held several native fish species. After a predatory fish from another continent is released by an aquarium owner, it multiplies rapidly, eats the native fish, and faces few natural enemies, and the native species decline. Which category of **biodiversity** loss best describes this situation?

options.text: **Habitat destruction**, because the shoreline is being paved over.
**Pollution**, because runoff adds excess nutrients to the water.
**Invasive species**, because a nonnative organism established and outcompeted native life.
**Overexploitation**, because the native fish are harvested faster than they can breed.

explanation: An introduced organism that spreads rapidly, harms native species, and faces few natural enemies is an invasive species, which is exactly what the stem describes. The stem shows no evidence of paving, runoff, or harvesting. Each distractor is a real threat, but none matches the introduced predator.

subject: biology-2
question: A rare plant species survives in only one wild population, and a wildfire could wipe it out. Botanists collect thousands of seeds and store them in a **seed bank**, a frozen climate-controlled facility that keeps them alive as a backup. What is this approach called?

options.text: **Sustainable use**, allowing careful harvesting of the wild plants.
**Habitat protection**, fencing off the wild population.
**Habitat corridors**, strips of protected land linking the population to other sites.
**Ex situ conservation**, preserving the species outside its natural habitat.

explanation: Keeping seeds alive in a facility away from the wild population is ex situ conservation, which acts as insurance against extinction. Harvesting and fencing keep the species dependent on the single wild site, and corridors connect habitats but do not store seeds.

subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: Which description correctly defines the carboxyl functional group?

options.text: A carbon atom bonded to nitrogen with no oxygen on that carbon (C—N)
A carbonyl carbon that also carries a hydroxyl group (—COOH)
A carbonyl carbon bonded to two other carbon atoms (C—CO—C)
An oxygen atom bridging two carbon-containing groups (C—O—C)

explanation:
A carboxyl group places a carbonyl (C=O) and a hydroxyl (—OH) on the same carbon, giving the condensed formula —COOH and two oxygen atoms per group. That arrangement is what makes carboxylic acids acidic (typical pKa 4 to 5), because loss of the —OH proton yields a carboxylate anion whose charge is delocalized over both oxygens. The distractors describe an amine linkage, a ketone, and an ether, none of which has an —OH bound to a carbonyl carbon and none of which is appreciably acidic.

ELI-10: A functional group is the reactive part bolted onto an otherwise unreactive carbon chain, and the carboxyl group is two parts bolted to one carbon: a double-bonded oxygen and an —OH. Neither part alone is acidic, but together the double-bonded oxygen pulls electron density away from the —OH, so that hydrogen leaves as H+ much more readily. Count the oxygens in —COOH and you get 1 + 1 = 2, which is the quickest way to tell a carboxyl from a plain alcohol on an exam structure.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: Which statement about alkanes is accurate?

options.text: They contain alternating single and double bonds within a closed ring
They contain at least one carbon–carbon double bond and follow the formula CnH2n
They contain a carbon–carbon triple bond and follow the formula CnH2n−2
They contain only carbon–carbon single bonds and follow the formula CnH2n+2

explanation:
Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons: every carbon–carbon bond is a single bond, so each carbon holds the maximum possible number of hydrogens, giving CnH2n+2. Propane (n = 3) therefore has 2(3) + 2 = 8 hydrogens. The other choices define alkenes (CnH2n), alkynes (CnH2n−2), and aromatic rings such as benzene, all of which are unsaturated because a pi bond or ring reduces the hydrogen count.

ELI-10: Each carbon must form four bonds. In an alkane, a carbon spends only one bond on each neighbor, so every leftover bond goes to a hydrogen and the molecule carries as much hydrogen as it structurally can, which is what saturated means. Check it with propane: 2(3) + 2 = 8 hydrogens, matching C3H8 on a propane tank label. This same counting rule is why saturated dietary fats have no double bonds while unsaturated fats do.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: Which term describes two compounds that share an identical molecular formula but differ in how their atoms are connected?

options.text: Structural isomers
Polymers
Homologs
Allotropes

explanation:
Structural (constitutional) isomers have the same molecular formula but a different bonding sequence, which gives them different physical and chemical properties. Butane and 2-methylpropane are both C4H10, each with 2(4) + 2 = 10 hydrogens, yet they differ in branching and boiling point. Allotropes are different forms of a single element, polymers are long repeating covalent chains, and members of a homologous series differ by successive —CH2— units, so their formulas are not identical.

ELI-10: Same parts list, different assembly, different product. C4H10 can be built as one straight chain of four carbons or as a three-carbon chain with a methyl branch, and both use 2(4) + 2 = 10 hydrogens because both are saturated. Because shape controls how tightly molecules pack together, the straight chain boils near 0 degrees Celsius while the branched one boils about 10 degrees lower. Recognizing isomers matters clinically because drug molecules with the same formula but different connectivity can act very differently in the body.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: Acetic acid (pKa about 4.8) is a far stronger acid than ethanol (pKa about 16), even though both molecules contain an O—H bond. Which explanation best accounts for this difference?

options.text: Acetic acid is the more polar molecule, and polarity by itself determines acid strength
The acetate anion delocalizes its negative charge over two equivalent oxygen atoms by resonance
Ethanol's alkyl group physically blocks water molecules from reaching its O—H bond
Acetic acid's carbonyl oxygen accepts a proton from water, releasing hydroxide ions

explanation:
Acid strength tracks the stability of the conjugate base. When acetic acid loses its proton, the resulting carboxylate has two resonance forms in which the negative charge sits on either oxygen, so the real ion carries half a negative charge on each equivalent oxygen and is substantially stabilized. Ethanol's ethoxide ion localizes the full charge on one oxygen with no resonance partner, so ionization is far less favorable, and the roughly 16 − 4.8 = 11.2 pKa unit gap corresponds to about eleven orders of magnitude in Ka. Polarity alone (choice A) does not predict acidity, and choice D describes basic rather than acidic behavior.

ELI-10: Whether a molecule gives up its proton depends on how comfortable the leftover negative charge will be. Ethoxide is stuck holding the entire charge on one oxygen, so ethanol rarely lets go. Acetate spreads that charge across two identical oxygens, which lowers its energy and makes the proton easy to release. Each pKa unit is a factor of 10 in the acid ionization constant, so a gap of 16 − 4.8 = 11.2 units means acetic acid's ionization constant (Ka) is roughly a hundred billion times larger than ethanol's.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: Ethanol (molar mass 46 g/mol) boils at 78 degrees Celsius while propane (molar mass 44 g/mol) boils at −42 degrees Celsius. Which explanation best accounts for this difference?

options.text: Ethanol's hydroxyl group allows hydrogen bonding between molecules, which propane cannot do
Propane is nonpolar, so its molecules have no intermolecular attractions to overcome
Boiling breaks covalent bonds, and ethanol's C—O bond is stronger than propane's C—C bonds
Ethanol has the larger molar mass, so far more thermal energy is required to vaporize it

explanation:
Boiling requires overcoming intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds, so choice C misstates the process. Ethanol's O—H group lets each molecule hydrogen bond to its neighbors, an attraction far stronger than the London dispersion forces holding nonpolar propane together; propane does have dispersion forces, so choice B is also wrong. The 46 − 44 = 2 g/mol mass difference cannot account for a 120 degree boiling point gap, which rules out choice D.

ELI-10: Vaporizing a liquid means separating molecules from each other, not tearing molecules apart. Propane molecules cling only through weak, fleeting dispersion forces, so mild warming frees them and propane is a gas at room temperature. Ethanol molecules link through hydrogen bonds between the —OH of one molecule and the oxygen of the next, and breaking that network takes much more heat. Since the molar masses differ by only 46 − 44 = 2 g/mol, the functional group, not the size, explains the 120 degree difference.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: A hypothetical primary amine whose conjugate acid has a pKa of 9.4 is placed in a buffered solution at pH 7.4. What is the most likely outcome?

options.text: The amine precipitates as a neutral solid because acid removes its hydrogen bonding ability
The nitrogen donates a proton to water, giving an anion that is less water soluble
The amine stays neutral because nitrogen's lone pair is already committed to bonding
The nitrogen lone pair accepts a proton, giving a cation that is more water soluble

explanation:
Amines are weak bases because the nonbonding electron pair on nitrogen can accept a proton, producing a substituted ammonium cation (R—NH3+). By the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship, the protonated form exceeds the neutral form by 10^(9.4 − 7.4) = 100 to 1 at pH 7.4, so the amine is overwhelmingly ionized. The full positive charge greatly strengthens ion-dipole interaction with water, which is why amine-containing drugs are commonly formulated as hydrochloride salts to improve dissolution.

ELI-10: Nitrogen in an amine has one pair of electrons not used in bonding, and a proton is simply a bare positive charge looking for electrons, so the two combine readily. When the pH sits below the conjugate acid's pKa, the protonated form wins, and here 9.4 − 7.4 = 2 pH units below means it wins by 10^2, or 100 to 1. That single charge is what makes the molecule dissolve well in water, the same reason sodium chloride dissolves and cooking oil does not.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: Which comparison of ester formation and ester hydrolysis is accurate?

options.text: Both reactions release water, differing only in the direction of electron flow
Formation releases water, while hydrolysis consumes water to regenerate acid and alcohol
Formation consumes water, while hydrolysis releases water and creates a carbon–carbon bond
Formation joins two alcohols, while hydrolysis yields two carboxylic acids

explanation:
Esterification joins a carboxylic acid and an alcohol with loss of one H2O per bond formed, the defining pattern of a condensation (dehydration synthesis) reaction. Hydrolysis is the exact reverse: water adds across the ester linkage and splits it into the parent carboxylic acid and alcohol. Building one triglyceride from glycerol plus 3 fatty acids therefore forms 3 ester bonds and releases 3 * 1 = 3 water molecules, and digesting that triglyceride consumes the same 3 waters.

ELI-10: Condensation and hydrolysis are one reaction read in two directions. Going forward, the acid gives up an —OH and the alcohol gives up an —H; those fragments combine into water and the two pieces bond directly. Going backward, adding water back across the bond splits the pieces apart, which is literally what hydrolysis means. The same bookkeeping applies to fats, starches, and proteins, so once you can count waters for a triglyceride (3 * 1 = 3) you can count them for any biological polymer.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: Lactic acid has the condensed structure CH3—CH(OH)—COOH. Which set of functional groups is present in this molecule?

options.text: Two hydroxyl groups and one ketone group
One ether linkage and one amine group
One aldehyde group and one ester group
One hydroxyl group and one carboxyl group

explanation:
The —OH on the middle carbon sits on a carbon with no double-bonded oxygen, so it is an alcohol (hydroxyl) group; the terminal —COOH is a carboxyl group. Lactic acid is therefore a hydroxy acid with molecular formula C3H6O3, containing 1 + 2 = 3 oxygen atoms. Students often miscount the —COOH as a separate hydroxyl plus a ketone, but a carbonyl bearing an —OH is by definition a carboxyl, and a ketone requires carbons on both sides of the carbonyl.

ELI-10: Work through the condensed formula one carbon at a time. CH3 is an unfunctionalized methyl end. CH(OH) puts an —OH on a carbon holding only hydrogens and carbons, which is the definition of an alcohol. COOH puts an —OH on a carbon that already holds a double-bonded oxygen, and that combination earns its own name and its own chemistry. Tally the oxygens you passed, 1 + 2 = 3, and you have confirmed the formula C3H6O3, which also explains why lactic acid is both very water soluble and weakly acidic.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: Which functional-group combination produces the amide linkage found in proteins?

options.text: A carboxyl group reacting with an amine group, with loss of water
Two hydroxyl groups reacting with each other, with loss of water
An amine reacting with an alcohol, with loss of water
An alcohol reacting with a carboxyl group, with loss of water

explanation:
An amide, called a peptide bond in proteins, forms when the carboxyl carbon of one amino acid bonds to the nitrogen of another amino acid's amine group with loss of H2O. The resulting C(=O)—N linkage has partial double-bond character from resonance, making it planar and unusually resistant to spontaneous hydrolysis, which is why proteins hold defined shapes. A carboxyl plus an alcohol would give an ester, two hydroxyls would give an ether, and an amine plus an alcohol does not condense under physiological conditions. Chaining 5 amino acids creates 5 − 1 = 4 peptide bonds and releases 4 water molecules.

ELI-10: Every amino acid carries an acid end (—COOH) and a base end (—NH2), so one molecule's acid end can always react with the next molecule's amine end. Each joining event expels one water and forms one amide bond, so the number of bonds is always one fewer than the number of residues: 5 − 1 = 4 for a pentapeptide. Notice that ester, ether, and amide bonds all form by losing water, so the identity of the product depends entirely on which two groups reacted, not on the water released.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: A hypothetical study compound consists of an unbranched 12-carbon hydrocarbon chain bearing a single terminal hydroxyl group. Which prediction about its behavior in water is best supported?

options.text: It will be freely miscible, because long carbon chains create strong dipole–dipole attractions to water
It will be freely miscible, because a single hydroxyl group hydrogen bonds strongly enough to carry the molecule into solution
It will be poorly soluble, because the large nonpolar chain outweighs one polar hydroxyl group
It will dissolve as an ionic solution, because hydroxyl groups release hydrogen ions in water

explanation:
Alcohol solubility falls sharply as the carbon-to-hydroxyl ratio rises: methanol, ethanol, and 1-propanol are miscible with water, 1-butanol is only partly soluble, and alcohols of five or more carbons per hydroxyl are increasingly insoluble. At a ratio of 12 / 1 = 12 carbons per hydroxyl, the hydrophobic surface that water must reorganize around dwarfs the hydrogen-bonding contribution of one —OH. Choice D also fails because alcohols have pKa near 16 and do not measurably ionize at physiological pH.

ELI-10: Solubility is a competition between the polar part of a molecule, which water welcomes, and the nonpolar part, which forces water into an ordered cage that costs energy. A short alcohol like 1-propanol has 3 carbons for its one —OH and the polar end wins. Stretch the chain to 12 carbons for the same single —OH and the ratio is 12 / 1, so the nonpolar side dominates and the compound behaves more like an oil or a wax than like rubbing alcohol. The same logic explains why fatty acids need bile salts to disperse in the aqueous contents of the intestine.
