source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: What would happen if a secondary alcohol such as 2-propanol were subjected to mild oxidation?

options.text: It would form an aldehyde that is then rapidly oxidized further to a carboxylic acid
It would form an ether by losing water and joining a second alcohol molecule
It would form a ketone, which resists further oxidation under the same conditions
It would resist oxidation, because its carbinol carbon carries no hydrogen atom

explanation:
Oxidation of an alcohol removes the hydroxyl hydrogen along with a hydrogen from the carbinol carbon. A secondary alcohol has exactly one hydrogen on that carbon, so oxidation stops at the ketone; 2-propanol (C3H8O, about 60 g/mol) becomes acetone (C3H6O, about 58 g/mol), a loss of 60 − 58 = 2 g/mol corresponding to two hydrogen atoms. Primary alcohols keep a second carbinol hydrogen after forming an aldehyde and can therefore proceed to a carboxylic acid, while tertiary alcohols have no carbinol hydrogen at all, which is what choice D actually describes.

ELI-10: Count the hydrogens on the carbon that holds the —OH, because that number sets how far oxidation can go. A primary alcohol's carbinol carbon has two, so it can be oxidized twice, first to an aldehyde and then to a carboxylic acid. A secondary alcohol's has one, so oxidation runs once and stops at a ketone. A tertiary alcohol's has none and is essentially inert to this reaction. The mass bookkeeping confirms it: 60 − 58 = 2 g/mol, exactly the two hydrogens removed when 2-propanol becomes acetone.
tags: primary versus secondary versus tertiary alcohols
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: organic-chemistry-1
question: An unknown hydrocarbon isolated in a teaching laboratory has the molecular formula C6H10. Which structural conclusion is best supported by this formula alone?

options.text: The compound is fully saturated, since it contains more hydrogens than carbons
The compound has one double bond and no rings, since it falls two hydrogens short of an alkane
The compound has two degrees of unsaturation, so it contains some combination of rings and pi bonds
The compound is a benzene derivative, since aromatic rings are the usual source of missing hydrogens

explanation:
The saturated six-carbon alkane is C6H14, so C6H10 is four hydrogens short, and each ring or pi bond costs two hydrogens: (2(6) + 2 − 10) / 2 = 2 degrees of unsaturation. Those two degrees can be satisfied by two double bonds, one triple bond, one ring plus one double bond, or two rings, so the formula constrains the structure without determining it, which is why choice B is too specific. Benzene is C6H6 with four degrees of unsaturation, so an aromatic ring alone cannot fit C6H10.

ELI-10: Start from the fully saturated benchmark for six carbons, 2(6) + 2 = 14 hydrogens, then compare with the 10 hydrogens actually present. Every time a molecule closes a ring or forms a pi bond, two hydrogen atoms are no longer needed, so the four missing hydrogens mean two such features: (14 − 10) / 2 = 2. The calculation tells you how many rings or pi bonds exist but not which, so cyclohexene, 1-hexyne, and 1,3-hexadiene all satisfy C6H10. Spectroscopy is what narrows the possibilities from there.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: An atom contains 15 protons, 16 neutrons, and 15 electrons. Which statement correctly identifies this atom's mass number and what that number represents?

options.text: 15, the number of protons in the nucleus
31, the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
16, the number of neutrons in the nucleus
30, the total number of protons and electrons in the atom

explanation:
Mass number (A) is the nucleon count, protons plus neutrons, so 15 + 16 = 31. The atomic number (Z = 15) counts protons alone and fixes the element's identity (phosphorus), while electrons are roughly 1/1836 the mass of a nucleon and are excluded from the mass number. Separating A from Z is the prerequisite for reading isotope notation and for calculating neutrons as A minus Z.

ELI-10: Two different counts get confused all the time. The atomic number counts only protons, and it decides which element you have. The mass number counts everything heavy in the nucleus, protons plus neutrons together, because those are the particles that actually weigh something. Electrons are so light they do not change the total in any meaningful way. So here: 15 protons plus 16 neutrons gives a mass number of 31, while the atomic number stays 15.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 each contain 6 protons, but carbon-14 contains 8 neutrons. Which term best describes the relationship between these two atoms, and why?

options.text: Isotopes, atoms of one element that differ in neutron number
Allotropes, different structural forms built from the same element
Ions, atoms of one element that differ in electron number
Isomers, substances with the same formula but different atomic arrangements

explanation:
Both atoms have Z = 6, so both are carbon; carbon-14 simply carries two extra neutrons (14 - 6 = 8 versus 12 - 6 = 6). Atoms of one element that differ only in neutron count are isotopes, and because their electron configurations are identical their chemical behavior is essentially the same. Ions differ in electron count and therefore carry charge, allotropes are different bonding arrangements of an element such as graphite versus diamond, and isomers are compounds with identical formulas but different structures.

ELI-10: The proton count is what makes an atom carbon, and it never changes without changing the element itself. Neutrons are different: they add mass to the nucleus but no charge, so you can add or subtract a couple and still have carbon. Carbon-14 carries 8 neutrons instead of the usual 6, which makes it heavier but chemically the same substance. Versions of one element that differ only in neutron count are called isotopes.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Fluorine, chlorine, and bromine all appear in Group 17 of the periodic table. Which statement best explains why these three elements show similar chemical behavior?

options.text: They occupy the same period, so their valence electrons fill the same principal energy level
They have nearly equal atomic masses, so their nuclei exert similar attraction
They have equal numbers of core electrons, so the same nuclear pull reaches each outer shell
They each hold 7 valence electrons, so they gain or share electrons in similar ways

explanation:
For main-group elements the group number gives the valence electron count; Group 17 members have 17 - 10 = 7 electrons in the outermost shell. Chemical behavior is governed almost entirely by valence electrons, so all three need one additional electron to reach an octet and react in parallel ways. They sit in different periods (n = 2, 3, and 4), have very different atomic masses, and have different core electron counts (2, 10, and 28), so none of those features can explain the shared chemistry.

ELI-10: Elements in the same column of the periodic table are grouped there for a reason: they have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell. Fluorine, chlorine, and bromine each have 7 outer electrons and each need just one more to reach the stable set of 8. That single shared gap is what makes them react in similar ways, even though the atoms differ greatly in size and mass. Outer electrons drive chemistry; the deeper electrons and the neutrons do not.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A proton has a mass of about 1.00728 amu and an electron about 0.00054858 amu. Which statement best explains why an atom's mass is treated as residing almost entirely in its nucleus?

options.text: Electrons are massless particles, so only nucleons can contribute to the mass of an atom
Electrons are excluded from mass totals because they carry negative rather than positive charge
A proton is roughly 1,836 times as massive as an electron, so protons and neutrons supply nearly all of the mass
The nucleus occupies most of the atom's volume, so it necessarily holds most of the atom's mass

explanation:
Dividing the two masses gives 1.00728 / 0.00054858, or about 1,836, and a neutron is slightly heavier still than a proton. In a carbon-12 atom the six electrons together contribute roughly 0.03 percent of the total mass, which is why mass number counts only nucleons. Charge is unrelated to mass; electrons have small but real mass; and the nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller in radius than the atom, so it holds nearly all the mass in a tiny fraction of the volume.

ELI-10: It takes about 1,836 electrons stacked together to match the mass of one proton. Neutrons weigh about the same as protons, so every particle in the nucleus is a heavyweight and every electron outside it is a featherweight. Even in a large atom with dozens of electrons, all of them together still add up to a rounding error compared with the nucleus. That is why chemists count only protons and neutrons when they talk about an atom's mass, and why the tiny nucleus carries nearly all of the weight despite taking up almost none of the space.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Which comparison of maximum electron capacity between the second (n = 2) and third (n = 3) principal energy levels is accurate?

options.text: The n = 3 level holds 18 electrons, 10 more than n = 2, since capacity follows the 2n^2 relationship
The n = 3 level holds 16 electrons, 8 more than n = 2, since each level doubles the one before it
The n = 3 level holds 8 electrons, the same as n = 2, since an octet fills every principal level
The n = 3 level holds 12 electrons, 4 more than n = 2, since each level adds a single orbital

explanation:
Maximum occupancy of a principal energy level is 2n^2, giving 2(2^2) = 8 for n = 2 and 2(3^2) = 18 for n = 3, a difference of 10 electrons. Those 10 additional slots are the five d orbitals that first become available at n = 3, which is why a transition series contains 10 elements. Capacity is not the same as row length: because 4s fills before 3d, the 3d orbitals are not occupied until the fourth period (scandium through zinc), so the third period contains only 8 elements even though n = 3 can hold 18. The octet rule describes the stable valence arrangement of main-group elements, not the absolute capacity of a shell.

ELI-10: Each principal energy level has a fixed number of electron spots, and the formula is 2 times the level number squared. Level 2 gives 2 x 4 = 8 spots. Level 3 gives 2 x 9 = 18 spots. The 10 extra spots at level 3 come from a new set of five d orbitals that did not exist at level 2, and each orbital holds 2 electrons. Careful, though: having the spots is not the same as filling them right away. Electrons fill the 4s orbital before the 3d ones, so those 10 d spots do not get used until the fourth row of the periodic table, where you see the block of 10 transition metals from scandium to zinc. That is why the third row has only 8 elements even though level 3 can hold 18.
tags: orbital filling order vs. period length
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Atomic radius decreases steadily across Period 3, from sodium (Z = 11) to chlorine (Z = 17). Which explanation best accounts for this trend?

options.text: Each added electron enters a new principal energy level, so shielding grows faster than nuclear charge
Nuclear charge rises by 6 protons while electrons fill the same energy level, pulling the valence shell inward
Neutron count rises from 12 to 18, and the heavier nucleus compresses the surrounding electron cloud inward
Electron-electron repulsion falls as the 3p subshell fills, letting the outer shell relax closer to the nucleus

explanation:
Across Period 3 the added electrons all enter the n = 3 shell and shield one another poorly, while nuclear charge climbs from 11 to 17, an increase of 6 protons. Effective nuclear charge therefore rises left to right, tightening the pull on the valence electrons and shrinking the radius. Shielding grows only slightly and never outpaces the added protons, no new shell opens until Period 4, neutrons add mass but no charge and do not attract electrons, and filling the 3p subshell increases rather than decreases mutual repulsion.

ELI-10: Going across a row, you add one proton and one electron at a time, but the new electrons all land in the same outer shell rather than starting a new one farther out. Electrons in the same shell are poor at blocking each other from the nucleus, so the growing positive charge in the center is felt more and more strongly by the outer electrons. Stronger pull on electrons that are not moving farther out means the whole atom is drawn in tighter. That is why atoms get smaller as you move to the right, even though they are gaining particles.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Which comparison between a neutral calcium atom (Z = 20) and a calcium ion carrying a 2+ charge is accurate?

options.text: The ion has 18 protons and 20 electrons, and that imbalance produces its 2+ charge
The ion has 22 electrons, gained in order to complete its outermost shell
Both particles have 20 electrons, but the ion contains 2 fewer neutrons
Both particles have 20 protons, but the ion has 18 electrons, leaving a net charge of 2+

explanation:
Ion formation changes only the electron count; the proton count stays at 20 or the particle would no longer be calcium. Losing the two 4s valence electrons leaves 20 positive charges against 18 negative ones, a net of 20 - 18 = 2+, and gives an argon-like arrangement. Note also that extra electrons would create a negative charge, not a positive one, and that neutron count is unaffected by ionization; this is why electrolytes such as calcium, sodium, and potassium circulate as charged particles while remaining the same elements.

ELI-10: Protons sit in the nucleus and are not removed in ordinary chemistry; changing them would change the element. Electrons sit on the outside and can be lost or gained fairly easily. Calcium gives up its two outermost electrons, so it still has 20 protons but now only 18 electrons, and the two unmatched positive charges are what the 2+ symbol means. The neutrons are untouched, so the ion has the same mass number as the atom it came from.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A hypothetical teaching sample is labeled as the potassium-39 ion with a 1+ charge (atomic number 19, mass number 39). How many neutrons and electrons does one of these ions contain?

options.text: 19 neutrons and 20 electrons
20 neutrons and 19 electrons
20 neutrons and 18 electrons
18 neutrons and 20 electrons

explanation:
Neutron count equals mass number minus atomic number: 39 - 19 = 20. The 1+ charge means one electron has been lost from the neutral count of 19, leaving 18 electrons, an argon-like arrangement. Reading isotope and ion notation as two independent pieces of information, one nuclear and one electronic, is what allows correct interpretation of electrolyte chemistry, where potassium circulates as a singly charged cation.

ELI-10: There are two separate calculations hidden in this label, and each uses a different number. For neutrons, subtract the atomic number from the mass number: 39 minus 19 gives 20 neutrons. For electrons, start from the proton count, 19, and adjust for charge: a 1+ means one electron was lost, so 18 remain. The mass number tells you nothing about electrons, and the charge tells you nothing about neutrons, so never let one substitute for the other.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: An unidentified neutral element has electrons distributed as 2, 8, 2 across its first three shells. Which prediction about its periodic placement and bonding behavior is best supported?

options.text: Period 2, Group 2; it loses 2 electrons to form a 2+ cation
Period 3, Group 2; it loses 2 electrons to form a 2+ cation
Period 3, Group 2; it gains 6 electrons to complete an octet, forming a 6- anion
Period 3, Group 12; it shares both valence electrons and forms no ions

explanation:
Summing the shells gives 2 + 8 + 2 = 12 electrons in a neutral atom, so Z = 12 and the element is magnesium. The highest occupied shell is n = 3, which sets the period at 3, and the 2 valence electrons place it in Group 2, not Group 12 (the group number is not the atomic number). Alkaline earth metals have low ionization energies, so shedding 2 electrons to reach a neon-like configuration is far more favorable than gaining 6, producing the 2+ cation found in body fluids.

ELI-10: Start by adding up the electrons: 2 + 8 + 2 = 12, so a neutral atom of this element also has 12 protons, making it magnesium. The period number is simply the highest shell in use, which is shell 3. The group number for a main-group element comes from the valence electrons, and there are 2 on that outer shell, so Group 2. Then ask which is easier: losing 2 electrons or finding 6 more. Losing 2 wins, so this atom forms a 2+ ion.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A data table for a hypothetical element lists two isotopes: mass 63 amu at 69.2 percent abundance and mass 65 amu at 30.8 percent abundance. Which value is closest to the average atomic mass, and what does the result indicate?

options.text: 63 amu; the tabulated mass is set by the most abundant isotope alone
65 amu; the heavier isotope contributes more mass and therefore dominates
64 amu; the average is the midpoint between the two isotope masses
63.6 amu; the average sits nearer 63 because that isotope is more abundant

explanation:
Converting percentages to decimals and weighting each mass gives (0.692)(63) + (0.308)(65) = 63.62 amu, or about 63.6. The value must fall between the two isotope masses, and it shifts toward the more abundant lighter isotope rather than landing on the midpoint of 64 or on either isotope mass exactly. Checking that a weighted average lies between the extremes and leans toward the dominant component is a quick way to catch arithmetic errors.

ELI-10: A weighted average asks not just what the values are but how many of each you have. Here nearly 70 percent of the atoms weigh 63 and only about 30 percent weigh 65, so the light group pulls the average down toward its own value. Multiply each mass by its share as a decimal and add: 0.692 x 63 = 43.6 and 0.308 x 65 = 20, for a total near 63.6. Two quick checks: the answer must land between 63 and 65, and it must sit closer to whichever isotope is more common.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Element M has 11 protons (Period 3, Group 1) and element Q has 19 protons (Period 4, Group 1). What happens to the first ionization energy going from M to Q, and why?

options.text: Higher for Q, because 8 additional protons raise the nuclear charge felt by the valence electron
Identical for both, because each atom has only a single valence electron to remove
Lower for Q, because its valence electron occupies the fourth shell behind 8 more core electrons
Lower for Q, because its greater atomic mass weakens the nucleus's hold on the outer electron

explanation:
Element Q has 18 core electrons versus 10 for element M, a difference of 8 shielding electrons, and its lone valence electron sits in the n = 4 shell rather than n = 3. Greater distance plus increased shielding lowers the effective nuclear charge acting on that electron, so less energy is needed to remove it, even though total nuclear charge is larger. Mass itself exerts no electrostatic attraction, and having one valence electron does not by itself fix ionization energy, which is why first ionization energy falls down a group and the heavier alkali metals are the more reactive ones.

ELI-10: Both atoms have exactly one loose outer electron, so the difference has to come from how tightly that electron is held. In Q, the electron sits one shell farther out, and electrostatic attraction weakens sharply with distance. On top of that, 8 extra inner electrons stand between it and the nucleus, cancelling much of the positive pull it would otherwise feel. The net pull, called effective nuclear charge, is weaker for Q, so its electron leaves more easily and its ionization energy is lower.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Two hypothetical laboratory nuclide samples each contain neutral atoms with 53 protons; sample 1 has mass number 127 and sample 2 has mass number 131. Which statement best integrates the nuclear and chemical properties of these two samples?

options.text: They are isotopes: matching proton and electron counts give nearly identical chemistry, while the 4-neutron difference alters nuclear stability
They are different elements, because mass number rather than proton count establishes elemental identity and therefore reactivity
They are ions of one element, because adding neutrons to a nucleus changes the net charge carried by each sample
They are isotopes, but the added neutrons require added valence electrons, so the two samples form different chemical bonds

explanation:
Both samples have Z = 53, so both are the same element, and neutral atoms of each carry 53 electrons with identical valence configurations, making their chemical reactions essentially indistinguishable. Their neutron counts differ by 131 - 127 = 4, and the neutron-to-proton ratio governs nuclear stability, so one nuclide can be stable while the other decays. Neutrons are uncharged and do not affect electron count, and elemental identity is set by protons, not by mass number; this separation of chemical identity from nuclear behavior is why a radioactive nuclide follows the same biological pathway as its stable counterpart.

ELI-10: An atom really has two independent identities. The outside identity, set by protons and the matching electrons, decides how it bonds and where the body sends it, and both samples are identical there with 53 of each. The inside identity is set by the mix of protons and neutrons in the nucleus, and the two samples differ by 4 neutrons. Certain neutron-to-proton ratios hold together and others do not, so one nuclide can sit there indefinitely while the other breaks down and emits radiation. Same chemistry, different nuclear stability.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: An aluminum atom has 13 protons and 13 electrons. If it loses 3 electrons during a chemical reaction, which term and charge correctly describe the resulting particle?

options.text: An anion carrying a 3- charge, because removing electrons leaves the particle negative
An isotope carrying a 3+ charge, because the number of nuclear particles has changed
A cation carrying a 3+ charge, because protons now outnumber electrons by three
A cation carrying a 13+ charge, because all 13 protons are now unopposed

explanation:
Net ionic charge equals protons minus electrons: 13 - 10 = +3. A positively charged ion is a cation, and cations form by losing electrons. The 10 remaining electrons still cancel 10 of the 13 protons, so the charge is 3+, not 13+. Isotopes differ in neutron count, and the proton count (element identity) does not change in a chemical reaction, so the species is Al3+.

ELI-10: Charge is a subtraction problem, not a count of what is left. Protons are fixed at 13 and each one contributes +1; each electron contributes -1. Start at 13 plus and 13 minus, which cancel to zero. Remove 3 electrons and you have 13 plus against 10 minus, so 10 pairs cancel and 3 pluses survive: a 3+ charge. Any positively charged ion is a cation (the 't' in cation is a handy stand-in for a plus sign), and losing electrons is the only way an atom becomes one.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Magnesium chloride (MgCl2) is classified as a strong electrolyte. Which statement best explains that classification and the moles of ions released per mole dissolved?

options.text: It dissociates only slightly, so a small equilibrium fraction of ions carries nearly all of the current
It dissociates essentially completely, releasing 3 mol of mobile ions per mole, so the solution conducts well
It dissolves as intact neutral units that reorient in the electric field and conduct by shifting polar bonds
It dissociates completely but releases 2 mol of ions per mole, since each unit gives one cation and one anion

explanation:
A strong electrolyte is defined by essentially complete dissociation into free, mobile ions, which are the charge carriers that make a solution conduct. Each MgCl2 formula unit supplies one Mg2+ and two Cl-, so 1 + 2 = 3 mol of ions per mole of solute. Partial dissociation describes a weak electrolyte (for example acetic acid), and dissolving without dissociating describes a nonelectrolyte such as glucose.

ELI-10: Two ideas are bundled here. First, conduction needs charged particles that are free to move; a strong electrolyte supplies them because it comes apart essentially completely in water. Second, count the ions from the formula, not from the number of ion types: MgCl2 has one Mg and two Cl written into it, so one formula unit yields three separate particles. Weak electrolytes come apart only a little, and nonelectrolytes not at all, which is why their solutions conduct poorly or not at all.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A physiology text lists the normal serum reference interval for the major extracellular cation as 135-145 mEq/L. Which ion is being described, and what is the midpoint of that interval?

options.text: Potassium (K+), midpoint 140 mEq/L, because K+ is the dominant cation of extracellular fluid
Calcium (Ca2+), midpoint 140 mEq/L, because Ca2+ is the chief cation dissolved in plasma
Sodium (Na+), midpoint 140 mEq/L, because Na+ is the dominant cation of extracellular fluid
Sodium (Na+), midpoint 280 mEq/L, because the two interval endpoints are added together

explanation:
Sodium is the principal extracellular cation, and the midpoint of its reference interval is the mean of the endpoints: (135 + 145)/2 = 140 mEq/L. Adding the endpoints without dividing gives 280, a unit-nonsensical value. Potassium is the principal intracellular cation and circulates at only about 3.5-5 mEq/L, and although calcium is the most abundant cation in the body by mass, over 99% of it is bound in bone rather than dissolved in plasma (total serum calcium is roughly 4.5-5.5 mEq/L).

ELI-10: Two separate skills are being checked. The identity part rests on compartments: sodium is concentrated in the fluid outside cells, potassium inside cells, which is why a blood sample is dominated by sodium. The arithmetic part is a midpoint, which is an average, not a sum: add 135 and 145 to get 280, then divide by 2 to get 140. Forgetting the division is the classic slip, and 280 mEq/L should look wrong immediately because it sits far outside any plausible serum value.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A student finds that distilled water barely conducts current, while a 0.9% (w/v) NaCl solution - 0.9 g of NaCl per 100 mL - conducts strongly. What is the primary reason for the difference?

options.text: The roughly 9 g/L of NaCl dissociates into mobile hydrated Na+ and Cl- that serve as charge carriers
The roughly 9 g/L of NaCl stays as intact neutral units that drift toward the electrodes and carry charge
The dissolved NaCl depresses the freezing point, and solutions with lower freezing points conduct better
The dissolved NaCl raises the polarity of the water, letting the solvent itself transmit electrons

explanation:
Pure water self-ionizes only to about 1 x 10^-7 M, so it holds almost no charge carriers. A 0.9% (w/v) solution contains 0.9 g per 100 mL, and since 1 L is ten 100-mL portions, 0.9 x 10 = 9 g/L of NaCl, which dissolves and dissociates into hydrated Na+ and Cl- that migrate toward opposite electrodes and complete the circuit. Freezing-point depression is a consequence of dissolved particles rather than a mechanism of conduction, and adding salt does not make water conduct on its own.

ELI-10: Conduction in solution is migration of charged particles, not electron flow through the liquid. Distilled water has almost nothing charged in it, so there is nothing to migrate. Salt changes that in two steps: it dissolves, and then it dissociates into separate Na+ and Cl- that water molecules surround (hydrate) and keep apart. Note that dissolving alone is not enough - sugar dissolves just as well and still does not conduct, because its particles stay neutral. Percent w/v converts easily: 0.9 g per 100 mL is 9 g in the ten 100-mL portions that make a liter.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: One mole of glucose and one mole of NaCl are each dissolved in separate 1 L beakers of water. Which comparison of the resulting solutions is accurate?

options.text: Both solutions contain the same number of dissolved particles, because equal moles of solute were used
Glucose gives more dissolved particles, because its molecules split into smaller fragments in water
Neither solution conducts current, because both solids dissolve as intact electrically neutral units
NaCl gives twice as many dissolved particles as glucose, because it dissociates into Na+ and Cl-

explanation:
Glucose is a nonelectrolyte that dissolves as intact C6H12O6 molecules, giving 1 mol of particles per mole. NaCl is a strong electrolyte that dissociates into Na+ and Cl-, giving 2 mol of particles per mole, a ratio of 2/1 = 2. Glucose is a monosaccharide and does not hydrolyze into smaller units on dissolving. Because the NaCl solution contains ions it conducts, and because it contains twice the particles its osmolarity is about twice as high.

ELI-10: Separate two questions: how much solute went in, and how many independent particles came out. Both beakers received 1 mol of solute, so the first answer is identical. But glucose enters the water whole and stays whole - one molecule in, one particle in solution - while each NaCl formula unit separates into two particles, a sodium ion and a chloride ion. Particle count, not molecular size, is what determines osmolarity and other colligative properties, and the presence of charge on those particles is what determines conductivity.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A lab measures a 0.05 M KCl solution, then a 0.1 M KCl solution, using the same electrodes and temperature. Which change is expected, and by what factor does the mobile-ion concentration change?

options.text: Conductivity falls, because the extra dissolved ions interfere with one another and stop migrating
Conductivity rises by a factor of 4, because K+ and Cl- each double independently
Conductivity is essentially unchanged, because KCl yields the same two ion types at any concentration
Conductivity rises, because the concentration of mobile ions increases by a factor of 2

explanation:
For a strong electrolyte well below saturation, the number of charge carriers per liter scales directly with concentration, so 0.1/0.05 = 2 means both [K+] and [Cl-] double and conductivity rises roughly twofold. The two ion concentrations rise together as part of the same doubling; they do not multiply to give a fourfold effect. KCl is far below its solubility limit, so nothing precipitates, and ion-ion interference is negligible at these dilute concentrations.

ELI-10: Conductivity depends on how many charged particles per liter are available to migrate. Doubling the amount of KCl in the same volume doubles that supply: 0.1 divided by 0.05 equals 2. It is tempting to double once for K+ and again for Cl-, but those two are not independent - one doubling of KCl produces one doubling of the whole ion population, so the factor is 2, not 4. Crowding effects that reduce ion mobility do exist, but only at concentrations far higher than these.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Clinical laboratories often report electrolytes in milliequivalents rather than millimoles. For calcium, 1 mmol of Ca2+ corresponds to how many mEq, and what does that reveal about the two units?

options.text: 1 mEq, because milliequivalents and millimoles are alternative names for the same quantity
0.5 mEq, because equivalents divide the amount of substance by the magnitude of the charge
2 mEq, because equivalents weight each ion by the magnitude of the charge it carries
40 mEq, because equivalents are obtained by applying the molar mass of the element

explanation:
Milliequivalents equal millimoles multiplied by the absolute value of the ionic charge, so for the divalent Ca2+ ion 1 x 2 = 2 mEq. The equivalent expresses charge-combining capacity, which is why clinicians use it when comparing cations with anions for electroneutrality. Molar mass converts between mass and moles and plays no part in this conversion. For monovalent ions such as Na+ and K+ the two values coincide numerically, which is precisely why the distinction is easy to overlook.

ELI-10: Millimoles answer 'how many ions are present', while milliequivalents answer 'how much charge do they bring'. Those questions give the same number only when each ion carries exactly one charge. Calcium carries two, so a single millimole of it delivers 1 x 2 = 2 milliequivalents of positive charge. The direction matters: multiply by the charge, never divide, because a more highly charged ion supplies more charge, not less.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A hypothetical teaching solution contains 0.02 mol of KCl dissolved per liter of water. Assuming complete dissociation, what is the concentration of K+ expressed in mEq/L?

options.text: 2 mEq/L, because the amount in moles is divided by the charge on the potassium ion
20 mEq/L, because 0.02 mol/L equals 20 mmol/L and K+ carries a single positive charge
40 mEq/L, because the K+ and the Cl- released by each formula unit are both counted
0.02 mEq/L, because for a monovalent ion the equivalent concentration equals the molarity

explanation:
Two steps are required. Convert the unit prefix: 0.02 mol/L x 1000 = 20 mmol/L. Then multiply by the charge magnitude of 1 for K+, giving 20 mEq/L. Option D correctly notes that mmol/L and mEq/L coincide for monovalent ions but fails to convert mol/L to mmol/L first. Chloride is a distinct anion reported separately and is never folded into the potassium result.

ELI-10: Work the prefix and the charge as separate operations. The prefix: a millimole is one thousandth of a mole, so 0.02 mol/L becomes 20 mmol/L by multiplying by 1000. The charge: potassium is K+, one unit of charge, so multiplying by 1 leaves the value at 20 mEq/L. The equality of mmol/L and mEq/L for monovalent ions is a useful check, but it holds only after the amounts are in the same prefix - 0.02 and 20 are not interchangeable.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A hypothetical teaching solution is analyzed for four cations: Na+ 5 mmol/L, Mg2+ 2 mmol/L, K+ 4 mmol/L, and Ca2+ 3 mmol/L. Which cation contributes the most positive charge per liter, and how much?

options.text: Na+, contributing 5 mEq/L, because it is present at the highest millimolar concentration
Mg2+, contributing 4 mEq/L, because its double charge outweighs every other cation listed
K+, contributing 4 mEq/L, because monovalent ions dominate the charge total in solution
Ca2+, contributing 6 mEq/L, because its 3 mmol/L is doubled by its 2+ charge

explanation:
Charge contribution is millimoles multiplied by charge magnitude: Na+ gives 5 x 1 = 5 mEq/L, Mg2+ gives 2 x 2 = 4 mEq/L, K+ gives 4 x 1 = 4 mEq/L, and Ca2+ gives 3 x 2 = 6 mEq/L. Calcium is highest even though sodium has the larger millimolar concentration, because the 2+ charge doubles calcium's contribution. Note that Mg2+ and K+ tie at 4 mEq/L from very different millimolar amounts, which shows that concentration ranking alone does not predict charge ranking.

ELI-10: Rank by charge, not by headcount. Convert each entry first by multiplying millimoles by the number of charges the ion carries: sodium 5 x 1 = 5, magnesium 2 x 2 = 4, potassium 4 x 1 = 4, calcium 3 x 2 = 6. Calcium wins at 6 even though sodium had the biggest raw number, because each calcium ion brings two units of charge. The magnesium and potassium tie makes the point sharply - 2 mmol/L of a divalent ion carries exactly as much charge as 4 mmol/L of a monovalent one.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A sample panel from a teaching case reports Na+ 140 mEq/L, Cl- 104 mEq/L, and HCO3- 24 mEq/L. Using the common formula anion gap = Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-), what is the value and what does it represent?

options.text: A gap of 36 mEq/L, representing the sodium remaining after chloride has been neutralized
A gap of 12 mEq/L, representing unmeasured anions such as proteins, phosphate, and sulfate
A gap of 80 mEq/L, representing the amount by which chloride exceeds bicarbonate
A gap of 12 mEq/L, demonstrating that the sample violates the rule of electroneutrality

explanation:
The arithmetic is 140 - (104 + 24) = 12 mEq/L. Both measured anions must be subtracted, so stopping at 140 - 104 = 36 or computing 104 - 24 = 80 misapplies the formula. Because bulk solutions are electrically neutral, no charge is genuinely missing; the gap simply reflects anions the routine panel does not measure, chiefly albumin along with phosphate, sulfate, and organic acids. The calculation is a bookkeeping device built on charge balance, not evidence against it.

ELI-10: Body fluid must carry equal positive and negative charge, so the anion gap is best read as an accounting remainder rather than a real imbalance. The panel measures one large cation (sodium, 140) and the two largest anions (chloride 104 plus bicarbonate 24, totaling 128). Subtracting leaves 12 units of negative charge unaccounted for. Those charges are physically present - they sit on plasma proteins and small anions the panel never reports - so the gap measures the laboratory's blind spot, and a widened gap suggests an unmeasured anion such as lactate has accumulated.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A student compares 0.1 M CaCl2 with 0.15 M NaCl, assuming ideal complete dissociation of both salts. Which comparison of their calculated osmolarities is accurate?

options.text: They are equal at 0.3 osmol/L, because CaCl2 releases 3 particles and NaCl releases 2
CaCl2 is lower at 0.2 osmol/L, because Ca2+ counts as one particle carrying a double charge
NaCl is higher at 0.45 osmol/L, because each formula unit releases three separate chloride ions
CaCl2 is higher at 0.6 osmol/L, because the ionic charge magnitudes multiply the particle count

explanation:
Osmolarity counts dissolved particles and ignores their charge: CaCl2 yields Ca2+ plus two Cl-, so 0.1 x 3 = 0.3 osmol/L, while NaCl yields two particles, so 0.15 x 2 = 0.3 osmol/L. The solutions are therefore isosmotic despite different molarities and different ionic charges. The discriminating idea is that osmolarity depends on particle number while milliequivalents depend on charge - two quantities students routinely conflate. Real solutions deviate slightly because of ion pairing, which is why the problem specifies ideal behavior.

ELI-10: Osmolarity is a particle census, and charge is not counted in that census - a 2+ calcium ion counts exactly the same as a 1+ sodium ion. So the only thing to track is how many pieces each formula unit produces. CaCl2 produces three, and 0.1 x 3 = 0.3. NaCl produces two, and 0.15 x 2 = 0.3. Equal particle concentrations mean the two solutions pull water across a membrane with equal force: they are isosmotic. If the question had asked about milliequivalents instead, charge would matter and the answers would differ.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A hypothetical laboratory solution contains 0.15 mol/L Na+ and 0.02 mol/L Ca2+, with chloride as the only anion present. What must the chloride concentration be, and what principle sets it?

options.text: 0.19 mol/L, because the total negative charge must balance the total positive charge
0.17 mol/L, because the total moles of anion must match the total moles of cation one for one
0.13 mol/L, because the divalent calcium offsets part of the sodium contribution
0.34 mol/L, because each dissolved cation requires two chloride ions to be neutralized

explanation:
Electroneutrality requires equal totals of positive and negative charge: 0.15 from Na+ plus 0.02 x 2 = 0.04 from Ca2+ gives 0.19 mol/L of positive charge. Chloride is monovalent, so 0.19 mol/L of Cl- is needed to balance it. Simply adding cation moles gives 0.17 and ignores calcium's 2+ valence, which is exactly the error that charge-based equivalents are designed to prevent. Bulk solutions cannot carry any appreciable net charge.

ELI-10: Balance charges, not particles. Sodium contributes 0.15 mol/L of ions each carrying one positive charge, so 0.15 units of positive charge. Calcium contributes only 0.02 mol/L of ions, but each carries two positive charges, so 0.02 x 2 = 0.04 units. The positive total is 0.19. Chloride carries one negative charge apiece, so its concentration must also be 0.19 mol/L. Counting calcium as 0.02 would leave the solution with net positive charge, which no real bulk solution can sustain.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A calcium atom has 20 protons. In calcium chloride, calcium is present as a particle containing 20 protons and 18 electrons. Which statement best describes how the bond in this compound forms?

options.text: Two atoms share a pair of valence electrons unequally, producing partial charges but no full ions.
Two atoms share one pair of valence electrons equally, so neither atom ends up carrying any charge.
One atom transfers valence electrons to another, and the resulting oppositely charged ions attract electrostatically.
Fixed metal cations are held in place by a sea of delocalized electrons shared among all the atoms.

explanation:
An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a cation and an anion generated by electron transfer, typically from a metal of low ionization energy to a nonmetal of high electron affinity. A particle with 20 protons and 18 electrons carries a net charge of 20 - 18 = 2+, confirming that calcium has lost two electrons; each chlorine gains one, becoming Cl-. Option B describes a nonpolar covalent bond, option A a polar covalent bond, and option D metallic bonding, none of which involves the full charge separation seen here.

ELI-10: Charge is just a proton-versus-electron headcount. Calcium normally has 20 of each, so it is neutral. Hand two electrons away and it still has 20 protons but only 18 electrons, leaving it two positive units short of balanced: Ca2+. The chlorine atoms that caught those electrons each end up one unit negative. Opposite charges pull on each other, and that pull between transferred-electron ions is the ionic bond.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: In an H2 molecule the two hydrogen atoms are joined by a single covalent bond, which consists of 1 shared pair, or 2 electrons. Which statement correctly defines a covalent bond?

options.text: The attraction of a cation for an anion within a repeating three-dimensional crystal lattice.
The mutual attraction of two nuclei for the same pair or pairs of shared valence electrons.
The attraction between the partially positive end of one molecule and the partially negative end of another.
The attraction of fixed metal cations for valence electrons that move freely throughout the solid.

explanation:
A covalent bond exists because both positively charged nuclei are simultaneously attracted to the same region of electron density concentrated between them; that shared density lowers the potential energy of the system relative to the separated atoms. A single bond holds 1 pair x 2 electrons = 2 electrons. Option A defines ionic bonding, option C describes dipole-dipole attraction between separate molecules, and option D describes metallic bonding.

ELI-10: A covalent bond is not one atom capturing an electron; it is two nuclei pulling on the same electrons at once. Put a pair of electrons in the space between two hydrogen nuclei and each nucleus is attracted to that negative cloud. Neither can pull away without giving up that attraction, so the atoms stay joined. One shared pair equals 2 electrons equals one single bond, which is exactly what holds H2 together.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Which example is best classified as an ionic compound, and how many ions are present in one of its formula units?

options.text: MgCl2, which contains 3 ions per formula unit
CO2, which contains 3 ions per formula unit
CH4, which contains 5 ions per formula unit
N2, which contains 2 ions per formula unit

explanation:
Ionic compounds typically form between a metal and a nonmetal; MgCl2 consists of one Mg2+ cation and two Cl- anions, giving 1 + 2 = 3 ions per formula unit. CH4, CO2, and N2 are molecular substances built entirely from nonmetal atoms joined by shared electron pairs, so they contain no ions at all, and counting their atoms is not the same as counting ions. Screening a formula for metal-plus-nonmetal composition is the fastest first test for ionic character.

ELI-10: Use a two-step sort. First, look for a metal paired with a nonmetal: magnesium is a metal and chlorine is not, so MgCl2 is ionic, while carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen are all nonmetals, making the other three molecular. Second, count charged pieces, not atoms. MgCl2 breaks into one Mg2+ and two Cl-, which is three ions. CH4 has five atoms but zero ions, which is the trap in that option.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Sodium chloride melts near 801 degrees C, while methane melts near -182 degrees C, a difference of 983 degrees C. What is the primary reason for this very large gap?

options.text: Melting sodium chloride breaks a lattice of strong ion-ion attractions, while melting methane overcomes only weak intermolecular forces.
Melting methane breaks the strong C-H covalent bonds inside each molecule, while melting sodium chloride leaves its ionic bonds fully intact.
Melting sodium chloride overcomes many weak attractions that add up, while melting methane breaks one unusually strong covalent bond.
Sodium chloride is built from much heavier atoms than methane, so far more thermal energy is needed to set its particles moving.

explanation:
In an ionic solid each ion is attracted to every oppositely charged neighbor throughout a continuous three-dimensional array, so melting must supply enough energy to overcome a large lattice energy. Methane is a molecular solid whose discrete molecules are held to one another only by weak London dispersion forces; melting separates the molecules while the strong C-H covalent bonds inside each molecule remain untouched. Option B reverses which particles come apart, option C wrongly treats the ionic lattice as a stack of weak additive attractions and methane as having a single covalent bond, and option D misattributes the gap to atomic mass rather than to the type of force being broken.

ELI-10: Melting always asks the same question: what has to let go for particles to start sliding past each other? In sodium chloride the answer is full positive-negative attractions running through the whole crystal, which is a lot to overcome. In methane the answer is only the faint stickiness between separate molecules; the bonds inside each CH4 stay put. Weak attractions give way at -182 degrees C, strong ionic ones not until 801 degrees C, a melting temperature 983 degrees C higher.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Using Pauling electronegativity values (H = 2.2, Cl = 3.16), the H-Cl bond has an electronegativity difference of 0.96. Which classification of this bond, with its consequence, is correct?

options.text: Nonpolar covalent, because the electrons are shared equally and no partial charges develop.
Ionic, because chlorine removes hydrogen's electron completely, so an isolated HCl molecule consists of H+ and Cl- ions.
Polar covalent, because the shared pair sits closer to chlorine, giving chlorine a partial negative and hydrogen a partial positive charge.
Coordinate covalent, because chlorine supplies both electrons of the shared pair while hydrogen supplies none.

explanation:
An electronegativity difference of roughly 0.4 to 1.7 marks a polar covalent bond: the pair is genuinely shared, but unequally. At 3.16 - 2.2 = 0.96, chlorine draws the bonding pair closer and carries a partial negative charge (delta minus) while hydrogen carries a partial positive charge (delta plus), giving HCl a permanent dipole moment. Complete transfer to separate ions requires a much larger difference, which is why gaseous HCl is a polar molecule rather than an ionic solid. In HCl each atom contributes one electron to the bond, so it is not coordinate covalent.

ELI-10: Bond polarity is about where the shared electrons spend their time, not about who owns them. Chlorine's electronegativity of 3.16 beats hydrogen's 2.2 by 0.96, so the pair is pulled toward the chlorine side without ever leaving hydrogen entirely. The result is a molecule with a slightly negative chlorine end and a slightly positive hydrogen end, written delta minus and delta plus. Partial charges like these, not full ionic charges, are the signature of a polar covalent bond.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A neutral nitrogen atom has 5 valence electrons and reaches an octet of 8 by sharing. How many covalent bonds does nitrogen typically form, and why?

options.text: Three, because sharing three pairs supplies the 3 additional electrons nitrogen needs to reach 8.
Four, because nitrogen has four valence orbitals available and places one bond in each of them.
Five, because an atom forms one covalent bond for every valence electron that it already possesses.
None, because nitrogen's 5 valence electrons already give it a stable half-filled outer shell.

explanation:
For a neutral main-group atom, the usual number of covalent bonds equals the number of electrons short of an octet: 8 - 5 = 3 for nitrogen. Each shared pair counts toward the octets of both bonded atoms, so three bonds bring nitrogen's count from 5 to 8 while leaving one lone pair, as in NH3 or the triple bond of N2. Option B applies carbon's pattern to nitrogen, option C confuses electrons owned with electrons needed, and option D misapplies half-filled subshell stability, which describes relative ionization trends rather than an atom's tendency to bond.

ELI-10: Ask how many electrons the atom is missing, not how many it has. Nitrogen holds 5 valence electrons and an octet needs 8, so it is short by 3. Every covalent bond lets nitrogen count one more electron from a partner toward its own octet, so three bonds close the gap exactly. That leaves the remaining two electrons as a lone pair, which is why ammonia is N with three H atoms plus one lone pair rather than four or five bonds.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but 0.5 mol of it dissolved in water releases a total of 1 mol of ions. What happens to the electrical conductivity of the sample, and why?

options.text: It conducts electricity, because dissolving breaks covalent bonds and releases free electrons into the water.
It conducts electricity, because dissolving frees the Na+ and Cl- ions to move independently and carry charge.
It does not conduct electricity, because intact NaCl molecules simply spread out among the water molecules.
It conducts only once molten, because water molecules surround the ions and neutralize their charges.

explanation:
Conduction in solution requires mobile charge carriers. In the crystal the ions are charged but locked into fixed lattice sites; dissolution (like melting) releases them so Na+ and Cl- can migrate toward opposite electrodes, making NaCl a strong electrolyte. Each formula unit supplies 2 ions, so 0.5 mol x 2 = 1 mol of ions. NaCl contains no discrete molecules and releases no free electrons, and hydration shells stabilize ionic charge rather than cancel it.

ELI-10: Electric current is charge in motion, so a substance needs charges that are both present and free to travel. Solid salt has the charges but not the freedom, since every ion is pinned in the lattice, so it is an insulator. Water surrounds each ion and pulls the lattice apart, and now those charges can drift toward electrodes and carry current. Because every NaCl unit yields two ions, 0.5 mol of salt sets 1 mol of charge carriers loose. Dissolved electrolytes are also why body fluids conduct the signals an ECG records.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: In carbon dioxide, carbon is joined to each oxygen by a double bond, so the two double bonds account for 8 bonding electrons in a linear O=C=O arrangement. Which statement about bonding and polarity in CO2 is correct?

options.text: The bonds are ionic, because oxygen pulls the bonding electrons completely away from carbon.
Each C=O bond is polar, but the linear symmetric geometry makes the two bond dipoles cancel.
The molecule is polar overall, because each oxygen atom carries a partial negative charge.
Both C=O bonds are nonpolar, because carbon and oxygen attract the shared electrons equally.

explanation:
Oxygen (3.44) is considerably more electronegative than carbon (2.55), so every C=O bond carries a dipole. Bond dipoles are vectors, however: in a linear, symmetric molecule the two equal dipoles point in opposite directions and sum to a net dipole moment of zero, so CO2 is a nonpolar molecule built from polar bonds. Molecular polarity therefore depends on geometry as well as bond polarity. The bonding framework is covalent, not ionic, and the electron count confirms it: 2 double bonds x 4 electrons = 8 bonding electrons.

ELI-10: Treat each polar bond as an arrow pointing toward the more electronegative atom. In CO2 the molecule is a straight line with an oxygen on each end, so the two arrows have equal length and point exactly opposite ways, and they add to zero. The bonds are still polar, and the oxygens really do carry partial negative charge, but the molecule as a whole has no positive end or negative end. Bend that same arrangement, as in water, and the arrows stop cancelling and the molecule becomes polar.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Aluminum forms Al3+ ions and oxygen forms O2- ions. Which formula for the compound they produce, together with its reasoning, is correct?

options.text: Al3O2, because each element's subscript is set equal to the size of that element's own charge.
AlO, because every ionic compound pairs one cation with one anion in a 1:1 ratio.
Al2O3, because the total positive charge (2 x 3+ = 6+) exactly balances the total negative charge (3 x 2- = 6-).
Al2O3, because each aluminum atom shares three pairs of electrons with each oxygen atom.

explanation:
An ionic formula gives the lowest whole-number ratio of ions that makes the compound electrically neutral. Two Al3+ contribute 2 x 3 = 6 units of positive charge and three O2- contribute 6 units of negative charge, so the formula is Al2O3. Option B assumes a universal 1:1 ratio, which holds only when the ion charges are equal in magnitude (as in NaCl). Option A copies each charge onto its own element instead of crossing it over, and option D gives the right formula with covalent reasoning, even though a metal oxide of this type is ionic.

ELI-10: Neutrality is the rule that sets every ionic formula. Each Al3+ adds 3 positive units and each O2- adds 2 negative units, so you need the smallest counts that make the totals match: two aluminums give 6 positive and three oxides give 6 negative, hence Al2O3. The crossover shortcut works because it lands on that same balance, but only if you cross the charges over, writing oxygen's 2 as aluminum's subscript and aluminum's 3 as oxygen's subscript, then reducing if possible.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A student looks up Pauling electronegativity values for potassium (0.82) and bromine (2.96) to predict the bonding in potassium bromide. Which interpretation of these data is best supported?

options.text: The difference is about 3.78, so the bond is ionic because the two electronegativity values add together.
The difference is about 2.14, so the bond is nonpolar covalent because both atoms are relatively large.
The difference is about 2.14, so the bond is polar covalent; the shared pair stays roughly midway between the two nuclei.
The difference is about 2.14, so the bond is largely ionic; potassium's valence electron transfers to bromine, forming K+ and Br- in a lattice.

explanation:
Electronegativity difference is found by subtraction, not addition: 2.96 - 0.82 = 2.14. Differences above roughly 1.7 to 2.0 indicate predominantly ionic character, which fits a group 1 metal combining with a halogen. The transferred electron yields K+ and Br-, and these ions assemble into an extended crystal lattice rather than discrete KBr molecules. Option A uses the wrong operation, option B ignores the size of the difference in favor of atomic radius, and option C pairs a very large difference with equal sharing, which is self-contradictory.

ELI-10: Electronegativity rates how strongly an atom pulls on shared electrons, so what matters is the gap between the two ratings, which means subtraction. Bromine at 2.96 against potassium at 0.82 leaves a gap of 2.14, well past the roughly 1.7 mark where sharing stops being realistic. At that point potassium does not merely lose the tug of war, it hands the electron over, producing K+ and Br- that stack into a salt crystal. Adding the values, as in option A, measures nothing meaningful.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: In a teaching data set, breaking an O-H covalent bond inside a water molecule requires about 460 kJ/mol, while breaking a hydrogen bond between two water molecules requires about 20 kJ/mol. Which conclusion is best supported by this comparison?

options.text: Boiling water breaks its O-H covalent bonds, which is why steam is chemically different from liquid water.
Water's high boiling point reflects individual hydrogen bonds that are each only 23 kJ/mol weaker than an O-H bond.
A hydrogen bond is a weak covalent bond in which two molecules share one hydrogen atom's single electron.
The O-H bond is about 23 times stronger than the hydrogen bond, so boiling separates whole molecules without breaking O-H bonds.

explanation:
Dividing the two values gives 460 / 20 = 23, an order-of-magnitude gap between an intramolecular covalent bond and an intermolecular attraction. Vaporization supplies far less energy than 460 kJ/mol, so it overcomes only the weaker hydrogen bonds; steam is still H2O with its O-H bonds intact. Option C misdefines a hydrogen bond, which is a strong dipole-dipole attraction rather than a shared-electron bond. Option B misreads the data: the two energies differ by a factor of 23, not by 23 kJ/mol, since 460 - 20 = 440.

ELI-10: Read the numbers as a ratio, because that tells you which attraction gives way first. At 460 versus 20 kJ/mol, the covalent O-H bond is about 23 times harder to break than a hydrogen bond, so any process supplying modest energy attacks the hydrogen bonds and nothing else. Boiling is exactly that: molecules separate from one another and drift off intact, which is why steam is still water and not loose H and O atoms. Hydrogen bonds are weak individually, but a liquid holds so many of them that water still needs unusual amounts of heat to boil.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Ammonium sulfate, (NH4)2SO4, contains 15 atoms per formula unit and dissolves in water to give NH4+ and SO4 2- ions. Which statement best explains the bonding present in this compound?

options.text: Every bond in the compound is ionic, because the substance is a salt that separates into ions in water.
Every bond in the compound is covalent, because the formula contains only nonmetal atoms.
The N-H and S-O bonds are ionic, while the attraction between the two polyatomic ions is covalent.
Covalent bonds hold the atoms together within each polyatomic ion, while ionic attractions hold NH4+ and SO4 2- to one another.

explanation:
Compounds built from polyatomic ions display both bonding types at once: shared electron pairs bind N to H and S to O inside each ion, while electrostatic attraction between the resulting NH4+ and SO4 2- units builds the lattice. That is precisely why dissolution releases intact polyatomic ions instead of free N, H, S, and O atoms, ruling out option A. Option B ignores that a cation and an anion are present despite the all-nonmetal composition, and option C reverses the two bond types. Counting confirms the composition: 2 x (1 + 4) + 1 + 4 = 15 atoms per formula unit.

ELI-10: Polyatomic ions force you to look at two levels at once. Inside NH4+, nitrogen and hydrogen share electron pairs, and inside SO4 2-, sulfur and oxygen do the same, so those internal links are covalent and survive dissolving. Between the two clusters there is nothing shared at all, only a positive group attracted to a negative group, which is ionic. The all-nonmetal formula fools people into calling it purely covalent, but the ions in solution prove otherwise. Atom count: two NH4 groups give 2 x 5 = 10, plus one S and four O, for 15.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Pauling electronegativity values are H = 2.2 and Cl = 3.16. Which statement best describes the bonding electrons in a molecule of HCl?

options.text: They are transferred completely from hydrogen to chlorine, producing full ionic charges.
They are shared equally, because a bond between two nonmetal atoms is always nonpolar.
They are shared unequally and held closer to chlorine, giving chlorine a partial negative charge.
They are held closer to hydrogen, because the smaller hydrogen nucleus attracts them more strongly.

explanation:
The electronegativity difference is 3.16 - 2.2 = 0.96, which falls in the polar covalent range (roughly 0.4 to 1.7 on the Pauling scale; differences above about 1.7 to 2.0 are treated as ionic). The pair remains shared, but chlorine's greater effective nuclear attraction for bonding electrons shifts electron density toward it, creating a partial negative charge on Cl and a partial positive charge on H. This permanent bond dipole (HCl has a measured dipole moment near 1.08 D) is the foundation for predicting molecular polarity and intermolecular forces.

ELI-10: Both atoms keep hold of the shared electrons, but chlorine pulls harder, so the electron cloud sits lopsided toward the chlorine side. Lopsided electron density means chlorine ends up slightly negative and hydrogen slightly positive, written as delta-minus and delta-plus. That is what 'polar covalent' means: still sharing, just not fairly. Complete transfer would be ionic, and that takes a much larger electronegativity gap than 0.96.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Which intermolecular force acts between every pair of neighboring molecules, whether those molecules are polar or nonpolar?

options.text: Hydrogen bonding
London dispersion forces
Ion-dipole attraction
Dipole-dipole attraction

explanation:
London dispersion forces arise from instantaneous fluctuations in an electron cloud that induce a matching temporary dipole in a neighboring particle. Because every atom and molecule contains electrons, dispersion is universal, while hydrogen bonding requires an H bonded to N, O, or F, dipole-dipole requires a permanent dipole, and ion-dipole requires an ion. Methane, with only 10 electrons and no permanent dipole, still condenses at about -161 degrees Celsius solely because of dispersion.

ELI-10: Electrons are constantly moving, so at any instant they can be bunched slightly to one side of a molecule. That momentary imbalance repels or attracts electrons in the molecule next door, creating a matching imbalance, and the two lopsided clouds attract. Since electrons exist in every molecule, this attraction never switches off, even in molecules with no permanent plus or minus end. The other three forces each need a special ingredient that many substances simply do not have.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A true hydrogen bond requires a hydrogen atom to be covalently bonded directly to which set of atoms?

options.text: Carbon, nitrogen, or sulfur
Nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine
Oxygen, sulfur, or chlorine
Any element more electronegative than hydrogen

explanation:
N, O, and F combine high electronegativity with small atomic radius, so they strip enough electron density from hydrogen to leave a highly concentrated partial positive charge on a very small, unshielded nucleus. That exposed proton can approach a lone pair on a nearby N, O, or F closely enough to give an unusually strong dipole-dipole interaction, typically 4 to 40 kJ/mol. The weakest qualifying case, N-H, still has an electronegativity difference of 3.04 - 2.2 = 0.84, whereas larger atoms such as S and Cl are too diffuse to produce the same effect despite reasonable electronegativity.

ELI-10: Hydrogen has only one electron, so when a very electronegative partner pulls that electron away, almost nothing is left shielding the proton. Size matters as much as pull: the partner has to be small enough that the stripped hydrogen sits close to it and stays exposed. Nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine are the only common atoms that are both small and greedy enough. Chlorine is electronegative but large, so its electron cloud spreads out and the effect fades.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A beaker of liquid water is heated until it boils completely away at 100 degrees Celsius. Which forces are overcome during this process?

options.text: Only London dispersion forces, because hydrogen bonds persist unchanged in steam
The O-H covalent bonds inside each molecule, releasing hydrogen and oxygen atoms
Both the O-H covalent bonds and the hydrogen bonds, in roughly equal proportion
Attractions between molecules, mainly hydrogen bonds, while O-H covalent bonds stay intact

explanation:
Boiling is a physical change that separates intact molecules from one another, so only intermolecular attractions are disrupted. The energy scale confirms this: the average O-H covalent bond enthalpy is about 463 kJ/mol, while a single hydrogen bond in water is roughly 21 kJ/mol, a gap of 442 kJ/mol, and water's enthalpy of vaporization is only 40.7 kJ/mol. Steam is still H2O; if covalent bonds were broken, boiling water would generate hydrogen and oxygen gas, which it does not.

ELI-10: Water molecules in the liquid are stuck to each other by hydrogen bonds, like magnets on a fridge. Boiling pulls the magnets apart, but each molecule stays a molecule, which is why steam is still water. Splitting the O-H bonds inside a molecule is a chemical change that costs more than ten times as much energy per bond and would give you hydrogen and oxygen gas instead of steam. Any time you see melting, boiling, or evaporating, think intermolecular, not intramolecular.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Carbon dioxide contains two strongly polar C=O bonds, yet the whole molecule is nonpolar. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: The molecule is linear, so two equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.
The individual C=O bond dipoles are too small to give the molecule measurable polarity.
Double bonds share four electrons, and that larger shared count cancels bond polarity.
Lone pairs on the central carbon atom offset the partial charges on the two oxygens.

explanation:
Molecular polarity is the vector sum of bond dipoles, so geometry matters as much as electronegativity. Each C=O bond is genuinely polar, with an electronegativity difference of 3.44 - 2.55 = 0.89, but the central carbon has no lone pairs, giving a linear 180-degree arrangement in which two identical dipoles point directly away from each other and sum to zero. Water contains comparably polar O-H bonds but is bent at about 104.5 degrees, so its bond dipoles cannot cancel and the molecule has a net dipole of 1.85 D.

ELI-10: Think of the two oxygens as equally strong pulls on the electrons, aimed in exactly opposite directions along a straight line. Real forces exist on each bond, but they add up to nothing overall, so the molecule has no plus end or minus end for a neighbor to grab. The key skill is checking geometry before declaring a molecule polar: identical polar bonds arranged symmetrically cancel, and the same bonds arranged asymmetrically, as in bent water, do not.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Fluorine (F2) is a gas at room temperature while iodine (I2) is a solid, even though both are nonpolar diatomic molecules. Which comparison is accurate?

options.text: Iodine molecules are polar and fluorine molecules are not, so iodine has dipole-dipole forces.
Iodine molecules hydrogen bond to one another, which fluorine molecules cannot do.
Iodine has far more electrons in a larger, more polarizable cloud, so dispersion is stronger.
Fluorine is more electronegative, so fluorine molecules attract one another more strongly.

explanation:
Both molecules are homonuclear, so neither has a permanent dipole and dispersion is the only force available to either. Dispersion strength tracks polarizability, which rises with the number of electrons and how loosely the outer ones are held: I2 carries 106 electrons versus 18 for F2, a difference of 88. Iodine's large, easily distorted cloud produces attractions strong enough to hold a crystalline solid melting at 113.7 degrees Celsius, while F2 boils at -188 degrees Celsius. Note that electronegativity describes electron pull within a bond, not attraction between separate molecules.

ELI-10: Dispersion depends on how easily an electron cloud can be pushed out of shape, and big loose clouds distort far more than small tight ones. Fluorine's eighteen electrons are held close to two small nuclei, so its momentary dipoles are tiny and the molecules barely stick. Iodine's one hundred six electrons sit in large outer shells that shift easily, producing much stronger momentary dipoles. More electrons and greater volume mean stronger dispersion, which is the usual reason substances get less volatile as you move down a group.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: When solid sodium chloride dissolves in water, which interaction primarily stabilizes the separated sodium and chloride ions in solution?

options.text: Ion-dipole attractions between each ion and the oppositely charged end of nearby water molecules
Hydrogen bonds formed directly between sodium ions and the oxygen atoms of water molecules
London dispersion forces between the ions and the electron clouds of water molecules
New covalent bonds formed between the sodium ions and the oxygen atoms of water

explanation:
Water is polar, with partial negative charge on oxygen and partial positive charge on the hydrogens, so oxygen ends orient toward Na+ and hydrogen ends orient toward Cl-. These ion-dipole attractions are the strongest of the intermolecular interactions and build hydration shells whose released hydration energy roughly offsets the 787 kJ/mol lattice energy of NaCl. Because each formula unit releases two ions, dissolving 0.15 mol NaCl yields 0.3 mol of solute particles, which is why saline solutions conduct current and exert osmotic pressure roughly double that of an equimolar nonelectrolyte.

ELI-10: An ion carries a full charge and water carries partial charges, so the two line up: oxygen ends crowd around the sodium ion and hydrogen ends crowd around the chloride ion. Each ion ends up wrapped in a shell of oriented water molecules that keeps it separated from its former partner. This is not a hydrogen bond, because no hydrogen is being shared with a lone pair on N, O, or F, and it is not covalent, because no electrons are shared. Full charge meeting partial charge is called ion-dipole.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: In a hypothetical lab exercise, Solid X dissolves in water to 36 g per 100 mL, while Solid Y dissolves to only 0.003 g per 100 mL. Which conclusion is best supported by these data?

options.text: Solid Y is the more polar substance, because polar solids resist dissolving in polar solvents.
Solid X is likely ionic or polar and solvates well, while Solid Y is likely nonpolar.
Solid X is nonpolar and Solid Y is polar, because nonpolar solids mix freely with water.
Both solids are nonpolar, and the gap reflects only the particle size of each solid.

explanation:
The rule that like dissolves like is an energetic statement: dissolving proceeds readily when new solute-solvent attractions repay the energy spent separating solvent molecules from each other and solute particles from each other. Solid X is 36 / 0.003 = 12,000 times more soluble, consistent with ion-dipole or hydrogen-bonding interactions strong enough to pay that cost, while a nonpolar Solid Y offers only weak dispersion forces and cannot compete with water's hydrogen-bond network. The same logic explains why glucose and electrolytes travel freely in plasma while lipids require carrier proteins or lipoproteins.

ELI-10: Water molecules already hold each other tightly with hydrogen bonds, so a solute has to offer something comparable to be let in. A charged or polar solid offers strong attractions to water's partial charges, so water rearranges around it and it dissolves. A nonpolar solid offers only weak dispersion, so water prefers its own company and the solid stays undissolved. A twelve-thousand-fold solubility gap is exactly the fingerprint of one solute matching water's polarity and the other not.
