source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Ethanol (CH3CH2OH) boils at 78 degrees Celsius, but dimethyl ether (CH3OCH3), which has the identical molecular formula C2H6O, boils near -24 degrees Celsius. Which statement best explains this difference?

options.text: Ethanol's O-H group can donate and accept hydrogen bonds; the ether oxygen can only accept.
Dimethyl ether is fully nonpolar, so only dispersion forces operate between its molecules.
Ethanol contains an extra carbon-oxygen bond that raises the energy needed to vaporize it.
Ethanol has the greater molar mass, so its London dispersion forces are much stronger.

explanation:
These isomers share the formula C2H6O and a molar mass of about 46 g/mol, so dispersion forces are comparable and cannot account for the 78 - (-24) = 102 degree Celsius gap. Hydrogen bonding requires a hydrogen covalently bound to N, O, or F: ethanol supplies that donor, so its molecules form an extended hydrogen-bonded network. Dimethyl ether's oxygen is flanked by two carbons and has lone pairs but no attached hydrogen, so in the pure liquid no donor exists and only dipole-dipole and dispersion forces remain. Both isomers are polar; polarity alone is not the deciding factor.

ELI-10: Hydrogen bonding takes two parts: a donor, meaning an H attached to N, O, or F, and an acceptor, meaning a lone pair. Ethanol has both, so its molecules link into chains that take a lot of heat to pull apart. Dimethyl ether has acceptors only, and an acceptor with no donor nearby has nothing to bond to, so pure ether molecules just brush past each other. Same atoms, different arrangement, and the presence or absence of one donor hydrogen shifts the boiling point by over 100 degrees.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Which change would most likely increase the rate at which a liquid evaporates from an open dish held at constant temperature?

options.text: Replacing the liquid with one whose molecules form an extensive hydrogen-bond network
Dissolving a nonvolatile solute that lowers the liquid's vapor pressure
Replacing the liquid with one whose molecules have weaker intermolecular attractions
Pouring the liquid into a narrow cylinder that exposes less surface area

explanation:
Evaporation occurs when surface molecules acquire enough kinetic energy to escape the attractions of their neighbors, so weakening those attractions increases the fraction of molecules that can escape at any given temperature. Liquids with weak intermolecular forces therefore show high vapor pressure and low enthalpy of vaporization, while water's extensive hydrogen bonding gives it an enthalpy of vaporization of about 40.7 kJ/mol, so 2 mol takes about 81.4 kJ to vaporize. The other options either strengthen the attractions holding molecules in the liquid or reduce the surface area from which escape occurs, both of which slow evaporation.

ELI-10: Only molecules at the surface with above-average kinetic energy can break free, so the question is how high the escape barrier sits. Weaker attractions lower that barrier, so a much larger share of surface molecules clears it every second and the dish empties faster. That is why isopropyl alcohol dries on skin within seconds while water lingers: alcohol has fewer hydrogen bonds per molecule. Surface area and added solutes change the rate too, but the options listed move both in the wrong direction.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A phospholipid molecule has one charged phosphate head group and two long hydrocarbon tails. What would happen if a large number of these molecules were placed in water?

options.text: They settle as a disordered solid, since a molecule with long hydrocarbon chains is nonpolar.
They dissolve completely as separate molecules, since the charged head makes each one soluble.
They dissolve because the hydrocarbon tails form hydrogen bonds with surrounding water.
They self-assemble with polar heads facing the water and nonpolar tails clustered away from it.

explanation:
Phospholipids are amphipathic: the charged phosphate head engages in ion-dipole and hydrogen-bonding interactions with water, while the hydrocarbon tails offer only dispersion forces and force surrounding water into an entropically costly ordered cage. The system minimizes free energy by sequestering the tails, and the shape of the aggregate follows the shape of the molecule: two bulky tails under one head make the molecule roughly cylindrical, so it packs into a bilayer that typically closes into a vesicle, whereas single-tailed amphiphiles such as soaps and detergents are cone-shaped and form micelles instead. An aggregate of 500 of these two-tailed phospholipids buries 2 * 500 = 1000 tails in a shielded hydrophobic core. Because the tails are shielded rather than dissolved, the assembly is a stable structure, not a precipitate, which is why cell membranes form and reseal without any energy input.

ELI-10: One molecule cannot satisfy both halves at once, since the head wants water contact and the tails want to avoid it. The compromise is collective: thousands of molecules point their heads outward into the water and tuck their tails inward against each other. Two fat tails under one head make this molecule shaped more like a cylinder than a cone, so the sheet it builds is two layers thick and usually curls around to close into a hollow bubble; single-tailed molecules like soap are cone-shaped and ball up into small micelles instead. The driving force is largely the water itself, which regains freedom once it no longer has to cage greasy chains, and this single polarity argument is why every cell membrane exists and why it heals over small punctures.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: For a hypothetical polar liquid, the total intermolecular attraction is 21 kJ/mol, of which 17 kJ/mol is attributed to London dispersion and the remainder to dipole-dipole attraction. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The substance behaves as a nonpolar liquid, since dispersion supplies most of the attraction.
Dipole-dipole attraction outweighs dispersion whenever a substance has a permanent dipole.
The substance is capable of hydrogen bonding, since the total attraction exceeds 20 kJ/mol.
Dispersion can dominate in a polar substance, with dipole-dipole supplying under one fifth.

explanation:
Dispersion and dipole-dipole contributions are additive, and dispersion grows steeply with electron count and polarizability, so in many polar molecules of moderate size dispersion supplies the larger share of the total attraction. Here the dipole-dipole term is 21 - 17 = 4 kJ/mol, or (21 - 17) / 21 * 100 = 19.05 percent of the total, which is below one fifth. A nonzero dipole-dipole term establishes that the substance is polar, so it cannot be treated as nonpolar, and a total near 21 kJ/mol says nothing about hydrogen bonding, which requires a hydrogen covalently bonded to N, O, or F rather than a threshold energy.

ELI-10: A common misconception is that once a molecule is polar, its permanent dipole becomes the main source of attraction. In reality the dispersion contribution keeps climbing as the electron cloud gets larger, and it routinely overtakes the dipole term in molecules bigger than a few atoms. Here the dipole part is about 19 out of every 100 units of attraction, so polarity is real but minor. Data like these are why chemists compare molecules on total attraction rather than assuming the presence of a dipole settles the ranking.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: In a sealed hypothetical reaction vessel, 4 g of hydrogen gas reacts completely with 32 g of oxygen gas to form water as the only product. Which value states the mass of water produced, and which principle requires it?

options.text: 34 g, because a small amount of mass is converted to the heat released
32 g, because the heavier reactant determines the mass of the product
18 g, because one mole of water has a mass of 18 g
36 g, because mass is conserved in a chemical reaction

explanation:
The law of conservation of mass states that atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical change, so in a closed system the total mass of products equals the total mass of reactants. Here 4 g of H2 (2 mol) and 32 g of O2 (1 mol) match the 2:1 ratio of 2 H2 + O2 to 2 H2O exactly, so both are fully consumed and all 36 g of matter appears as water. The energy released is real but the associated mass change is far too small to measure chemically, which is why chemical equations are balanced on an atom-for-atom basis.

ELI-10: A chemical reaction rearranges atoms; it never deletes them or invents new ones. Take apart a 36-piece structure and rebuild it into a different shape inside a sealed box, and the box still holds 36 pieces. So 4 g in plus 32 g in must come out as 36 g of water. Reactions release energy, but that does not make measurable matter disappear.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Which set of coefficients, written in the order N2, H2, NH3, balances the equation N2 + H2 -> NH3 using the smallest whole numbers?
explanation:
With 1, 3, 2 the left side has 2 N and 6 H and the right side has 2 N and 6 H, so every element balances with the smallest possible whole numbers. Each other set fails an atom count: 1, 2, 2 gives 4 H on the left against 6 H on the right; 2, 3, 2 gives 4 N on the left against 2 N on the right; 1, 3, 3 gives 2 N on the left against 3 N on the right. Balancing is done only by adjusting coefficients, because changing a subscript would change the identity of a substance.

ELI-10: Count atoms on each side and adjust only the numbers written in front. One N2 supplies 2 nitrogen atoms, and each NH3 uses 1 nitrogen, so 2 NH3 can be built. Those 2 NH3 need 6 hydrogen atoms, and hydrogen arrives as H2 pairs, so 3 H2 are required. Final tally: 2 N and 6 H on both sides.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Which equation is an example of a decomposition reaction?

options.text: AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) -> AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq)
Zn(s) + 2 HCl(aq) -> ZnCl2(aq) + H2(g)

explanation:
Decomposition follows the pattern AB -> A + B: a single reactant breaks apart into two or more simpler substances. Hydrogen peroxide breaking down into water and oxygen gas is exactly that pattern. The distractors are a single-replacement reaction (zinc displacing hydrogen from the acid), a combination or synthesis reaction (two elements forming one compound), and a double-replacement precipitation reaction.

ELI-10: Classify by counting what starts and what ends. Decomposition has exactly one starting substance that comes apart into several products. Synthesis is the reverse: several reactants combine into one product. Replacement reactions start with two substances that swap partners. Only the peroxide equation begins with a single compound, so only it is decomposition.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A student tries to "balance" H2 + O2 -> H2O by rewriting the product formula as H2O2. What is wrong with this approach?

options.text: The mass on each side changes, but the identity of the product stays the same
The equation stays chemically valid because a subscript was changed, not a coefficient
The equation is acceptable because subscripts and coefficients both scale the product amount
The equation no longer describes water; it describes hydrogen peroxide, a different compound

explanation:
Subscripts specify the fixed composition of a compound, so changing one produces a different substance rather than a different quantity of the same substance. H2O and H2O2 differ by one oxygen atom per molecule and have entirely different chemical properties: water is stable and drinkable, hydrogen peroxide is a reactive oxidizer that decomposes readily. Balancing is legitimate only when correct formulas are held fixed and coefficients in front of them are adjusted.

ELI-10: A formula is the substance's identity; a coefficient is how many units of it are present. If a reaction needs more water, you write a larger number in front of H2O. Editing the subscript instead changes what the substance is, the way changing letters inside a word changes the word rather than giving you two copies of it.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A hypothetical laboratory burner combusts propane completely: C3H8 + 5 O2 -> 3 CO2 + 4 H2O. How many moles of O2 are consumed when 2 mol of propane burns completely?

options.text: 2.5 mol, because the 2 mol of propane is divided by the 5:1 ratio
10 mol, because the 5:1 mole ratio is applied to 2 mol of propane
5 mol, because the coefficient of O2 in the balanced equation is 5
8 mol, because the water coefficient of 4 is scaled to the 2 mol of propane

explanation:
Coefficients in a balanced equation express mole ratios, and this equation requires 5 mol O2 per 1 mol C3H8. Multiplying that ratio by 2 mol of propane gives 2 x 5 = 10 mol O2. Reading a coefficient as a fixed absolute amount, inverting the ratio, or picking the coefficient of the wrong species are the three common errors represented by the distractors.

ELI-10: Treat the balanced equation as a ratio, not a fixed quantity. It says every 1 propane pairs with 5 oxygen molecules. Doubling the propane doubles everything tied to it, so 2 propane pairs with 10 oxygen. The key move is to set up the ratio as 5 mol O2 per 1 mol C3H8 and multiply, so the propane units cancel and moles of O2 remain.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: In a teaching demonstration, hydrochloric acid is neutralized by calcium hydroxide: 2 HCl + Ca(OH)2 -> CaCl2 + 2 H2O. How many moles of Ca(OH)2 are required to neutralize 0.4 mol of HCl completely?

options.text: 0.2 mol, because each mole of Ca(OH)2 supplies two moles of hydroxide
0.4 mol, because an acid and a base always neutralize in a 1:1 ratio
0.1 mol, because each of the two hydroxide ions neutralizes two moles of acid
0.8 mol, because each mole of HCl requires two moles of the base

explanation:
The balanced equation sets a 2:1 mole ratio of HCl to Ca(OH)2, so 0.4 mol HCl requires 0.4 / 2 = 0.2 mol of the base. Each formula unit of Ca(OH)2 releases two hydroxide ions, so one mole of it neutralizes two moles of a monoprotic acid such as HCl. Assuming every acid-base pairing is 1:1 is a frequent misconception that produces a twofold error in the amount of base.

ELI-10: Neutralization pairs one H+ with one OH-. HCl delivers one H+ per formula unit, while Ca(OH)2 delivers two OH- per formula unit. So each unit of base can handle two units of this acid, and you need only half as many moles of base as acid: 0.4 divided by 2 is 0.2 mol.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Which statement about the complete ionic and net ionic equations for AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) -> AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq) is accurate?

options.text: The net ionic equation lists all four ions, since each of them is dissolved in water
The net ionic equation drops Ag+ and Cl-, since ions that form a solid are not written
The net ionic equation drops the spectator ions Na+ and NO3-, leaving Ag+ + Cl- -> AgCl(s)
The complete ionic equation writes AgCl as separate Ag+ and Cl- ions in solution

explanation:
In the complete ionic equation, soluble strong electrolytes are written as dissociated ions while the insoluble product AgCl is written as an intact solid. Na+ and NO3- appear unchanged on both sides, so they are spectator ions and cancel, leaving Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> AgCl(s). The net ionic equation isolates the chemical change that actually occurs, which is why it is the standard representation for precipitation and neutralization reactions.

ELI-10: Write out every dissolved ion first, but keep the insoluble solid together because it is not dissociated. Then cross off any ion that appears identically on both sides; it entered and left unchanged, so it did nothing. Here Na+ and NO3- cancel, and what survives is the silver ion joining the chloride ion to form solid AgCl.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: A sealed hypothetical vessel is charged with 4 mol H2 and 3 mol O2, which react by 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O. Which outcome is expected once the reaction goes to completion?

options.text: 3 mol of water forms, with 1 mol of H2 left unreacted
6 mol of water forms, with all 3 mol of O2 consumed
4 mol of water forms, with 1 mol of O2 left unreacted
7 mol of water forms, with both gases fully consumed

explanation:
Divide each amount by its coefficient: H2 gives 4 / 2 = 2 reaction units, O2 gives 3 / 1 = 3, so H2 is limiting. The 4 mol of H2 produces 4 mol of H2O and consumes only 2 mol of O2, leaving 1 mol of O2 in excess. The limiting reactant is set by stoichiometric demand, not by which reactant simply has the smaller number of moles or the smaller coefficient.

ELI-10: Ask how many complete reactions each reactant could support. Hydrogen is used two at a time, so 4 mol of H2 supports 2 rounds. Oxygen is used one at a time, so 3 mol of O2 supports 3 rounds. Only 2 rounds can actually run, and each round makes 2 water, giving 4 mol of water. Those 2 rounds use 2 mol of O2, so 1 mol of O2 sits unused.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: In a hypothetical student synthesis, the calculated theoretical yield of a salt is 25 g and the mass actually isolated after purification is 20 g. What is the percent yield of the reaction?

options.text: 125%, found by dividing the theoretical yield by the actual yield
80%, found by dividing the actual yield by the theoretical yield
20%, because the isolated mass in grams is reported directly as the percentage
0.8%, found from the ratio of actual to theoretical without converting to a percentage

explanation:
Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100 = (20 / 25) x 100 = 80%. Theoretical yield comes from the balanced equation applied to the limiting reactant; actual yield is what is physically recovered, and it is normally lower because of side reactions, incomplete reaction, and losses during transfer and filtration. A reported yield above 100% almost always signals an impure or incompletely dried product rather than extra material.

ELI-10: Percent yield compares what you got with what the stoichiometry promised. You were promised 25 g and recovered 20 g, so you kept 20 out of every 25, which is 4 out of every 5, or 80 out of 100. Two habits prevent errors here: put the actual amount on top, and remember to multiply the ratio by 100.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: In a hypothetical furnace demonstration, calcium carbonate decomposes completely: CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g). Using 44 g/mol as the molar mass of CO2, what mass of CO2 is released when 2 mol of CaCO3 decomposes?

options.text: 22 g, obtained by dividing the 44 g/mol molar mass between the 2 mol of CaCO3
200 g, because the 100 g/mol molar mass of CaCO3 is applied to the 2 mol
44 g, because one mole of CO2 leaves the solid no matter how large the sample is
88 g, because 2 mol of CO2 forms and each mole has a mass of 44 g

explanation:
The balanced equation has a 1:1 mole ratio of CaCO3 to CO2, so 2 mol of carbonate releases 2 mol of CO2. Converting moles to mass with the molar mass of the gas gives 2 mol x 44 g/mol = 88 g. The two-step pattern of moles of reactant, then mole ratio, then molar mass of the requested substance is the standard route for every mass-based stoichiometry calculation, and the molar mass used must belong to the substance being asked about.

ELI-10: Work in two steps. First use the equation's ratio: one CaCO3 releases one CO2, so 2 mol in means 2 mol of gas out. Then convert moles of gas to grams using the molar mass of that gas: 2 x 44 = 88 g. The common trap is grabbing the molar mass of the starting solid instead of the substance the question asks for.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Butane undergoes complete combustion according to the unbalanced equation C4H10 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O. When the equation is balanced with the smallest possible whole-number coefficients, what is the sum of all four coefficients?
explanation:
Balancing carbon and hydrogen first gives C4H10 + 13/2 O2 -> 4 CO2 + 5 H2O, and multiplying every coefficient by 2 clears the fraction to give 2 C4H10 + 13 O2 -> 8 CO2 + 10 H2O, so the coefficients sum to 2 + 13 + 8 + 10 = 33. The atom inventory confirms 8 C, 20 H, and 26 O on each side, since 13 x 2 = 26 and (8 x 2) + 10 = 26. The sums 24 and 29 arise from doubling only some of the coefficients after clearing the fraction (24 = 2 + 13 + 4 + 5 and 29 = 2 + 13 + 4 + 10), while 31 is simply a nearby total that no correct balancing produces.

ELI-10: Balance carbon and hydrogen first because each appears in only one product, and leave oxygen for last because it appears in two. That gives 4 CO2 and 5 H2O, which need 13 oxygen atoms, or 6.5 O2 molecules. Since half a molecule is not allowed, multiply every coefficient in the equation by 2, exactly as you would double a whole recipe rather than one ingredient. The result is 2, 13, 8, 10, which adds to 33.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-1
question: Ammonia is produced by N2 + 3 H2 -> 2 NH3. A sealed hypothetical reactor is charged with 2 mol N2 and 3 mol H2. Using 17 g/mol as the molar mass of NH3, what is the theoretical yield of ammonia?

options.text: 51 g, because each mole of H2 charged yields one mole of NH3
68 g, because N2 is limiting and yields 4 mol of NH3
34 g, because H2 is limiting and yields 2 mol of NH3
85 g, because all 5 mol of reactant charged is converted to product

explanation:
Divide each amount by its coefficient: N2 gives 2 / 1 = 2 reaction units while H2 gives 3 / 3 = 1, so hydrogen is the limiting reactant and 1 mol of N2 remains in excess. Applying the 3:2 ratio, 3 mol of H2 produces 2 mol of NH3, and 2 mol x 17 g/mol = 34 g. Comparing raw mole counts would point to N2 as limiting because only 2 mol were charged, which is exactly the error behind choice B; only the moles-divided-by-coefficient comparison correctly identifies H2 as the limiting reactant.

ELI-10: Each complete reaction consumes 1 N2 and 3 H2. With 3 mol of H2 you can run exactly one such reaction, and with 2 mol of N2 you could run two, so hydrogen runs out first and 1 mol of nitrogen is left over. That single reaction produces 2 mol of NH3, and at 17 g per mole that is 34 g. Notice that nitrogen is the one you have less of by simple count, yet hydrogen is what runs out, so always divide each amount by its coefficient before deciding which reactant limits the yield.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Which statement best defines the molar mass of a substance?

options.text: The mass in grams of one representative particle of the substance, read directly from an analytical balance
The mass in grams of one mole of the substance, numerically equal to its atomic or formula mass in amu
The combined count of protons and neutrons in one representative particle, expressed in atomic mass units
The volume in liters that one mole of the substance occupies at standard temperature and pressure

explanation:
Molar mass is the mass of exactly one mole (6.022 x 10^23 representative particles) of a substance, with units of grams per mole. Its numerical value matches the atomic mass (for elements) or the formula/molecular mass (for compounds) expressed in atomic mass units, which is why the periodic table can be read directly as a table of molar masses: for water, 2(1.008) + 15.999 = 18.015 g/mol. A single particle has a mass of only about 10^-23 g, and molar volume is a separate quantity that varies with phase, temperature, and pressure.

ELI-10: Weighing is easy; counting atoms is impossible. Molar mass is the trick that turns one into the other: it tells you what one mole-sized batch of particles weighs. The convenient part is that the number is already printed on the periodic table. Hydrogen reads 1.008 and oxygen reads 15.999, so one mole of water weighs 1.008 + 1.008 + 15.999 = 18.015 grams. Same number, two different scales: amu when you are talking about one particle, grams when you are talking about a mole of them.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Which value correctly states the number of representative particles contained in exactly one mole of any substance?

options.text: 6.022 x 10^23 particles, the value known as Avogadro's number that defines the mole
1.008 x 10^23 particles, since the mole is anchored to the molar mass of hydrogen
6.022 x 10^-23 particles, since the exponent is negative for quantities as small as atoms
1.204 x 10^24 particles, since the mole is referenced to a 12-gram sample of carbon-12

explanation:
The Avogadro constant is 6.02214076 x 10^23 mol^-1 (an exact defined value in the SI system since 2019), commonly rounded to 6.022 x 10^23. It applies to whatever the representative particle is: atoms for elements, molecules for molecular compounds, formula units for ionic compounds. Because the count is fixed, one mole of any substance contains the same number of particles even though the masses differ widely. A negative exponent would describe a fraction of a particle, and 12 g of carbon-12 contains one mole, not two.

ELI-10: A dozen always means 12, whether the items are eggs or bricks; only the weight changes. A mole always means 6.022 x 10^23, whether the items are gold atoms or water molecules. The number is enormous because atoms are so small that you need hundreds of thousands of billions of billions of them before the pile is big enough to see and weigh. Note the sign of the exponent: 10^23 is a huge count. A negative exponent would mean less than one particle, which cannot be what a mole means.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A laboratory sample contains 116.88 g of sodium chloride (molar mass 58.44 g/mol). How many moles of sodium chloride are present?

options.text: 0.5 mol, obtained by dividing the molar mass by the sample mass
2 mol, obtained by dividing the sample mass by the molar mass
58.44 mol, since the molar mass reports the mole count of the sample directly
6830 mol, obtained by multiplying the sample mass by the molar mass

explanation:
Moles are obtained by dividing the measured mass by the molar mass: 116.88 g / 58.44 g/mol = 2 mol. Dimensional analysis confirms the setup, because grams divided by grams per mole leaves moles. Option A inverts the ratio, giving 0.5 with units of mol^-1 (grams per mole divided by grams leaves 1/mol), and option D multiplies, giving about 6830 with units of g^2/mol; neither result carries the unit mol, so checking units catches both errors before the number is reported. Option C simply repeats the molar mass value and ignores the sample mass entirely.

ELI-10: If one sack of flour weighs 5 pounds and you are holding 10 pounds of flour, you have 10 / 5 = 2 sacks. Molar mass is the weight of one sack of particles, 58.44 g per mole for table salt, and your sample weighs 116.88 g. Divide and you get 2 sacks, meaning 2 moles. Carry the units through the arithmetic as a check: g divided by g/mol leaves mol, which is what the question asked for. If you divide or multiply the other way around, the leftover units are not moles, which is your signal to flip the setup and try again.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Two beakers each hold 100 g of solid: one holds glucose (180.16 g/mol) and the other holds water ice (18.02 g/mol). Which comparison of the two samples is accurate?

options.text: The two samples hold equal numbers of moles, since their masses are equal
The glucose sample holds about 10 times more moles, since its molar mass is larger
The two samples hold equal numbers of molecules, since molar mass affects only the mass
The water sample holds about 10 times more moles, since its molar mass is about 10 times smaller

explanation:
Moles equal mass divided by molar mass, so at fixed mass the mole count is inversely proportional to molar mass. Since 180.16 / 18.02 is about 9.998, the same 100 g yields roughly ten times as many moles of water as of glucose (about 5.55 mol versus 0.555 mol). Equal masses therefore do not imply equal mole counts or equal particle counts, which is precisely why chemists convert to moles before comparing amounts or setting up reactions.

ELI-10: Picture 100 grams of marbles beside 100 grams of bowling balls. The scale reads the same, but you have far more marbles because each one is light. A water molecule is the marble here at 18.02 g per mole, and a glucose molecule is the bowling ball at 180.16 g per mole, roughly ten times heavier. So the same 100 g gives you about ten times as many water molecules. Heavier particles means fewer of them in every gram.
tags: inverse relationship of mass and molar mass
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: The periodic table lists the molar mass of chlorine as 35.45 g/mol, yet no individual chlorine atom has that mass. What accounts for this non-whole-number value?

options.text: Electrons contribute a small fractional mass that pulls the value away from a whole number
It is the abundance-weighted average of the masses of chlorine's naturally occurring isotopes
It is the plain average of the mass numbers 35 and 37, since both isotopes occur in nature
It is the mass of a single chlorine-35 atom, rounded to two decimal places for tabulation

explanation:
Natural chlorine is about 75.76% chlorine-35 (34.969 amu) and 24.24% chlorine-37 (36.966 amu), giving (0.7576)(34.969) + (0.2424)(36.966) = 35.45 amu. Because any real sample is a mixture of isotopes, the tabulated atomic mass is an abundance-weighted average rather than the mass of any single atom. An unweighted average of 35 and 37 would give 36, electron mass is negligible at this precision, and 34.969 rounds to 34.97 rather than 35.45.

ELI-10: Suppose a group has 76 members weighing 35 kg and 24 members weighing 37 kg. The group average is about 35.5 kg, even though no single member weighs that. Chlorine is the same situation: most chlorine atoms are the lighter chlorine-35 type and a smaller share are chlorine-37. The periodic table reports the average, weighted so the more common isotope counts more heavily. Note that a plain average of 35 and 37 would give 36, so the weighting is what pulls chlorine's listed value down to 35.45.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Which comparison of 1 mol of neon gas and 1 mol of nitrogen gas (N2) is accurate?

options.text: Neon holds more representative particles, because its particles are single atoms rather than molecules
Nitrogen holds more representative particles, because each of its molecules is built from two atoms
Both hold the same number of representative particles, but the nitrogen sample holds twice as many atoms
Both hold the same number of atoms, because one mole fixes the atom count at 6.022 x 10^23

explanation:
One mole of any substance contains 6.022 x 10^23 representative particles, so both samples contain that count: atoms for neon, molecules for N2. Each N2 molecule holds two nitrogen atoms, so the nitrogen sample contains 2(6.022 x 10^23) = 1.2044 x 10^24 atoms while neon contains 6.022 x 10^23 atoms. Identifying the representative particle before converting is what prevents this very common error in mole-to-particle work.

ELI-10: A mole counts whatever unit the substance is made of. For neon the unit is a lone atom; for nitrogen gas the unit is a molecule of two bonded atoms. One mole of each gives the same number of units, like one dozen single socks versus one dozen pairs of socks. The dozens match, but the pairs contain twice as many actual socks. So 1 mol of N2 holds 6.022 x 10^23 molecules and 1.2044 x 10^24 nitrogen atoms. Always ask which particle the question wants counted.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: What is the primary purpose of the mole concept in chemistry?

options.text: It links a countable number of particles to a mass that can be measured on a laboratory balance
It converts the volume of a liquid sample into its density without any mass measurement
It fixes the number of atoms written as subscripts when a chemical formula is constructed
It sets the volume that one mole of any liquid occupies, so samples can be compared by volume

explanation:
Substances react in whole-number particle ratios, yet no balance can count individual particles. The mole is the conversion bridge: molar mass turns a weighable mass into a particle count, so 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate (100.09 g/mol) corresponds to a measurable 25.02 g and to about 1.5 x 10^23 formula units. This macroscopic-to-microscopic link underpins stoichiometry, solution concentration, and clinical dosage calculations. Subscripts come from bonding and charge balance, and molar volume is a separate concept that applies mainly to gases.

ELI-10: You cannot count grains of rice before dinner, but you can weigh out a cup and know approximately how many you have. Chemists face the same problem in a harsher form, since atoms are far too small to count at all. So they weigh instead, and molar mass is the conversion card: one mole of this substance weighs this many grams. Need 0.25 mol of chalk? Weigh 25.02 g and you have counted about 1.5 x 10^23 formula units without counting anything.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A student measures out 9 g of pure water (18.02 g/mol) for a classroom demonstration. Approximately how many water molecules does this sample contain?

options.text: 3 x 10^23 molecules, obtained by converting to moles and then multiplying by Avogadro's number
1.2 x 10^24 molecules, obtained by doubling Avogadro's number for the two hydrogen atoms
5.4 x 10^24 molecules, obtained by multiplying the mass in grams by Avogadro's number
3.3 x 10^22 molecules, obtained by dividing Avogadro's number by the molar mass

explanation:
Mass-to-particle problems take two steps: 9 g / 18.02 g/mol = 0.4994 mol, then 0.4994 mol x 6.022 x 10^23 mol^-1 = 3.008 x 10^23 molecules. Multiplying grams by Avogadro's number without the mole step inflates the result by a factor of the molar mass, giving 5.4 x 10^24. The answer is reasonable because 9 g is about half of water's 18.02 g/mol, so the count should be about half of Avogadro's number.

ELI-10: Treat this as a two-leg trip with moles as the connecting stop. There is no direct route from grams to molecules. Leg one: 9 g divided by 18.02 g per mole is about half a mole. Leg two: half a mole times 6.022 x 10^23 particles per mole is about 3 x 10^23 molecules. The sanity check is quick, since half a mole should give half of Avogadro's number, and it does. Any answer larger than 10^24 for such a small sample means the mole step was skipped.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A chemistry exercise calls for preparing exactly 0.5 mol of glucose (C6H12O6, molar mass 180.16 g/mol). Which mass should be weighed out, and why?

options.text: 180.16 g, because the molar mass is the mass to weigh whenever a mole quantity is specified
360.32 g, because the molar mass is divided by the requested mole quantity
90.08 g, because mass equals the requested moles multiplied by the molar mass
0.00278 g, because the requested moles are divided by the molar mass

explanation:
Converting moles to mass uses mass = moles x molar mass, so 0.5 mol x 180.16 g/mol = 90.08 g. The units confirm the setup, since moles multiplied by grams per mole leaves grams. Dividing instead produces 360.32 g or 0.00278 g, both of which fail the estimation check that half a mole must weigh half of the molar mass.

ELI-10: If one full container of a substance weighs 180.16 grams, half a container weighs half that, which is 90.08 grams. That is the whole calculation: moles times molar mass. Build in the estimate before you compute. When the requested amount is less than one mole, the mass must come out smaller than the molar mass; when it is more than one mole, the mass must come out larger. An answer that breaks this rule means the multiplication was flipped into a division.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A hypothetical teaching solution is prepared by dissolving 11.1 g of calcium chloride, CaCl2 (110.98 g/mol), in water so that it fully dissociates. How many moles of chloride ions does the solution contain?

options.text: 0.05 mol, because the compound's moles are split evenly between the two kinds of ions
0.1 mol, because each formula unit releases one chloride ion into solution
2 mol, because the subscript 2 states the chloride mole quantity directly
0.2 mol, because each formula unit releases two chloride ions into solution

explanation:
First convert to moles of compound: 11.1 g / 110.98 g/mol = 0.1 mol CaCl2. The formula shows two chloride ions per formula unit, so the ratio of 2 mol Cl- per 1 mol CaCl2 gives 0.2 mol chloride (alongside 0.1 mol Ca2+). Subscripts in a formula are per-unit ratios, not absolute mole quantities, which is the misconception behind the 2 mol option.

ELI-10: Each CaCl2 formula unit arrives as a set: one calcium ion and two chloride ions, like a bicycle with one frame and two wheels. Weighing tells you the number of sets, here 0.1 mole of them. The number of wheels is twice that, so 0.2 mole of chloride. The subscript 2 never means two moles on its own; it means two per unit. The order matters: find moles of the whole compound first, then apply the subscript as a multiplier.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A 21.5 g sample of a purified unknown compound is determined to contain 0.25 mol of that compound. What is its molar mass, and what does this value represent?

options.text: 5.375 g/mol, representing the mass contributed by each individual molecule in the sample
0.0116 g/mol, representing the fraction of a mole contained in each gram of the sample
21.5 g/mol, representing the mass of the sample reported on a per-mole basis
86 g/mol, representing the mass of 6.022 x 10^23 molecules of the compound

explanation:
Molar mass is mass divided by moles: 21.5 g / 0.25 mol = 86 g/mol. Conceptually that is the mass of one full mole, meaning 6.022 x 10^23 molecules of the compound. Determining molar mass this way reverses the usual conversion and is how an unknown is identified once its empirical formula is known, since the molecular formula must be a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula mass.

ELI-10: You have a quarter of a container and it weighs 21.5 grams, so a full container weighs four times as much, which is 86 grams. Molar mass is that full-container weight, where a full container means 6.022 x 10^23 molecules. Dividing by 0.25 is the same as multiplying by 4, so watch the direction: the answer must be larger than 21.5 g, because a whole mole always outweighs a quarter of one. Options smaller than 21.5 g can be ruled out before any arithmetic.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Four sealed vials each contain exactly 1 g of a pure gas: hydrogen (H2, 2.016 g/mol), helium (He, 4.003 g/mol), nitrogen (N2, 28.02 g/mol), and oxygen (O2, 32 g/mol). Which vial contains the greatest total number of atoms?

options.text: The oxygen vial, because its larger molar mass supplies more atomic material per gram
The helium vial, because single atoms give more particles per gram than bonded molecules do
The hydrogen vial, because it has both the smallest molar mass and two atoms per molecule
The nitrogen vial, because its molar mass balances particle count against atoms per molecule

explanation:
At fixed mass, moles rise as molar mass falls, and the total atom count then scales with the atoms per formula unit. Hydrogen gives (1 g / 2.016 g/mol) x 2 = 0.992 mol of atoms, compared with 0.25 mol for helium, 0.0714 mol for nitrogen, and 0.0625 mol for oxygen. Being monatomic does not help helium enough, since each helium atom is nearly twice the mass of an entire H2 molecule, so the diatomic gas still wins on both factors combined.

ELI-10: Two factors decide atoms per gram: how light each particle is, and how many atoms each particle carries. Hydrogen leads on both. It is the lightest molecule there is, so 1 g gives about half a mole of molecules, and each molecule carries two atoms, doubling that to about 0.992 mole of atoms. Helium comes as single atoms, which sounds like an advantage, but one helium atom outweighs a whole H2 molecule, so 1 g yields only 0.25 mole of atoms. Lightest plus doubled beats single but heavier.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A laboratory solution is prepared by dissolving 5 g of sodium chloride in 95 g of water. Which term correctly identifies the water in this mixture, and what mass of it is present?

options.text: The solute, 5 g, because it is the component dispersed throughout the mixture
The solvent, 5 g, because it is the component that is no longer visible
The solute, 95 g, because it establishes the final volume of the mixture
The solvent, 95 g, because it is the component present in greater amount and does the dissolving

explanation:
In a solution the solvent is the component present in the greatest amount and it disperses the solute to the level of individual particles or ions; here water (95 g) is the solvent and NaCl (5 g) is the solute. The total solution mass is 100 g, so 100 g minus the 5 g of solute leaves 95 g of solvent. Identifying solute versus solvent correctly is the first step in every concentration calculation, because concentration is always some measure of solute relative to either the solvent or the total solution.

ELI-10: Two jobs exist in any solution: one substance does the dissolving and one substance gets dissolved. The dissolver is the solvent, and it is normally the component you have far more of; the dissolved substance is the solute. Here the numbers decide it for you: 95 g of water against 5 g of salt, so water is the solvent. Note that the salt does not vanish when it disappears from view, it has simply spread out as separate sodium and chloride ions too small to see.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Which statement correctly defines molarity, and what is the molarity of a solution containing 0.5 mol of glucose in a total volume of 2 L?

options.text: Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent; the molarity is 0.25 M
Grams of solute per liter of solution; the molarity is 0.25 M
Moles of solute per liter of solution; the molarity is 0.25 M
Moles of solute per liter of solution; the molarity is 4 M

explanation:
Molarity (M) is moles of solute divided by liters of final solution, so 0.5 mol / 2 L = 0.25 M. Choice A gives the definition of molality (mol solute per kg solvent), a distinct unit used for colligative-property work; choice D applies the right definition but inverts the division (2 / 0.5). Molarity is referenced to the finished solution volume rather than the volume of solvent added, because dissolving a solute changes the final volume of the mixture.

ELI-10: Molarity answers one question: how many moles of solute sit in each liter of the finished liquid? Two details carry all the weight. First, the numerator is moles, not grams, so a mass must be converted before you can use it. Second, the denominator is the volume after mixing, not the volume of water you started with. Here, 0.5 mol spread over 2 L means each liter holds only a quarter of a mole, so the value is 0.25 M. If you ever get a number larger than the moles you started with, check that you did not divide backwards.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Percent mass/volume (% w/v) is a concentration unit used frequently in health science laboratories. Which description matches this unit, and how much solute is in 1000 mL of a 0.9% w/v solution?

options.text: Grams of solute per 100 g of solution; 9 g of solute
Grams of solute per 100 mL of solution; 9 g of solute
Grams of solute per liter of solution; 0.9 g of solute
Milligrams of solute per 100 mL of solution; 9 mg of solute

explanation:
Percent mass/volume is defined as grams of solute per 100 mL of solution, so 0.9% w/v supplies 0.9 g per 100 mL, and 1000 mL contains 0.9 g x 10 = 9 g. Choice A describes percent by mass (% w/w), which uses 100 g of solution rather than 100 mL, and choice D misassigns the mass unit as milligrams. Because laboratory and clinical fluids are measured out by volume rather than weighed, % w/v is the practical labeling unit for them.

ELI-10: Percent means per hundred, and the w/v version pins that hundred to 100 mL of finished solution while the solute is counted in grams. So 0.9% w/v translates to 0.9 g in every 100 mL. One liter is ten of those 100 mL portions, giving ten helpings of 0.9 g, or 9 g total. The mismatch between grams on top and milliliters on the bottom is deliberate and is the single thing that separates % w/v from % w/w, which weighs both parts.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A student adds pure water to 50 mL of a 2 M solution until the total volume is 250 mL. What happens to the amount of solute and the concentration, and what is the new molarity?

options.text: Moles of solute decrease and concentration decreases; the new molarity is 0.4 M
Moles of solute are unchanged and concentration decreases; the new molarity is 0.4 M
Moles of solute are unchanged and concentration is unchanged; the new molarity is 2 M
Moles of solute are unchanged and concentration decreases; the new molarity is 10 M

explanation:
Dilution adds solvent only, so the number of moles of solute is conserved while the volume rises, which lowers the concentration. Applying M1V1 = M2V2 gives M2 = (2 M)(50 mL) / 250 mL = 0.4 M. Choice D pairs the correct concept with the inverted ratio (2 x 250 / 50), and choice A misstates conservation of solute. The constancy of moles is precisely what makes the dilution equation valid, since M1V1 and M2V2 are both expressions for the same quantity of solute.

ELI-10: Adding water changes only the denominator of the concentration ratio. The solute particles already in the flask are not created or destroyed; you simply give them more room, so the number per liter falls. Check the direction before you trust the arithmetic: the volume went from 50 mL to 250 mL, five times larger, so the concentration must be one-fifth of 2 M, which is 0.4 M. A diluted solution that came out more concentrated than the original is always a signal that the ratio was flipped.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: The solubility of a salt is 36 g per 100 mL of water at 20 degrees C. A student stirs 90 g of this salt into 250 mL of water at 20 degrees C until no more dissolves. Which description of the resulting solution is accurate?

options.text: Supersaturated, because the 90 g of dissolved salt exceeds the 36 g in the solubility value
Unsaturated, because additional salt would still dissolve if the mixture were stirred longer
Supersaturated, because the mixture was stirred until no further solid would dissolve
Saturated, because 250 mL of water dissolves exactly 90 g at this temperature

explanation:
Solubility is a ratio that scales with the quantity of solvent: (36 g / 100 mL) x 250 mL = 90 g, so this solution contains exactly the maximum dissolvable amount and is saturated with no excess solid present. Choices A and C confuse saturated with supersaturated; a supersaturated solution holds more solute than the equilibrium value and must be produced indirectly, typically by saturating at a higher temperature and cooling slowly without disturbance. Stirring longer cannot exceed the equilibrium limit, so choice B misattributes an equilibrium ceiling to slow kinetics.

ELI-10: The number 36 is meaningless without the phrase per 100 mL attached to it, so never compare 90 g to 36 g directly. Scale the ratio to the solvent you actually have: 250 mL is 2.5 times 100 mL, so the ceiling is 2.5 x 36 = 90 g. Adding exactly the ceiling amount gives a saturated solution, meaning it holds the maximum at that temperature and any further solid would sit undissolved. Supersaturated is a different, unstable state produced by a temperature trick, not by stirring harder or waiting longer.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A dissolved gas has a solubility of 0.04 g/L in water when the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid is 1 atm at constant temperature. Which change would most likely occur if the partial pressure is tripled to 3 atm?

options.text: Solubility falls to about 0.013 g/L, because added pressure drives gas out of solution
Solubility rises to about 0.12 g/L, because greater pressure raises the temperature of the water
Solubility remains 0.04 g/L, because pressure changes affect only solid and liquid solutes
Solubility rises to about 0.12 g/L, because gas solubility is directly proportional to partial pressure

explanation:
Henry's law states that at constant temperature the solubility of a gas is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid, so tripling the pressure triples the solubility: 0.04 g/L x 3 = 0.12 g/L. Choice B reaches the right value through a false mechanism, since the problem holds temperature constant and, in any case, a temperature increase decreases gas solubility. This proportionality explains why the amount of dissolved gas in a liquid changes with the pressure of the gas phase in contact with it.

ELI-10: Dissolved gas sits in a balance: molecules leave the liquid as fast as they enter it. Raising the partial pressure above the surface increases how often molecules strike and enter, so the balance shifts and more gas stays dissolved until equilibrium is restored. Triple the pressure and you triple the dissolved amount, so 0.04 g/L becomes 0.12 g/L. Temperature pushes the opposite way for gases, which is why a warm carbonated drink loses its dissolved gas much faster than a cold one.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Which comparison of a 0.1 M sodium chloride solution and a 0.1 M glucose solution is accurate with respect to dissolved particle concentration?

options.text: The NaCl solution is about 0.2 osmol/L because NaCl dissociates into two ions, while glucose stays as one particle
The glucose solution is about 0.2 osmol/L because each glucose molecule splits into two particles in water
Both are about 0.2 osmol/L because molarity already accounts for dissociation of the solute
Both are about 0.1 osmol/L because equal molarity means equal numbers of dissolved particles

explanation:
Sodium chloride is a strong electrolyte that dissociates essentially completely into Na+ and Cl-, so each mole yields approximately 2 osmoles and 0.1 M x 2 = 0.2 osmol/L. Glucose is a nonelectrolyte that dissolves as intact molecules, giving 0.1 osmol/L. Osmolarity rather than molarity governs osmotic pressure and the direction of water movement across a semipermeable membrane, which is why two equimolar solutions can behave very differently.

ELI-10: Molarity counts formula units before they dissolve; osmolarity counts the independent particles that exist afterward. Glucose dissolves intact, so one mole in gives one osmole of particles. NaCl separates into a sodium ion and a chloride ion, so one mole in gives about two osmoles. That is why the salt solution reaches 0.2 osmol/L at the same 0.1 M label. Osmosis responds to the number of dissolved particles rather than their identity or size, so the particle count is the figure that predicts water movement.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A student must prepare 500 mL of a 0.2 M aqueous solution of a compound with a molar mass of 58.5 g/mol for a laboratory exercise. What mass of the compound is required?

options.text: 5.85 g, found by multiplying molarity by volume in liters and then by molar mass
0.1 g, found by multiplying molarity by the volume in liters only
29.25 g, found by multiplying molar mass by the volume in liters and omitting the molarity
11.7 g, found by multiplying molarity by molar mass and by 1 L

explanation:
Moles required = M x V(L) = 0.2 mol/L x 0.5 L = 0.1 mol, and mass = moles x molar mass = 0.1 mol x 58.5 g/mol = 5.85 g. Choice D is the classic error of leaving the volume as 500 mL and effectively treating it as 1 L, which doubles the result; choice B stops after the mole step and mislabels moles as grams; choice C multiplies the molar mass by the 0.5 L volume but drops the 0.2 mol/L factor entirely. Volume must be converted to liters before molarity is applied, because molarity is defined per liter of solution.

ELI-10: Split the problem at the mole. Step one converts concentration and volume into an amount: 0.2 mol/L x 0.5 L = 0.1 mol. Step two converts that amount into something weighable using molar mass as the exchange rate: 0.1 mol x 58.5 g/mol = 5.85 g. Watch the units cancel and the path is obvious, because L cancels in the first step and mol cancels in the second. The usual failure is entering 500 instead of 0.5, so convert milliliters to liters before anything else touches the calculator.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Using a 5 M stock solution, a technician needs to prepare 250 mL of a 0.4 M working solution for a teaching laboratory. What volume of stock solution should be measured out, and how should it be handled afterward?

options.text: 50 mL of stock, then add solvent until the total volume reaches 250 mL
20 mL of stock, then add solvent until the total volume reaches 250 mL
20 mL of stock, then add exactly 250 mL of solvent to that portion
125 mL of stock, then add solvent until the total volume reaches 250 mL

explanation:
Rearranging M1V1 = M2V2 gives V1 = (0.4 M x 250 mL) / 5 M = 20 mL of stock. That aliquot is then brought up to a final total volume of 250 mL rather than having 250 mL of solvent added to it, which would produce 270 mL and a concentration of about 0.37 M. Distinguishing dilute to a final volume from add this volume of solvent is a core laboratory technique point, and it is why volumetric flasks are filled to a calibration mark.

ELI-10: Work from the solute the final solution must contain: 0.4 mol/L x 0.25 L = 0.1 mol. The stock carries 5 mol in every liter, so 0.1 mol occupies 0.1/5 = 0.02 L, which is 20 mL. Transfer that 20 mL to the flask and add solvent until the meniscus reaches the 250 mL mark. Filling to a mark is not the same instruction as adding 250 mL, since the second approach overshoots the target volume and leaves the solution slightly too dilute.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A laboratory water sample used in a teaching exercise contains 0.012 g of a dissolved mineral in 4 kg of solution. Expressed as parts per million by mass, what is the concentration?

options.text: 12 ppm, taking the solute mass expressed in milligrams as the ppm value
3000 ppm, using the solution mass in kilograms rather than converting it to grams
3 ppm, dividing the solute mass by the solution mass in grams and multiplying by one million
0.003 ppm, dividing the two masses in grams and multiplying by one thousand

explanation:
Parts per million by mass is (mass of solute / mass of solution) x 10^6 with both masses in the same unit: (0.012 g / 4000 g) x 10^6 = 3 ppm. Equivalently, 1 ppm by mass equals 1 mg per kg, and 12 mg / 4 kg = 3 mg/kg = 3 ppm. Choice B fails to convert 4 kg to 4000 g, and choice D applies the parts-per-thousand factor instead of parts per million. Trace concentrations are reported this way because expressing them as a percent would require awkwardly small decimals.

ELI-10: Parts per million is just a mass ratio rescaled so small numbers become readable. First put both masses in the same unit: 0.012 g of mineral in 4000 g of solution. The raw ratio is 0.000003, which is hard to read, so multiply by one million to get 3 ppm. A useful shortcut for dilute aqueous samples is that 1 ppm equals 1 mg of solute per kg of solution, so 12 mg spread through 4 kg gives 3 mg per kg, the same 3 ppm. Forgetting the kilogram-to-gram conversion inflates the answer by a factor of one thousand.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: In a laboratory exercise, 100 mL of 0.2 M potassium chloride is combined with 300 mL of 0.6 M potassium chloride, and the mixture is stirred. Assuming the volumes are additive, what is the resulting concentration?

options.text: The two concentrations are averaged without weighting and the concentration becomes 0.4 M
The concentrations add directly and the concentration becomes 0.8 M, above both starting values
The moles from each portion add and the concentration becomes 0.5 M, between the two starting values
The concentration stays 0.6 M because the more concentrated portion sets the final value

explanation:
Total moles = (0.1 L)(0.2 mol/L) + (0.3 L)(0.6 mol/L) = 0.02 + 0.18 = 0.2 mol, and total volume = 0.4 L, giving 0.2 mol / 0.4 L = 0.5 M. Choice A is the common error of averaging 0.2 and 0.6 while ignoring that three times as much of the concentrated solution was used. Because no solute is added or removed, the result must lie between the two starting concentrations and be weighted toward the one contributing the larger volume.

ELI-10: Mixing solutions is a bookkeeping problem: total the solute, total the volume, then divide. The 100 mL portion contributes 0.02 mol and the 300 mL portion contributes 0.18 mol, for 0.2 mol in a combined 0.4 L, which is 0.5 M. Use the answer's position as a check. It must land between 0.2 M and 0.6 M, and it should sit near 0.6 M because three-quarters of the liquid came from the stronger solution. An unweighted average of 0.4 M would ignore that imbalance, and any value outside the 0.2 to 0.6 range is impossible.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A textbook reports a glucose concentration of 90 mg/dL and asks students to express it in mmol/L, given that the molar mass of glucose is 180 g/mol. Which sequence of conversions and result is correct?

options.text: Multiply 90 by 10 to convert dL to L, then divide by 180 to get 5 mmol/L
Multiply 90 by 180 and divide by 1000 to get 16.2 mmol/L
Divide 90 by 10 and then by 180 to get 0.05 mmol/L, since 1 L equals 10 dL
Divide 90 by 180 to get 0.5 mmol/L, since milligrams convert directly to millimoles

explanation:
One liter contains 10 deciliters, so 90 mg/dL equals 900 mg/L, and dividing by the molar mass expressed as 180 mg/mmol gives 5 mmol/L. Choice C inverts the deciliter conversion by dividing when it should multiply, which is the most frequent error here; choice D skips the volume conversion entirely. Mass-per-volume and amount-per-volume units describe the same solution, and 180 g/mol is numerically identical to 180 mg/mmol, which is what makes the second step a direct division.

ELI-10: Two independent conversions are needed, so handle them one at a time. Fix the volume first: a deciliter is one-tenth of a liter, so a liter holds ten times as much and 90 mg/dL becomes 900 mg/L. Then fix the amount unit using molar mass, which says 180 mg of glucose is one millimole, giving 900 / 180 = 5 mmol/L. Decide the direction of the volume step by asking whether a liter should contain more or less than a deciliter; the answer is more, so multiply rather than divide.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Which statement best describes a Brønsted–Lowry acid?

options.text: A substance that accepts a proton from another substance
A substance that donates a proton (H+) to another substance
A substance that accepts a pair of electrons to form a bond
A substance that releases H+ only when dissolved in water

explanation:
In the Brønsted–Lowry framework an acid is defined by proton transfer: it donates H+ to a proton acceptor, which is the base. Option A is the Brønsted–Lowry definition of a base, option C is the Lewis definition of an acid (electron-pair acceptor), and option D is the narrower Arrhenius definition, which is restricted to aqueous solution. The proton-transfer definition is the one used in physiology because it also covers species such as HCO3- and NH3 acting as bases in nonaqueous or biological settings.

ELI-10: Acid-base chemistry is bookkeeping for one particle: the proton, H+. In any such reaction one species hands off an H+ and another takes it; the donor is the acid, the acceptor is the base. Defining acids this way is broader than saying 'makes H+ in water,' because it also describes reactions in blood, in gases, and in nonwater solvents. It also means every acid automatically creates a base when it loses its proton.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: The pH scale is logarithmic. A solution at pH 4 has a hydronium ion concentration how many times greater than a solution at pH 7?

options.text: 3 times greater
100 times greater
1,000 times greater
10,000 times greater

explanation:
Because pH = -log[H3O+], each whole pH unit corresponds to a tenfold change in hydronium concentration. A difference of 3 pH units is therefore 10 raised to the third power, a 1,000-fold difference in [H3O+]. Option A treats the scale as linear, the most common misconception about pH; option B corresponds to a 2-unit difference and option D to a 4-unit difference.

ELI-10: pH counts powers of ten, not equal steps. Moving from pH 7 to pH 6 multiplies the hydronium concentration by 10, from 7 to 5 by 100, and from 7 to 4 by 1,000. Concretely, pH 7 is 0.0000001 mol/L and pH 4 is 0.0001 mol/L. That compression is why a change of even a few tenths of a unit in a patient's blood is chemically large.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Normal arterial blood is maintained in the pH range 7.35 to 7.45. Which description of that range is accurate?

options.text: Strongly acidic, far below the neutral point of water
Slightly alkaline, just above the neutral point of water
Strongly alkaline, near the upper end of the pH scale
Exactly neutral, identical to pure water at 25 °C

explanation:
Pure water at 25 °C is neutral at pH 7, so a range centered near 7.4 lies slightly above neutral and is correctly described as slightly alkaline. It is not strongly alkaline; solutions of strong bases occupy pH values near 12 to 14. Recognizing that blood sits only a few tenths of a unit above neutral explains why deviations of even 0.1 unit are reported as clinically meaningful.

ELI-10: On the 0 to 14 scale, 7 marks the point where hydronium and hydroxide are equal. Blood at 7.4 sits just past that point on the basic side, not far out toward the strongly basic end. In concentration terms, 7.4 means about 4 × 10^-8 mol/L hydronium versus 1 × 10^-7 mol/L in neutral water, so blood holds roughly two and a half times less hydronium than plain water. 'Slightly alkaline' is the precise description.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A laboratory solution measured at 25 °C has a pOH of 4.5. What is its pH, and how should the solution be classified?

options.text: pH 4.5; acidic
pH 9.5; basic
pH 9.5; acidic
pH 18.5; basic

explanation:
At 25 °C the ion product of water (Kw = 1 × 10^-14) gives pH + pOH = 14, so a pOH of 4.5 corresponds to a pH of 14 - 4.5 = 9.5. Because 9.5 is above 7, hydroxide exceeds hydronium and the solution is basic. Option D comes from adding rather than subtracting, option A from assuming pH equals pOH, and option C from misclassifying a pH above 7.

ELI-10: pH and pOH are two readings of the same solution, and at 25 °C they always sum to 14. A pOH of 4.5 is low, which means hydroxide is relatively plentiful, so the solution must be basic and its pH must be the complement, 9.5. A quick check: any pOH below 7 forces a pH above 7. That single relationship lets you convert between the two scales without recalculating concentrations.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Which comparison between a strong acid and a weak acid prepared at the same molar concentration is accurate?

options.text: The strong acid has the higher pH because it holds its protons tightly
Both solutions have the same hydronium concentration because molarity sets pH
The weak acid ionizes completely but neutralizes added base more slowly
The strong acid ionizes essentially completely, so it has the lower pH

explanation:
Acid strength describes the extent of ionization, not the amount of acid dissolved. A strong acid such as HCl dissociates essentially completely, releasing far more hydronium per mole than a weak acid such as acetic acid, which establishes an equilibrium with most molecules still undissociated. More hydronium means a lower pH, so at equal molarity the strong acid gives the more acidic solution.

ELI-10: Concentration counts how much acid you added; strength counts what fraction of it actually lets go of its proton. In 0.1 mol/L HCl essentially every molecule releases H+, giving about 0.1 mol/L hydronium and a pH near 1. In 0.1 mol/L acetic acid only about 1 percent releases H+, giving roughly 0.001 mol/L and a pH near 3. Same amount dissolved, about a hundredfold difference in hydronium.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: What is the primary purpose of the bicarbonate buffer system in extracellular fluid?

options.text: To increase the rate at which cells generate carbon dioxide
To excrete metabolic hydrogen ions from the body permanently
To hold extracellular fluid at pH 7, the value of pure water
To resist large shifts in pH when acid or base is added

explanation:
A buffer is a weak acid paired with its conjugate base; added H+ is consumed by the base member and added OH- is consumed by the acid member, so the pH change is blunted rather than eliminated. In extracellular fluid, HCO3- neutralizes added acid while H2CO3 (from dissolved CO2) neutralizes added base. Permanent removal of acid is the job of the lungs and kidneys, not the buffer itself, and buffers hold pH near their working range, which for this system is about 7.4, not 7. Note that this system's apparent pKa is 6.1, which is outside the usual pKa ± 1 window for pH 7.4; it is nonetheless effective in the body because it is an open system, in which the lungs continuously adjust dissolved CO2 (and the kidneys adjust HCO3-) so the acid member is replenished or vented rather than exhausted.

ELI-10: A buffer behaves like a shock absorber for pH. When acid enters, bicarbonate captures the H+ and turns it into carbonic acid, a much weaker acid; when base enters, carbonic acid gives up an H+ to neutralize it. The added particles are not destroyed, only converted into a less disruptive form, so pH moves a little instead of a lot. In a sealed beaker this pair would be a mediocre buffer at 7.4, since its pKa of 6.1 is more than a unit away, but the body keeps it open to the air: breathing sets how much CO2 stays dissolved. Actually clearing that acid load requires exhaling CO2 and renal excretion.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Which example correctly illustrates a neutralization reaction?

options.text: Hydrochloric acid reacting with sodium hydroxide to give NaCl and water
Sodium chloride crystals dissolving in water to give Na+ and Cl- ions
Acetic acid partially ionizing in water to give H3O+ and acetate ions
Zinc metal reacting with oxygen gas to form solid zinc oxide

explanation:
Neutralization is the reaction of an acid with a base to yield a salt and water, driven by H+ combining with OH- to form H2O. HCl + NaOH gives NaCl plus water, the standard example. Option B is dissociation of an already formed salt, option C is ionization of a weak acid (which produces hydronium rather than consuming it), and option D is an oxidation-reduction reaction with no proton transfer.

ELI-10: To spot a neutralization, look for an acid and a base as the two reactants and for water among the products. The essential step is H+ + OH- forming H2O; the leftover cation and anion simply remain in solution as dissolved salt. Dissolving a salt only separates ions that already existed, ionizing a weak acid releases hydronium instead of removing it, and metal oxidation transfers electrons, not protons.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A hypothetical laboratory solution is reported to have a pH of 3. Which value correctly gives its hydronium ion concentration?
explanation:
Because pH = -log[H3O+], the concentration is recovered as [H3O+] = 10^-pH, so a pH of 3 gives 1 × 10^-3 mol/L. Option B is the hydroxide concentration of this same solution, since pOH = 14 - 3 = 11. Options A and C treat the digit 3 as a coefficient rather than as the exponent, a frequent error when converting between pH and concentration.

ELI-10: The pH value is an exponent, so undoing it means raising 10 to the negative of that number. A pH of 3 becomes 10^-3, which is 0.001 mol/L; the leading coefficient is 1, not 3. If the pH had been 3.5, the concentration would fall between 10^-4 and 10^-3, closer to 3 × 10^-4. Whenever a pH is a whole number, the concentration is a 1 sitting in that decimal place: pH 3 gives 0.001 and pH 5 gives 0.00001.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A blood sample's pH is reported as 7.2, compared with a previous value of 7.4 in the same person. Which interpretation of this change is most accurate?

options.text: Hydronium ion concentration rose roughly 1.6-fold
Hydronium ion concentration rose roughly 100-fold
Hydronium ion concentration fell roughly 1.6-fold
Hydronium ion concentration rose by about 0.2 mol/L

explanation:
A fall in pH always corresponds to a rise in hydronium concentration, and the magnitude of that rise is 10 raised to the pH difference: 10^(7.4 - 7.2) = 10^0.2, which is about 1.58. So a 0.2-unit drop represents roughly a 58 percent increase in [H3O+]. Option B would require a 2-unit fall, option C reverses the direction of the relationship, and option D misreads a pH difference as a concentration difference in mol/L.

ELI-10: Two features of pH have to be applied together here: it runs in reverse, so a lower number means more hydronium, and it is logarithmic, so even a fractional change multiplies the concentration. Raising 10 to the 0.2 power gives about 1.6, meaning roughly 60 percent more hydronium than before. In absolute terms the shift is from about 4 × 10^-8 to about 6 × 10^-8 mol/L, tiny numbers whose ratio is what matters physiologically.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Which change would most likely raise the pH of a bicarbonate-buffered solution that is in contact with a gas phase?

options.text: Bubbling additional carbon dioxide gas through the solution
Adding a measured volume of hydrochloric acid solution
Sweeping dissolved carbon dioxide out of the solution
Adding a neutral salt that does not react with water

explanation:
Dissolved CO2 combines with water to form carbonic acid, the acid member of the bicarbonate buffer pair. Removing CO2 shifts the equilibrium CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3- to the left, lowering H+ and raising the bicarbonate-to-acid ratio, so pH increases. Adding CO2 or a strong acid lowers pH, and an unreactive salt leaves the buffer ratio essentially unchanged.

ELI-10: Dissolved carbon dioxide functions as a hidden acid: combine it with water and carbonic acid forms, which then releases H+. Because that whole sequence is an equilibrium, taking CO2 away pulls the reaction backward and consumes H+, so the pH climbs. This is exactly the chemistry behind hyperventilation raising blood pH and hypoventilation lowering it, since ventilation controls how much CO2 stays dissolved.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A hypothetical laboratory buffer must hold a test solution near pH 7.4. Four weak acid/conjugate base pairs are available, with pKa values of 3.75, 4.76, 7.21, and 9.25. Which choice and reasoning are correct?

options.text: The pKa 7.21 pair, because buffering is strongest within about 1 unit of the pKa
The pKa 4.76 pair, because a lower pKa resists added acid more effectively
The pKa 9.25 pair, because the target pH lies on the alkaline side of neutral
The pKa 3.75 pair, because the strongest weak acid provides the most capacity

explanation:
From pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), a buffer holds appreciable amounts of both members only when the target pH is within roughly 1 unit of its pKa; there the ratio stays between about 1:10 and 10:1 and capacity is greatest. A pKa of 7.21 is only 0.19 unit from 7.4, requiring a near-equimolar mixture. The pKa 4.76 and 3.75 pairs would exist almost entirely as conjugate base at pH 7.4, and the pKa 9.25 pair almost entirely as the protonated acid, leaving little of the partner species to absorb an insult in either direction.

ELI-10: A buffer works because both partners are present in usable amounts; whichever one runs out first sets the limit. The pKa is the pH at which the two are equal, and each pH unit away from it tilts the mixture tenfold toward one side. Two units away the minority species is only about 1 percent of the pair, so the buffer is nearly exhausted before it starts. Matching the pKa to the target pH keeps both partners stocked.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: In a model of extracellular fluid, the bicarbonate-to-dissolved-CO2 ratio falls from 20:1 to 10:1 while the pKa remains 6.1. What would happen to the pH?

options.text: It rises from about 7.4 to about 7.7
It stays near 7.4 because the pKa did not change
It falls from about 7.4 to about 7.1
