It falls from about 7.4 to about 6.4

explanation:
Using pH = pKa + log([HCO3-]/[CO2]), the 20:1 ratio gives 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4, while the 10:1 ratio gives 6.1 + 1 = 7.1. Halving the ratio lowers pH by log 2, about 0.3 unit, not a full unit, because the relationship is logarithmic. Option D would require a 2:1 ratio and option A would require the ratio to increase rather than fall.

ELI-10: In the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation only the ratio of the two buffer members, not their absolute amounts, sets the pH once the pKa is fixed. Because the ratio enters as a logarithm, cutting it in half subtracts log 2, which is about 0.3 unit. That is why a pH of 7.1 can arise either from losing bicarbonate or from retaining CO2: both change the same ratio, and 0.3 unit is already a large clinical move.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Which statement best describes what a buffer solution does?

options.text: It slowly returns the pH to exactly its original value after acid is added
It neutralizes all hydrogen ions so the solution becomes chemically neutral
It resists large changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added
It raises the pH of any solution it is added to until the solution becomes basic

explanation:
A buffer blunts, but does not abolish, changes in pH when limited amounts of strong acid or strong base are introduced. It works because it holds an appreciable reservoir of both a proton donor and a proton acceptor, converting strong acids or bases into weak ones. The pH does shift slightly and stays shifted; nothing restores the original value. Buffer capacity is also finite, so once one component is largely consumed the pH moves sharply, which is exactly what happens clinically when body buffers are overwhelmed.

ELI-10: Think of a buffer like the shock absorbers on a car. The bumps in the road are still there, but the ride only jiggles instead of throwing you out of your seat. Add enough acid to blood to use up 2 of its 24 bicarbonates, while breathing keeps dissolved CO2 at about 1.2, and the pH only nudges from 7.4 to about 7.36 rather than crashing, because 6.1 + log(22/1.2) works out to 7.36. Notice the ride does not un-bump itself: the pH stays a little lower. And like shocks, buffers wear out, so enough acid eventually makes the ride rough again.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Which pair of substances could function together as a buffer system?

options.text: A weak acid and its conjugate base
A strong acid and the salt of a different strong acid
A strong acid and a strong base in equal concentration
Two weak acids with widely separated pKa values

explanation:
Buffering requires appreciable amounts of both a weak proton donor (HA) and its conjugate proton acceptor (A-), so that added base is absorbed by HA and added acid is absorbed by A-. Strong acids and strong bases ionize essentially completely, leaving no undissociated reservoir to trade protons with, and mixing them simply produces water and a neutral salt. Two unrelated weak acids are not a conjugate pair and buffer only in separate, non-overlapping pH windows. In plasma the working pair is carbonic acid (as dissolved CO2) and bicarbonate, normally near a 20:1 base-to-acid ratio.

ELI-10: A buffer is like a shop that both buys and sells the same item. The weak acid is the seller of hydrogen ions; the conjugate base is the buyer. With only strong acid, every ion has already been sold off and there is nothing left in stock to trade. In blood, bicarbonate at about 24 mmol/L is the buyer and dissolved CO2 at about 1.2 mmol/L is the seller, so there are roughly 20 buyers for every seller.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: What is the primary buffer system of the extracellular fluid?

options.text: The hemoglobin buffer system of red blood cells
The dihydrogen phosphate/hydrogen phosphate system
The bicarbonate/carbonic acid system
The ammonia/ammonium system of the renal tubule

explanation:
Bicarbonate paired with carbonic acid and its volatile partner, dissolved CO2, dominates extracellular buffering because bicarbonate is present at high concentration (about 24 mmol/L) and because both members of the pair are under active physiologic control. Applying the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation with a pKa of 6.1 and a 20:1 ratio gives 6.1 + log 20, and log 20 is about 1.3, so pH is about 7.4. Phosphate buffers matter mainly inside cells and in urine, hemoglobin buffers within erythrocytes, and the ammonia/ammonium pair operates in tubular fluid rather than plasma.

ELI-10: Blood has several buffer teams, but bicarbonate is the star because there is a lot of it and the body can deliberately change how much there is. A buffer pair is perfectly balanced, half acid and half base, at its pKa, which for this pair is 6.1. Blood is not balanced that way: it keeps about 20 bicarbonates for every dissolved CO2, and that lopsided ratio adds about 1.3 to the pKa. So 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4, right where blood likes to sit.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: When a strong acid enters the bloodstream, which sequence of events describes how the bicarbonate buffer handles it?

options.text: Bicarbonate binds sodium, and the resulting salt is excreted unchanged by the kidney
Carbonic acid donates a proton to the strong acid, converting it into a weaker acid
Bicarbonate is converted directly into carbonate, which precipitates out of the plasma
Bicarbonate accepts the proton to form carbonic acid, which becomes CO2 and is exhaled

explanation:
Bicarbonate is the proton acceptor: H+ plus HCO3- yields H2CO3, which carbonic anhydrase rapidly dehydrates to CO2 and water, and ventilation eliminates the CO2. Because the acid product is physically removed rather than accumulating, the system is described as open, which greatly increases its effectiveness. The cost is consumption of the bicarbonate pool, so a hypothetical acid load of 6 mEq/L titrates a starting bicarbonate of 24 mEq/L down to about 18 mEq/L, which is why a falling bicarbonate is the laboratory signature of metabolic acidosis.

ELI-10: Picture bicarbonate as a sponge that soaks up loose hydrogen ions. Once it soaks one up it becomes carbonic acid, which falls apart almost instantly into water and carbon dioxide gas, and you breathe the gas out. That is why the acid genuinely leaves the body instead of piling up in the blood. The catch is that every sponge used is a sponge gone: start with 24 and spend 6, and only 18 remain for the next acid load.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Which comparison of respiratory and renal regulation of acid-base balance is accurate?

options.text: The respiratory system adjusts bicarbonate while the kidneys adjust carbon dioxide
The respiratory response begins within minutes, while full renal compensation takes days
Both systems reach their maximal effect at about the same rate after an acid load
The kidneys respond first because they filter the entire plasma volume many times daily

explanation:
Chemoreceptor-driven changes in ventilation alter PaCO2 within minutes, making the lungs the rapid responder, whereas the kidneys adjust bicarbonate reabsorption and net acid excretion over roughly one to three days. The division of labor also runs the opposite way from option A: the lungs control the volatile acid component (CO2) and the kidneys control the metabolic component (HCO3-). Comparing about 15 minutes (0.25 hour) with about 72 hours shows the renal route is roughly 288 times slower, so the two systems cannot peak together.

ELI-10: Your lungs are the emergency brake and your kidneys are the repair crew. Within a minute or two of an acid load you can breathe faster and blow off carbon dioxide, which is fast but limited. The kidneys fix the problem more completely by excreting acid and generating new bicarbonate, but they need days to do it. Put the two on the same clock: 72 hours against a quarter of an hour is about 288 times longer.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: Which change would most likely lower blood pH in a person whose kidneys and bicarbonate stores are normal?

options.text: An increase in alveolar ventilation that lowers PaCO2
An increase in plasma bicarbonate concentration
A decrease in alveolar ventilation that raises PaCO2
A rise in both bicarbonate and dissolved CO2 that leaves their ratio unchanged

explanation:
Retained CO2 drives the hydration equilibrium toward carbonic acid and then toward H+ and HCO3-, raising hydrogen ion concentration and lowering pH, which defines respiratory acidosis. CO2 is the acid term in the denominator of the Henderson-Hasselbalch ratio, so raising it lowers pH, while options A and B move that ratio the other way and raise pH. Option D changes nothing, because pH depends on the ratio and not on either concentration alone. Applying the standard acute rule of a 0.08 pH fall per 10 mm Hg rise, a PaCO2 going from 40 to 60 mm Hg predicts a pH near 7.24.

ELI-10: Carbon dioxide is essentially acid in gas form: dissolve it in water and carbonic acid appears. Breathe too slowly and CO2 backs up like traffic, so the blood turns more acidic. A useful bedside rule is that each 10 mm Hg of acute CO2 buildup drops pH about 0.08. Going from 40 to 60 is two steps, so 7.4 minus 0.16 lands near 7.24. And if bicarbonate and CO2 both rise together, the ratio is unchanged, so the pH does not move at all.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A buffer has its greatest capacity to resist pH change under which condition?

options.text: When the weak acid has been nearly completely titrated
When the conjugate base greatly exceeds the weak acid
When the solution pH is at least two units above the pKa
When the concentrations of weak acid and conjugate base are equal

explanation:
Buffer capacity peaks when [A-] equals [HA], because equal reservoirs absorb added acid and added base equally well. That condition corresponds to pH equal to pKa, since log 1 is 0 in the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation. For the phosphate pair with a physiologic pKa near 6.8, maximal buffering therefore occurs at pH 6.8, conveniently close to intracellular pH. Each of the other three conditions describes a ratio far from 1:1: nearly complete titration of the weak acid leaves almost no HA to neutralize added base, a large excess of conjugate base leaves almost no HA for the same reason, and a pH two or more units above the pKa means the base-to-acid ratio is at least 100:1. In every one of those cases one reservoir is nearly exhausted and pH becomes highly sensitive to further additions; useful buffering is generally limited to about one pH unit on either side of the pKa.

ELI-10: Picture a seesaw with sandbags on both ends. With equal loads, removing one bag from either side barely tilts it. If one end is nearly empty, a single bag slams it down. Equal amounts of acid and base is the balanced seesaw, and the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation tells you where that happens: when the two are equal their ratio is 1, the logarithm of 1 is 0, so the pH sits exactly at the pKa. For phosphate that balance point is pH 6.8.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: In a hypothetical teaching sample the dissolved CO2 is 1.2 mmol/L and the pH is 7.4. Using pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3-]/[CO2]) and given that log 20 equals 1.3, what bicarbonate concentration must the sample contain?

options.text: 24 mmol/L
20 mmol/L
12 mmol/L
26 mmol/L

explanation:
Rearranging the equation, pH minus pKa equals 7.4 minus 6.1, or 1.3, and the ratio whose logarithm is 1.3 is 20. The bicarbonate concentration is therefore 20 times the dissolved CO2, or 20 multiplied by 1.2, which equals 24 mmol/L, matching the normal plasma value. Choosing 20 mmol/L mistakes the ratio itself for a concentration, and 12 mmol/L corresponds to a ratio of only 10, which would give pH 7.1. The exercise reinforces that pH is fixed by the ratio, so a 48:2.4 mmol/L pair would yield the same 7.4.

ELI-10: Work the equation backward. The pH sits 1.3 units above the pKa of 6.1, and 1.3 is the logarithm of 20, so bicarbonate must outnumber dissolved CO2 twentyfold. Multiply the CO2 you were given by that ratio: 20 times 1.2 equals 24 mmol/L, the familiar normal bicarbonate. Do not confuse the ratio with the amount; 20 is how many times bigger one is than the other, not the concentration itself.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A teaching data set shows pH 7.3, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, sodium 140 mEq/L, chloride 110 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 15 mEq/L. Which interpretation fits these values?

options.text: Respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
Metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory compensation
Respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation
Metabolic alkalosis with partial respiratory compensation

explanation:
The pH is acidemic and the bicarbonate is low, so the primary disturbance is metabolic acidosis; the low PaCO2 reflects compensatory hyperventilation, since a compensating system always moves in the direction that opposes the primary problem and never overshoots normal. Winter's formula predicts an expected PaCO2 of 1.5 times 15 plus 8, or about 30.5 mm Hg, so the respiratory response is appropriate in magnitude yet the pH remains below 7.35, which is why compensation is called partial rather than complete. The anion gap, 140 minus the sum of 110 and 15, equals 15 mEq/L, mildly above the usual 8 to 12 mEq/L range and suggesting an added-acid cause.

ELI-10: Read the pH first: 7.3 is on the acid side. Then ask who caused it. Bicarbonate is low, and bicarbonate is the metabolic number, so the metabolic side is the culprit. The low CO2 is the lungs helping by blowing off acid gas; they are helping about as hard as expected, yet the pH is still under 7.35, so the fix is incomplete. Finally check the anion gap: 140 minus (110 + 15) is 15, a bit above the usual 8 to 12, hinting that an unmeasured acid is in play.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: A student prepares a hypothetical laboratory acetate buffer containing equal concentrations of acetic acid and acetate, so its pH equals the pKa of 4.76. Which change would produce a buffer with a pH above the pKa?

options.text: Diluting the buffer with an equal volume of pure water
Adding more of the weak acid so it exceeds the conjugate base
Adding a small volume of a strong acid to the finished buffer
Adding conjugate base until it is twice the weak acid concentration

explanation:
Henderson-Hasselbalch gives pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]), so any ratio greater than 1 produces a positive logarithm and a pH above the pKa. With [A-] at 0.2 mol/L and [HA] at 0.1 mol/L the ratio is 2, log 2 is about 0.3, and the pH is about 5.06. Adding weak acid or adding strong acid shifts the ratio below 1 and lowers pH instead. Equal-volume dilution reduces both concentrations by the same factor, leaving the ratio and therefore the pH essentially unchanged, although it does reduce total buffer capacity.

ELI-10: Think of the pKa as home base, with the ratio deciding which way you drift. Add more base and pH rises; add more acid and pH falls. Doubling the base makes the ratio 2, and log 2 is about 0.3, so you land three tenths of a unit above home base: 4.76 + 0.3 = 5.06. Dilution is the interesting case. Watering down soup halves every ingredient but keeps the recipe's proportions, so the flavor, like the pH, stays the same, even though there is less of it to go around.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: The carbonic acid/bicarbonate pKa of 6.1 is well below the normal plasma pH of 7.4, yet this pair is still the body's most important extracellular buffer. What best explains this?

options.text: Its pKa shifts upward to 7.4 at body temperature, placing it at maximal capacity
It is an open system in which the lungs and kidneys independently regulate CO2 and bicarbonate
Carbonic acid is a strong acid, so it neutralizes added base faster than weak buffers do
Bicarbonate is more concentrated in plasma than chloride and all other anions

explanation:
In a sealed beaker, a buffer operating 1.3 pH units above its pKa would be poor, because that requires a base-to-acid ratio of about 20 to 1 and leaves very little proton donor in reserve. Physiologically, ventilation continuously removes CO2 while the kidneys reclaim and regenerate bicarbonate, so numerator and denominator are separately and continuously adjustable rather than fixed. The alternatives are false as written: the pKa does not migrate to 7.4, chloride at about 100 mEq/L exceeds bicarbonate at about 24 mEq/L, and carbonic acid is a weak acid.

ELI-10: On paper this looks like a badly chosen buffer, since it is strongest at pH 6.1 while blood sits at 7.4. That 1.3-unit gap forces bicarbonate to outnumber dissolved CO2 by roughly 20 to 1, because 10 raised to the 1.3 power is about 19.95. What rescues it is that the body cheats. The lungs vent CO2 out of the bottom of the fraction and the kidneys make fresh bicarbonate at the top, so both dials are under active control. A buffer with two adjustable dials beats a fixed one with a better starting number.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: chemistry-2
question: In a hypothetical teaching case, prolonged loss of gastric hydrochloric acid leaves bicarbonate at 36 mmol/L and PaCO2 at 48 mm Hg. Using dissolved CO2 = 0.03 x PaCO2, pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3-]/[CO2]), and log 25 = 1.4, what are the calculated pH and the interpretation?

options.text: About 7.5, indicating metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
About 7.5, indicating respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation
About 7.3, indicating metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
About 7.3, indicating respiratory acidosis with renal compensation

explanation:
Dissolved CO2 equals 0.03 multiplied by 48, or 1.44 mmol/L, so the ratio is 36 divided by 1.44, which is 25; adding log 25, about 1.4, to the pKa of 6.1 gives a pH near 7.5. Losing hydrochloric acid strips H+ from the body and leaves bicarbonate in excess, so the primary disorder is metabolic alkalosis, identified by the high bicarbonate accompanying an alkalemic pH. The elevated PaCO2 is compensatory hypoventilation retaining acidic CO2, which blunts the alkalemia without normalizing the pH; a primary respiratory alkalosis would instead show a low PaCO2.

ELI-10: Vomiting stomach acid is like pouring acid down the drain, and what remains in the blood is left too basic. First put both numbers in the same units: 0.03 times 48 gives 1.44 mmol/L of dissolved CO2. Now compare: 36 to 1.44 is a ratio of 25, higher than the usual 20, so the base side is winning. Log 25 is about 1.4, so 6.1 + 1.4 = 7.5. The body answers by breathing more slowly to hold acidic CO2 in, which is exactly why the PaCO2 drifted up to 48 instead of down.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept A diploid pea plant carries two alleles at the flower color locus. According to Mendel's law of segregation, what happens to these two alleles during gamete formation?

options.text: The two alleles blend into a single mixed allele before entering a gamete
The two alleles separate so that each gamete receives exactly one of them
Alleles at different loci enter gametes independently of one another
Both alleles are packaged together into the same gamete

explanation: The law of segregation states that the two alleles carried at a locus are separated during gamete formation so each gamete receives one allele, which is why a heterozygote produces the two gamete types in equal numbers. A describes blending inheritance, the idea Mendel's counts ruled out. C states the law of independent assortment, which governs alleles at different loci. D describes the opposite of segregation, with both alleles entering the same gamete.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept Mendel crossed pea plants that differed at two loci and found that the allele combinations in the offspring were shuffled freely. Which statement describes the law of independent assortment?

options.text: Alleles at different loci are transmitted to offspring independently of one another
The two alleles at a single locus separate during gamete formation
The phenotype of a heterozygote is an exact blend of the two parental phenotypes
Alleles at loci on the same chromosome are always transmitted together

explanation: Independent assortment holds that alleles at different loci are distributed to gametes independently, so a dihybrid produces the four gamete classes in equal proportions. B states the law of segregation, which concerns a single locus. C is blending inheritance, which Mendel's results ruled out. D describes complete linkage, which is broken whenever crossing over separates the loci.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept In 1910, Thomas Hunt Morgan found a white eyed male fly among the red eyed Drosophila in his laboratory. What key conclusion came from this experiment?

options.text: The white eye trait is carried on the Y chromosome only
Eye color in Drosophila is inherited through the cytoplasm
The white eye allele is X linked, establishing that genes are carried on chromosomes
White eye is a dominant autosomal trait

explanation: In the decisive crosses, a white eyed male with genotype *X^w Y* passed the mutant allele to daughters who were red eyed carriers, and their sons showed white eyes again, a pattern that places the gene on the X chromosome and made this the first trait tied to a specific chromosome. A fails because the allele moved through daughters, who never receive a Y chromosome. B describes cytoplasmic inheritance, which would pass through the egg to all offspring. D is ruled out because the trait is recessive and appears almost exclusively in males.

question: **Type:** application A researcher wants to map the positions of many genes along chromosomes by counting recombinant offspring in many crosses. Which model organism is the best first choice for this work?

Arabidopsis thaliana, because its genome is small
Drosophila melanogaster, because its short generation time and large progeny counts make recombination easy to score

explanation: Linkage mapping requires many offspring from many controlled crosses, and Drosophila melanogaster delivers both with a generation time of about two weeks, which is why Morgan's school used it to build the first linkage maps. Escherichia coli is a workhorse for molecular genetics, but bacterial recombination is not scored by counting offspring of controlled crosses. Xenopus laevis is chosen for its large oocytes and cell cycle biochemistry. Arabidopsis thaliana is chosen for plant development and flowering research.

question: **Type:** calculation A pea plant is heterozygous at two unlinked loci with genotype *AaBb*. What proportion of the gametes produced by this plant is expected to carry both recessive alleles, a and b?
explanation: Each locus segregates independently, so the probability that a gamete carries a is 1/2 and the probability that it carries b is 1/2, and the product rule gives 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4. A keeps only one of the two 1/2 events. B is not any gamete class and confuses gamete proportions with genotypic classes. D is the fraction of offspring homozygous recessive at both loci from an *AaBb* x *AaBb* cross, 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16, not a gamete frequency.

question: **Type:** cross-problem Two pea plants heterozygous for flower color with genotype *Aa* x *Aa* are crossed, with complete dominance of A over a and normal segregation at this single locus. What phenotypic ratio is expected among the offspring?

1:2:1 genotypic classes

explanation: Each parent makes A and a gametes with probability 1/2 each, so the offspring genotypes are 1 *AA* : 2 *Aa* : 1 *aa*, which sum to 4, and with complete dominance the *AA* and *Aa* classes show the dominant phenotype, giving a 3:1 phenotypic ratio (sums to 4). B gives the 1:2:1 genotypic ratio (sums to 4) rather than the phenotypic ratio that was asked. C is the two locus 9:3:3:1 ratio (sums to 16) expected from a dihybrid cross. D is the 1:1 ratio (sums to 2) seen in a testcross of a heterozygote.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** ethics The history of genetics includes the eugenics movement, which misused heredity claims to justify forced sterilization, and many modern geneticists say the field needs safeguards because of that history. Which statement best reflects the ethical debate?

options.text: The past misuse of genetics proves that genetic research should be stopped entirely
The benefits of genetics are so great that the history of misuse has no relevance to current practice
Some argue that this history requires stronger oversight of genetic research, while others warn that excessive restrictions could slow beneficial research
Decisions about genetic research should be made only by government agencies, never by individual scientists

explanation: The eugenics movement shows that heredity claims can be used to harm people, so one position holds that genetic research needs stronger ethics oversight and consent safeguards, while the competing position holds that overcorrection could slow research with real medical benefit. C states both positions fairly. A and B are one sided extremes that ignore either the benefits or the history. D proposes a decision structure that is not supported by either side of the debate.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** application Mendel selected the garden pea for his breeding experiments in the 1860s. Which combination of features made the pea a good experimental model for discovering the laws of inheritance?

options.text: Its genome is small and was among the first plant genomes sequenced
It is a mammal whose physiology closely matches human physiology
Its oocytes are large enough to be injected with DNA
It is easy to self pollinate or cross, produces many offspring, and has clearly contrasting traits

explanation: The pea has clearly contrasting traits such as round versus wrinkled seeds, can be self fertilized or crossed by hand, and produces many offspring in a single season, which let Mendel count large progeny classes and infer the laws of segregation and independent assortment. A describes modern genome sequencing, which played no role in Mendel's experiments. B matches the mouse as a mammalian model. C describes Xenopus laevis, used for oocyte injection.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept A cell in the G1 phase sustains DNA damage, and the DNA damage checkpoint responds by stopping the cell cycle. Which protein is responsible for this arrest?

options.text: cyclin dependent kinase 2
cyclin dependent kinase 1
retinoblastoma protein
p53 tumor suppressor

explanation: The p53 tumor suppressor, encoded by *TP53*, is the effector of the DNA damage response: it triggers cell cycle arrest so the cell can repair the damage or undergo apoptosis. Cyclin dependent kinase 2 (encoded by *CDK2*) drives entry into S phase and cyclin dependent kinase 1 (encoded by *CDK1*) drives entry into mitosis, so neither mediates arrest. The retinoblastoma protein (encoded by *RB1*) enforces the G1 restriction point in undamaged cells, but the damage-triggered arrest tested here runs through p53.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** application A human spermatocyte with 46 chromosomes (2n = 46) completes meiosis I without any errors. What is the chromosome content of each of the two daughter cells produced at the end of meiosis I?

options.text: 46 chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids
46 chromosomes, each with one chromatid
23 chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids
23 chromosomes, each with one chromatid

explanation: Meiosis I is the reductional division: homologous chromosomes separate, so the chromosome number is cut in half, from 46 to 23 chromosomes per daughter cell. Sister chromatids remain joined through meiosis I, so each of the 23 chromosomes still carries two chromatids. Option D describes the post-meiosis II products, and options A and B keep the diploid count instead of halving it.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** application During meiosis II in a human testis, the sister chromatids of one chromosome fail to separate while all other chromosomes behave normally. If a sperm that is aneuploid as a result of this error fertilizes a normal egg, which chromosome numbers are possible in the resulting zygote?
explanation: Sister chromatids separate in meiosis II, so their failure to separate sends both copies into one sperm and none into another: one sperm carries n + 1 = 24 chromosomes and one carries n - 1 = 22. Fertilizing a normal egg with 23 chromosomes gives 24 + 23 = 47 or 22 + 23 = 45, and both outcomes are possible depending on which aneuploid sperm fuses. Option D keeps only the 47 outcome, option A assumes the error is corrected, and option C double-counts the mis-segregated chromosome.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept During mitosis, replicated chromosomes are pulled to opposite poles of the cell. Which structure of the chromosome is the site where spindle microtubules attach?

options.text: the centromere
the telomere
the origin of replication
the nucleosome

explanation: The centromere is the constricted region where the sister chromatids of a replicated chromosome are held together and where the kinetochore assembles, providing the site of spindle microtubule attachment that pulls the chromosome apart. The telomere caps the chromosome ends and protects them from degradation, the origin of replication is where DNA synthesis starts, and the nucleosome is a DNA packaging unit. Mixing the centromere with the telomere is the classic error here.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** application A karyotype prepared from a patient's blood sample shows 47 chromosomes, including two X chromosomes and one Y chromosome. Which condition is indicated by this karyotype?

options.text: Down syndrome (trisomy 21)
Turner syndrome (45,X)
Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)
Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18)

explanation: A 47,XXY karyotype is the finding in Klinefelter syndrome, a sex chromosome aneuploidy listed as an extra X chromosome. Down syndrome and Edwards syndrome are autosome trisomies (trisomy 21 and trisomy 18) with 47 chromosomes as well, but their karyotypes show an extra autosome, not an XXY sex chromosome constitution. Turner syndrome has only 45 chromosomes with a single X, so it is excluded by the count.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** calculation A human liver cell contains 46 chromosomes in G1. How many chromosomes does each daughter cell contain immediately after this cell completes mitosis and cytokinesis?
explanation: S phase replicates each of the 46 chromosomes into a pair of sister chromatids, giving 92 chromatids, and mitotic anaphase splits every pair equally, so each daughter cell receives 92/2 = 46 chromosomes. Mitosis is equational: the chromosome number is preserved, not halved and not doubled. Option B applies meiotic halving, option C counts chromatids as chromosomes, and option D inserts a nondisjunction error that a normal mitosis does not make.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** application Each round of DNA replication shortens the ends of linear chromosomes, and the enzyme telomerase counteracts this loss in cells that need many divisions. Which molecule provides the RNA template used by telomerase to extend telomeres?

options.text: the *TERT* gene product, telomerase reverse transcriptase
the *BRCA1* protein
the *DNMT1* protein
the *TERC* RNA component

explanation: Telomerase is a ribonucleoprotein, and the *TERC* RNA component (3q26.2) is the template for the telomere repeat sequence, which the *TERT* reverse transcriptase (5p15.33) then extends. Option A names the catalytic enzyme rather than the template, option B misassigns the *BRCA1* homologous recombination repair protein, and option C misassigns *DNMT1*, the maintenance DNA methyltransferase that copies CpG methylation through division.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept The second meiotic division is described as equational. What does equational mean in this context?

options.text: homologous chromosomes segregate
sister chromatids separate so chromosome number stays constant
the DNA content is doubled before division
crossing over occurs between homologs

explanation: Meiosis II is equational because the chromosome number is unchanged: sister chromatids separate, and each daughter cell keeps the same chromosome count as the cell that entered the division. Homologous chromosome segregation is the reductional event of meiosis I, not meiosis II. Crossing over happens in prophase I, and DNA doubling occurs in S phase before meiosis I begins.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** application A researcher treats a population of dividing cells with a drug that specifically inhibits cyclin dependent kinase 1, the kinase that drives entry into mitosis. In which phase of the cell cycle would the treated cells accumulate?

options.text: G2 phase
G1 phase
S phase
M phase

explanation: Cyclin dependent kinase 1 (encoded by *CDK1* at 10q21.2) drives the G2 to M transition, so inhibiting it blocks entry into mitosis and cells accumulate in G2. Cyclin dependent kinase 2 (encoded by *CDK2* at 12q13.2) drives entry into S phase, so a G1 block would be produced by a CDK2 inhibitor, not a CDK1 inhibitor. Cells blocked at the G2/M border never reach M phase itself.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** calculation A karyotype of a newborn infant shows three copies of chromosome 18 and the normal complement of all other chromosomes. How many chromosomes does this karyotype contain in total?
explanation: A normal diploid karyotype has 46 chromosomes, and an extra copy of chromosome 18 adds exactly one chromosome, so the total is 46 + 1 = 47, the trisomy 18 karyotype of Edwards syndrome. Option A is the 45-chromosome count of a monosomy such as Turner syndrome, option C is the euploid count, and option D adds two chromosomes as if a whole extra pair were present.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** application A child's karyotype shows 45 chromosomes with a single X chromosome (Turner syndrome). Which statement about how this aneuploidy could have arisen is correct?

options.text: It requires nondisjunction in the egg
It requires nondisjunction in the sperm
It can arise from nondisjunction in either the egg or the sperm
It arises from failure of sister chromatids to separate in mitosis

explanation: A 45,X zygote forms when a gamete lacking a sex chromosome fuses with a normal gamete, and nondisjunction of the sex chromosomes in either parent can produce such a gamete: meiosis I or meiosis II errors in the egg or the sperm can yield a gamete with no sex chromosome. Options A and B each wrongly restrict the error to one parent. Option D mistakes a somatic mitotic error for the meiotic origin of a constitutional aneuploidy.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept Mitosis and meiosis are both types of nuclear division, but they differ in specific events. Which event occurs in meiosis but never in mitosis?

options.text: replication of DNA before division
separation of sister chromatids
condensation of chromosomes
pairing of homologous chromosomes

explanation: Pairing of homologous chromosomes (synapsis) occurs in prophase of meiosis I and is the prerequisite for crossing over; mitosis never pairs homologs because each chromosome segregates independently. DNA replication, chromosome condensation, and sister chromatid separation all occur in mitosis as well as in meiosis, so none of them distinguishes the two divisions.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** cross-problem A true-breeding tall pea plant (*TT*) is crossed with a true-breeding dwarf pea plant (*tt*), and the F1 plants are self-crossed. Assuming complete dominance and a single locus, what phenotypic ratio is expected among the F2 plants?
explanation: Every F1 plant is *Tt* and makes *T* and *t* gametes in equal proportions, so the F2 genotype classes are 1 *TT* : 2 *Tt* : 1 *tt* (sums to 4). Because *T* is completely dominant, the *TT* and *Tt* classes both appear tall, giving the 3:1 phenotypic ratio (sums to 4). A is the genotypic ratio 1:2:1 (sums to 4), which describes genotypes rather than phenotypes. C is the two locus ratio 9:3:3:1 (sums to 16), and D is the test cross ratio (sums to 2).

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** application Two independently assorting loci control seed color and seed shape, with *A* yellow dominant over *a* green and *B* round dominant over *b* wrinkled. An *AaBb* plant is crossed with an *aabb* plant. What is the probability that an offspring is yellow and wrinkled?
explanation: At the color locus, *Aa* x *aa* gives 1/2 yellow offspring, and at the shape locus, *Bb* x *bb* gives 1/2 wrinkled offspring. The loci assort independently, so the product rule gives 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4. A is the probability of a single locus in isolation, C adds a third independent factor, and B uses 1/4 single locus probabilities as though both parents were heterozygous at both loci.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept A plant shows the dominant phenotype at a single locus, but its genotype could be *AA* or *Aa*. How does a test cross distinguish between these two genotypes?

options.text: Cross to a homozygous recessive *aa* plant and score the offspring phenotypes.
Cross to a homozygous dominant *AA* plant and score the offspring phenotypes.
Self the plant and count only the dominant offspring.
Cross to a heterozygous *Aa* plant and count only the recessive offspring.

explanation: A test cross mates the dominant phenotype individual with a homozygous recessive individual, because every allele the recessive parent contributes is *a* and cannot mask what the tested individual passes on. If the tested plant is *AA*, all offspring are *Aa* and look dominant; if it is *Aa*, half the offspring are *aa* and recessive, showing the 1:1 ratio (sums to 2). B never exposes the hidden allele, and C and D produce classes that do not distinguish the two genotypes.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** calculation A monohybrid cross with complete dominance at one locus is expected to produce two phenotype classes in a 3:1 ratio (sums to 4). A student counts 160 F2 plants and calculates chi square to test goodness of fit. How many degrees of freedom does the test use?
explanation: Degrees of freedom equal the number of phenotype classes minus one, and the monohybrid cross has two phenotype classes, so the test uses 2 - 1 = 1 degree of freedom. C would apply if the test used three classes, as in a genotypic ratio 1:2:1 (sums to 4), and D would apply to a dihybrid phenotypic ratio 9:3:3:1 (sums to 16). A forgets that the total count is fixed, which removes one degree of freedom.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** calculation A test cross of a dominant phenotype plant is expected to give a 1:1 ratio (sums to 2) of dominant to recessive offspring. Among 100 offspring, 55 show the dominant phenotype and 45 show the recessive phenotype. What is the chi square value for goodness of fit?
explanation: The expected count is 1/2 x 100 = 50 in each class, and each class contributes (observed - expected) squared divided by expected, so chi square = 25/50 + 25/50 = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.00. A divides the squared deviation by the total 100 instead of the expected 50, B keeps only one class's contribution, and C squares the summed deviations 5 + 5 = 10, giving 100/50 = 2.00.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** cross-problem Two pea plants heterozygous at two independently assorting loci with complete dominance are crossed. What phenotypic ratio is expected among the offspring?
explanation: Each locus segregates independently, so the two single locus phenotypic ratios 3:1 (sums to 4) multiply to give the dihybrid ratio 9:3:3:1 (sums to 16). A keeps only one locus, and B is the single locus genotypic ratio 1:2:1 (sums to 4). D would appear in a test cross of a dihybrid, 1:1:1:1 (sums to 4), not in a self cross.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** cross-problem Two plants both *AaBb* at two independently assorting loci are crossed. Assuming complete dominance, what is the probability that an offspring has the genotype *AABb*?
explanation: At the first locus, *Aa* x *Aa* gives *AA* with probability 1/4, and at the second locus, *Bb* x *Bb* gives *Bb* with probability 1/2. Because the loci assort independently, the product rule gives 1/4 x 1/2 = 1/8. C is the probability of *AABB* (1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16), D is the probability of *AA* combined with the dominant phenotype at the second locus (1/4 x 3/4 = 3/16), and B keeps only the first locus.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** cross-problem A plant with round yellow seeds shows the dominant phenotype at two independently assorting loci, *A* and *B*. It is test crossed to an *aabb* plant, and all 100 offspring are round and yellow. What is the tested plant's genotype?

options.text: *AaBb*
*AABB*
*AaBB*
*AABb*

explanation: A test cross exposes every allele the tested plant passes on, because the *aabb* parent contributes only *a* and *b* gametes. If the tested plant carried any recessive allele, at least some offspring would show the recessive trait at that locus, but none do, so it must be homozygous dominant at both loci, *AABB*. A would give a 1:1:1:1 ratio (sums to 4), and C and D would each give a 1:1 ratio (sums to 2), both of which would be visible in the offspring.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept A plant with genotype *AaBb* at two independently assorting loci goes through meiosis. How many genetically different gamete types can it produce, and what are they?

options.text: Two types, *AB* and *ab* only
Two types, *Ab* and *aB* only
Four types, *AB*, *Ab*, *aB*, and *ab*
Four types, *AA*, *Aa*, *aA*, and *aa*

explanation: Independent assortment combines the *A* or *a* choice at one locus freely with the *B* or *b* choice at the other, giving 2 x 2 = 4 gamete classes in equal proportion. A and B each keep only two of the four combinations and miss the other two. D writes genotypes that a gamete can never carry, since a gamete holds one allele per locus.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept In a monohybrid cross of two *Tt* heterozygotes with complete dominance for plant height, which statement about the F2 offspring is correct?

options.text: The genotypic ratio 3:1 (sums to 4) and the phenotypic ratio 1:2:1 (sums to 4) describe the same classes.
The genotypic ratio 9:3:3:1 (sums to 16) applies whenever dominance is complete.
The phenotypic ratio 1:1 (sums to 2) appears whenever both parents are heterozygous.
The phenotypic ratio 3:1 (sums to 4) hides the underlying 1:2:1 genotypic ratio (sums to 4).

explanation: With complete dominance, the *TT* and *Tt* classes look identical, so the three genotype classes collapse into the 3:1 phenotypic ratio (sums to 4) even though the genotypes remain 1:2:1 (sums to 4). A swaps which ratio describes which level, and B imports the two locus ratio 9:3:3:1 (sums to 16). C is the test cross ratio (sums to 2), which requires a homozygous recessive parent.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** calculation A dihybrid cross with complete dominance is expected to follow a 9:3:3:1 ratio (sums to 16). Among 160 offspring, how many are expected in the double dominant class?
explanation: The double dominant class occupies 9 parts of the 9:3:3:1 ratio (sums to 16), so the expected count is 9/16 x 160 = 90. B takes one of the 3 part classes, 3/16 x 160 = 30, and C takes the 1 part class, 1/16 x 160 = 10. D applies the single locus probability 3/4 instead of the two locus 9/16, giving 3/4 x 160 = 120.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** application Two heterozygous *Aa* plants at a single locus with complete dominance are crossed. What is the probability that an offspring is homozygous at this locus, either *AA* or *aa*?
explanation: The *AA* and *aa* classes are mutually exclusive, so the sum rule adds their probabilities: 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2. A counts only the *AA* class, and D answers the dominant phenotype, which also includes *Aa* and is 3/4. B comes from splitting one class's probability in half.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** cross-problem Two true-breeding snapdragon strains, one with red flowers (*RR*) and one with white flowers (*rr*), are crossed to produce F1 plants with pink flowers (*Rr*). Two F1 plants are then crossed. Assuming incomplete dominance at a single locus and complete viability, what phenotypic ratio is expected in the F2?

options.text: 1:2:1 red:pink:white (sums to 4)
3:1 red:white (sums to 4)
1:1 pink:white (sums to 2)
1:2:1 red:white:pink (sums to 4)

explanation: In **incomplete dominance** the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype, so the *Rr* F1 plants are pink. Two *Rr* plants produce *RR*, *Rr*, and *rr* in a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio (sums to 4), and because each genotype maps to its own phenotype the F2 phenotypic ratio is the same 1:2:1 (sums to 4). B is the complete dominance ratio, which hides the heterozygote, C is the ratio of a testcross, and D lists the correct classes in the wrong order, swapping the pink and white positions.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** cross-problem At the *ABO* locus the *I^A* and *I^B* alleles are codominant, so an *I^A I^B* individual has blood type AB. A woman of blood type A with genotype *I^A I^A* and a man of blood type AB with genotype *I^A I^B* have children. Assuming all genotypes are equally viable, what fraction of their children is expected to have blood type AB?
explanation: Because the *I^A* and *I^B* alleles are **codominant**, an *I^A I^B* child shows both the A and the B sugar and is type AB. The mother is homozygous *I^A I^A*, so every egg carries *I^A* (probability 1), while the father produces *I^A* and *I^B* gametes in equal proportions, giving the chain 1 x 1/2 = 1/2. A would result from multiplying 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4 as if both parents were heterozygous, C inverts the correct fraction, and D ignores the father's *I^A* gametes entirely.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** calculation A woman of blood type A has genotype *I^A i* and a man of blood type B has genotype *I^B i*. Assuming the *I^A* and *I^B* alleles are codominant, *i* is recessive to both, and all genotypes are viable, what is the probability that their child has blood type O?
explanation: Blood type O requires the genotype *ii*, and each parent is heterozygous with one *i* allele, so each contributes *i* with probability 1/2. The product rule gives 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4 for the child to be *ii*. A is the answer if the chain were expanded to 1/4 x 1/4, as for two heterozygous loci, and B is 1/2 x 1/4, a hybrid of the two. D is only the probability that the mother passes *i*, without requiring the father to pass it too.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** cross-problem In Labrador retrievers, coat color is set by two unlinked loci: the *B* locus (dominant *B* gives black, *bb* gives brown) and the *E* locus, where *ee* is epistatic and gives yellow regardless of the *B* locus. Two black dogs heterozygous at both loci (*BbEe* x *BbEe*) are crossed. Assuming independent assortment and complete viability, what phenotypic ratio is expected in the puppies?

options.text: 9:3:4 black:brown:yellow (sums to 16)
12:3:1 black:brown:yellow (sums to 16)
15:1 black:yellow (sums to 16)
3:1 black:yellow (sums to 4)

explanation: Each locus segregates independently, giving the baseline 9:3:3:1 ratio (sums to 16). **Recessive epistasis** pools the two *ee* classes: 9 *B_E_* are black, 3 *bbE_* are brown, and 3 *B_ee* plus 1 *bbee* are yellow, so the ratio is 9:3:4 (sums to 16). B is dominant epistasis (12:3:1, sums to 16), C is duplicate gene action (15:1, sums to 16), and D treats the problem as a single locus (3:1, sums to 4).

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** calculation In shepherd's purse, seed capsule shape is controlled by two unlinked duplicate loci: a dominant allele at either locus gives a triangular capsule, and only the double recessive *aabb* gives an ovoid capsule. Two *AaBb* plants are crossed. Assuming independent assortment and complete viability, what fraction of the F2 is expected to have ovoid capsules?
explanation: The ovoid class is the double recessive *aabb*, whose probability is 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16, the single non-triangular class in the 15:1 ratio (sums to 16). A is the class *aaBb* (1/4 x 1/2 = 1/8), and D is the probability of being *aa* at just one locus. B has no arithmetic route here and typically comes from misreading the 9:6:1 cumulative ratio (sums to 16) as containing a 1/12 class.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** cross-problem In summer squash, fruit shape is set by two unlinked loci with a cumulative effect: dominant alleles at both loci give disc shape, a dominant allele at exactly one locus gives sphere shape, and the double recessive *aabb* gives long shape. Two *AaBb* plants are crossed. Assuming independent assortment and complete viability, what fraction of the F2 is expected to have sphere shape?
explanation: Sphere shape comes from exactly one dominant locus, and the two classes *A_bb* and *aaB_* are independent: 3/4 x 1/4 = 3/16 and 1/4 x 3/4 = 3/16. Adding the two classes gives 3/16 + 3/16 = 6/16, the middle class of the 9:6:1 ratio (sums to 16). A is only one of the two sphere classes, C is the disc class (3/4 x 3/4 = 9/16), and D is the long class (1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16).

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** cross-problem In mice, the *Ay* allele at the agouti locus is dominant for yellow coat color and is homozygous lethal, so *Ay Ay* embryos die before birth. Two yellow mice (*Ay a* x *Ay a*) are crossed. Assuming the lethal class is never observed and the two surviving genotypes are equally viable, what phenotypic ratio is expected among the live-born pups?

options.text: 3:1 yellow:non-yellow (sums to 4)
1:2:1 dead:yellow:non-yellow (sums to 4)
1:1 yellow:non-yellow (sums to 2)
2:1 yellow:non-yellow (sums to 3)

explanation: The cross produces *Ay Ay*, *Ay a*, and *aa* in a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio (sums to 4), but the *Ay Ay* class is a **lethal allele** combination and never appears. Restricting to live pups gives 2 *Ay a* to 1 *aa*, a 2:1 ratio (sums to 3). A counts the dead class as yellow, B reports the full genotypic ratio as if the lethal class survived, and C is the ratio of a testcross.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept A trait is described as having 70 percent penetrance among individuals who carry the disease-causing allele. Which statement best describes what this means?

options.text: 70% of individuals with the allele show the trait, and 30% carry it with no sign of the trait.
70% of the population carries the allele, and the rest does not.
Individuals with the allele show the trait to a 70% degree of severity.
70% of affected individuals have a family history of the trait.

explanation: **Penetrance** is the proportion of individuals carrying a genotype who express the associated phenotype at all, so 70% (70 of every 100 carriers) would show the trait and 30% would not. C describes expressivity, which is variation in severity among people who do express the trait, and B confuses penetrance with allele frequency in the whole population. D describes a family history statistic, not a property of the genotype.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept In neurofibromatosis type 1, caused by *NF1* loss of function, one affected family shows only cafe au lait spots in some members and cafe au lait spots plus neurofibromas in others. What genetic phenomenon does this variation among affected members illustrate?

options.text: Incomplete penetrance
Pleiotropy
Complementation
Variable expressivity

explanation: **Variable expressivity** means individuals with the same genotype show the phenotype to different degrees, which is exactly what the family illustrates. Incomplete penetrance would instead require some allele carriers to show no features at all, which the stem does not say. Although *NF1* is also pleiotropic, the stem contrasts affected members with each other, and complementation concerns the outcome of crossing two mutants.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept Marfan syndrome is caused by a defect in fibrillin, the protein product of *FBN1*, and affected individuals may show aortic dilation, lens dislocation, and unusually tall stature. Which term describes a single gene contributing to several seemingly unrelated features?

options.text: Variable expressivity
Pleiotropy
Epistasis
Incomplete penetrance

explanation: **Pleiotropy** is the phenomenon in which one gene influences multiple distinct phenotypes, and fibrillin is a single protein used in the aorta, the lens, and the skeleton. Variable expressivity would describe differences in severity among people with the same genotype, which is not what the stem emphasizes. Epistasis is the masking of one gene's phenotype by another gene, and incomplete penetrance would mean some *FBN1* carriers show nothing at all.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** application You cross two true-breeding white-flowered mutants of a plant whose wild-type flowers are purple, and all F1 plants have purple flowers. What does this result indicate about the two mutations?

options.text: The mutations are in the same gene, so the F1 is expected to be white.
The mutations are dominant alleles of the same gene.
The mutations are in different genes, and each parent supplies a functional allele the other lacks.
The F1 shows incomplete dominance at a single gene.

explanation: **Complementation** occurs when two recessive mutations lie in different genes: the F1 receives a functional copy of gene 1 from one parent and a functional copy of gene 2 from the other, restoring purple. If both mutations were in the same gene, no F1 plant would have a functional allele and the F1 would be white, contradicting A and B. Incomplete dominance would give an intermediate color at a single locus, not full purple.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** pedigree A mother of blood type A and a father of blood type B have two children: a son of blood type AB and a daughter of blood type O. ```text PEDIGREE: Generation I: A mother of blood type A and a father of blood type B have two children. Generation II: A son of blood type AB and a daughter of blood type O. Key inference: The type O daughter must be ii, so each parent must contribute an i allele. Most consistent mode: Multiple alleles at the ABO locus with codominance. ``` Which parental genotypes at the *ABO* locus are consistent with this family?

options.text: Mother *I^A I^A*, father *I^B I^B*
Mother *I^A i*, father *I^B I^B*
Mother *I^A I^A*, father *I^B i*
Mother *I^A i*, father *I^B i*

explanation: A type O child must be *ii*, receiving one *i* from each parent, so both parents must carry the recessive allele; only D satisfies this. The genotypes in D also explain the son of type AB, who inherits *I^A* from the mother and *I^B* from the father. Any parent homozygous at the *ABO* locus, as in A, B, or C, could not contribute an *i* allele and could not have a type O child.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept In the mammalian XX/XY sex determination system, what determines that an embryo develops testes and male anatomy?

options.text: Carrying a single X chromosome and no Y chromosome
The *SRY* gene on the Y chromosome, which encodes the testis determining factor and initiates testis development
Carrying two X chromosomes
The presence of one Barr body in each somatic cell

explanation: Maleness is determined by the *SRY* gene on the Y chromosome, which encodes the testis determining factor and initiates testis development in the bipotential gonad. A 47,XXY individual with Klinefelter syndrome is male despite having two X chromosomes, because the Y chromosome carries *SRY*, while a 45,X individual with Turner syndrome is female. A single X with no Y does not produce testes, and the Barr body is a product of X dosage compensation in females, not a sex determinant.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept A man is described as hemizygous at the *F8* locus on the X chromosome. What does hemizygosity mean at this locus?

options.text: He has only one allele at the locus, because his single X chromosome has no homolog on the Y chromosome
He carries two copies of the same allele, one on each X chromosome
He carries one allele on the X chromosome and a matching allele on the Y chromosome
He has no functional allele at the locus, because his single X chromosome is inactivated as a Barr body

explanation: Males carry one X and one Y chromosome, and the Y chromosome has no allele at the *F8* locus, so a male has exactly one copy of the gene and is hemizygous; any allele he carries is expressed. B describes a homozygous condition that requires two X chromosomes, C wrongly assumes matching alleles on the Y chromosome, and D confuses hemizygosity with the X inactivation that occurs in female cells.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** application In female mammals, one X chromosome in each somatic cell is transcriptionally silenced so that X linked gene dosage matches that of males. Which gene initiates this inactivation?

options.text: *SRY*, which encodes the testis determining factor
*SOX9*, the transcription factor that initiates testis determination
*XIST*, a long noncoding RNA that coats and silences one X chromosome
*FMR1*, which is silenced by a CGG repeat expansion

explanation: *XIST* produces a long noncoding RNA that coats one X chromosome and silences it, forming the Barr body, which is the visible outcome of dosage compensation. *SRY* and *SOX9* act in the testis determination pathway, not in X inactivation, and *FMR1* is the fragile X locus that is silenced by a CGG repeat expansion, a different mechanism.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** cross-problem Hemophilia A is X linked recessive, caused by loss of function of *F8*. A carrier woman (*X^H X^h*) mates with an unaffected man (*X^H Y*). Assume complete penetrance, no new mutations, and a 1:1 sex ratio (sums to 2). What fraction of their sons is expected to have hemophilia A?
explanation: A son receives his Y chromosome from his father with probability 1 and one X chromosome from his mother, which carries the *X^h* allele with probability 1/2, so 1/2 x 1 = 1/2 of sons are affected. A is the fraction of all offspring that are affected sons rather than the fraction of sons, and C wrongly multiplies by an extra 1/2. D reverses the allele probabilities, treating the mother as if she transmitted *X^h* three quarters of the time.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** cross-problem An X linked dominant trait with complete penetrance is segregating in a family. An affected woman who is heterozygous (*X^D X^d*) mates with an unaffected man (*X^d Y*). Assume no new mutations and a 1:1 sex ratio (sums to 2). What fraction of all offspring, sons and daughters combined, is expected to be affected?
explanation: The mother is heterozygous, so each child inherits *X^D* with probability 1/2, and because the trait is dominant with complete penetrance any child carrying *X^D* is affected, so 1/2 x 1 = 1/2 of all offspring are affected. Sons who inherit *X^D* are hemizygous (*X^D Y*) and daughters are heterozygous (*X^D X^d*), and both are affected. A (1/4) counts only affected daughters, C (3/4) assumes all daughters are affected and adds affected sons, and B (1) assumes the dominant allele reaches every child, which a heterozygous mother does not guarantee.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** cross-problem A trait is inherited strictly on the Y chromosome, with complete penetrance. An affected man (*X Y*) mates with an unaffected woman (*X X*). Assume no new mutations and a 1:1 sex ratio (sums to 2). What fraction of his sons is expected to show the trait?
explanation: A son always receives his Y chromosome from his father, and the trait allele rides that Y, so 1 x 1 = 1, meaning every son shows the trait. Daughters never show it, because they receive the father's X chromosome instead. B is the fraction of all offspring that are sons rather than the fraction of sons affected, A treats the locus as autosomal with two recessive alleles required, and D confuses Y linked inheritance with a sex influenced trait that only some males express.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** cross-problem Red green color blindness is X linked recessive, caused by defects in the cone opsin genes *OPN1LW* and *OPN1MW*. A carrier woman (*X^C X^c*) mates with a color blind man (*X^c Y*). Assume complete penetrance, no new mutations, and a 1:1 sex ratio (sums to 2). What fraction of their daughters is expected to be color blind?
explanation: A daughter receives one X from each parent: the father contributes *X^c* with probability 1 and the mother contributes *X^c* with probability 1/2, so 1 x 1/2 = 1/2 of daughters are *X^c X^c* and color blind, while the other half are carriers (*X^C X^c*). A is the fraction of all offspring that are affected daughters, and D (1) applies the X linked dominant rule to a recessive trait. C (3/4) adds the two probabilities (1/2 + 1/4) instead of multiplying them.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** cross-problem In a breed of sheep, wool color is sex influenced: allele B produces dark wool in males whether homozygous or heterozygous, but in females only the homozygote (*BB*) is dark. A heterozygous ram (*Bb*) is crossed with a heterozygous ewe (*Bb*). Assume complete dominance within each sex and a 1:1 sex ratio (sums to 2). What fraction of the male offspring is expected to have dark wool?
explanation: The cross *Bb* x *Bb* gives a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio (sums to 4), with *BB* at 1/4, *Bb* at 1/2, and *bb* at 1/4. In males the dark phenotype appears in both *BB* and *Bb*, so 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4 of male offspring are dark. B (1/4) applies the female threshold to males, C (1/2) counts only the heterozygotes, and D (9/16) wrongly multiplies 3/4 by a 3/4 fraction of males instead of the true 1/2 fraction.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** calculation In somatic cells, all but one X chromosome is inactivated, and each inactivated X appears as a Barr body. How many Barr bodies are present in each somatic cell of a 47,XXY individual with Klinefelter syndrome?
explanation: The number of Barr bodies equals the number of X chromosomes minus one, because one X must remain active in every cell. A 47,XXY cell has two X chromosomes, so 2 - 1 = 1 Barr body. A (0) applies the normal male rule of no inactivation to an XXY cell, B (2) counts one Barr body per X without leaving one active, and D (3) adds the Y chromosome into the count.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** calculation Hemophilia A is X linked recessive, caused by loss of function of *F8*. A man with hemophilia A has a daughter, and she mates with an unaffected man. Assume no new mutations and a 1:1 sex ratio (sums to 2). What is the probability that this couple's first child is a son with hemophilia A?
explanation: The affected father (*X^h Y*) passes his *X^h* chromosome to every daughter, so the daughter is an obligate carrier (*X^H X^h*) with probability 1. The probability that the first child is a son is 1/2, and a son receives *X^h* from his mother with probability 1/2, so 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4. A (1/2) conditions on the child being a son, B (1/8) wrongly multiplies by a 1/2 carrier probability even though the daughter is an obligate carrier, and C (1/3) invents a distorted sex ratio.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** pedigree Duchenne muscular dystrophy is X linked recessive, caused by loss of dystrophin encoded by *DMD*. In the pedigree below, what is the probability that the unaffected woman II-2 is a carrier? ```text PEDIGREE: Generation I: I-1 unaffected male x I-2 unaffected female Generation II: II-1 affected male, II-2 unaffected female, II-3 unaffected male Generation III: III-1 unaffected male (son of II-2) Key inference: The affected male II-1 received his single X chromosome from his unaffected mother I-2, making her an obligate carrier. Most consistent mode: X linked recessive ```
explanation: I-2 is an obligate carrier because her affected son II-1 received his only X chromosome from her. II-2 is an unaffected daughter of the carrier (*X^H X^h*) and an unaffected man (*X^H Y*), so her father contributes *X^H* with probability 1 and her mother contributes *X^h* with probability 1/2, giving 1/2 x 1 = 1/2. B (2/3) incorrectly applies the autosomal recessive unaffected sibling correction, which does not apply here because the father's *X^H* contribution to every daughter is certain.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** pedigree The pedigree below shows a family with an X linked dominant trait. An affected father has three daughters, all affected, and two sons, both unaffected. Which statement best explains this pattern? ```text PEDIGREE: Generation I: I-1 affected male x I-2 unaffected female Generation II: II-1 affected female, II-2 affected female, II-3 affected female, II-4 unaffected male, II-5 unaffected male Key inference: An affected father transmits the trait to all daughters and to no sons. Most consistent mode: X linked dominant ```

options.text: Daughters are affected because they inherit two X chromosomes, one from each parent
An affected father passes the mutant allele to all of his children, but only daughters express it
The sons are unaffected because X inactivation silences the mutant allele in males
An affected father passes his mutant X chromosome to every daughter and his Y chromosome to every son, so all daughters are affected and no sons are

explanation: An affected male has genotype *X^D Y* and passes his *X^D* chromosome to every daughter with probability 1 and his Y chromosome to every son, so all daughters are affected and all sons are unaffected. A describes the mechanics of X inheritance in daughters but does not explain why the trait appears, B is contradicted by the sons, who never receive the paternal X at all, and C confuses dosage compensation with transmission, because males do not inactivate their single X chromosome.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** mapping In Drosophila, a female heterozygous for three recessive mutations in the linked genes *a*, *b*, and *c*, with the arrangement *a b c* / + + +, is test crossed to a male homozygous for all three recessives. The progeny classes and counts are: *a b c* 592, wild type 592, *b c* 108, *a* 108, *a b* 94, *c* 94, *a c* 4, *b* 4. Which locus lies in the middle of the genetic map?

options.text: The order cannot be determined from these data

explanation: A double crossover exchanges the middle gene while the flanking genes stay in their parental arrangement, so the gene whose allele differs between the parental classes (*a b c*, + + +) and the double crossover classes (*a c*, *b*) is the middle locus; only *b* is swapped, so the order is *a*-*b*-*c*. Choosing *a* or *c* comes from reading order off the largest classes rather than comparing the parental with the double crossover classes, which never reveals the middle gene. D fails because the four *a c* and four *b* progeny are exactly the class needed to establish order.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** calculation A female Drosophila heterozygous for two recessive mutations *d* and *e*, with the arrangement *d e* / + +, is test crossed to a male homozygous *d e* / *d e*. Among 1000 progeny, 482 show both recessive traits, 478 are wild type, 20 show only *d*, and 20 show only *e*. What is the map distance between *d* and *e*?

options.text: 2 cM
4 cM
8 cM

explanation: The recombinant classes are the 20 progeny showing only *d* and the 20 showing only *e*, because they differ from both parental arrangements (*d e* and + +). The recombination frequency is (20 + 20)/1000 = 0.04, so the map distance is 0.04 x 100 = 4 cM. A counts only one of the two reciprocal recombinant classes, giving 20/1000 x 100 = 2 cM. C doubles the recombinants to 80/1000 x 100 = 8 cM, and D reports the fraction 0.04 without converting it to map units.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept Two genes on the same chromosome are 70 map units apart, yet a two point test cross between them reports a recombination frequency near 50%, the same value expected for genes on different chromosomes. Why does the recombination frequency not reach 70%?

options.text: Crossovers occur less often between distant genes, so the recombination frequency is depressed.
Genes that far apart are not actually on the same chromosome.
An even number of crossovers between two genes restores the parental combination, so the observed recombination frequency saturates near 50%.
Recombination frequency is capped at 50% by the map distance formula, regardless of crossover number.

explanation: Each crossover produces a single exchange between the genes, but two crossovers between them restore the parental combination, so only an odd number of crossovers yields recombinant chromosomes. When genes are far apart, an odd and an even number of crossovers become about equally likely, driving the recombination frequency toward a maximum of 50%. A reverses the real relationship, because distant genes have more crossovers, not fewer, and B is false because the genes are on the same chromosome by definition of the map. D misidentifies the biological limit as a formula artifact: map distances can exceed 50 cM even though recombination frequency cannot.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** mapping In a three point test cross producing 1000 progeny, the *a*-*b* interval is 10 map units and the *b*-*c* interval is 20 map units. If 16 double crossover progeny are observed, what is the coefficient of coincidence, and what does it indicate?

options.text: CoC = 0.8, positive interference
CoC = 0.8, negative interference
CoC = 0.2, positive interference
CoC = 1.25, negative interference

explanation: The expected double crossover count is the product of the two single crossover fractions times the total, 0.10 x 0.20 x 1000 = 20, so the coefficient of coincidence is CoC = observed DCO / expected DCO = 16/20 = 0.8. Interference is I = 1 - CoC = 0.2, which is greater than zero, so the interference is positive. B pairs the correct CoC with the wrong sign, C swaps the CoC and the interference values, and D inverts the ratio, 20/16 = 1.25, which would indicate negative interference.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** calculation A three point test cross between a triply heterozygous female (*a b c* / + + +) and a homozygous recessive male yields 1000 progeny: 410 *a b c*, 410 wild type, 30 *a*, 30 *b c*, 50 *a b*, 50 *c*, 10 *a c*, 10 *b*. What is the map distance between the outside genes *a* and *c*?

options.text: 16 cM
18 cM
12 cM
20 cM

explanation: The distance between the outside genes includes every crossover event between them: the 60 single crossovers in the *a*-*b* interval plus the 100 single crossovers in the *b*-*c* interval plus both exchanges in each double crossover, so the 20 double crossover progeny are counted twice: (60 + 100 + 2 x 20)/1000 x 100 = 200/1000 x 100 = 20 cM. A omits the double crossovers entirely, (60 + 100)/1000 x 100 = 16 cM. B counts each double crossover once, (60 + 100 + 20)/1000 x 100 = 18 cM, and C reports only the *b*-*c* interval, (100 + 20)/1000 x 100 = 12 cM.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** application A genome wide association study finds a SNP near the *HBB* gene strongly associated with sickle cell disease in a population. Which conclusion is best supported by this finding alone?

options.text: The SNP itself is the variant that causes sickle cell disease.
The associated SNP must lie inside the coding sequence of *HBB*.
The SNP is likely in linkage disequilibrium with the causal variant, so the association narrows the region for follow up mapping.
The association proves the two loci assort independently.

explanation: Genome wide association studies test hundreds of thousands of SNPs, and an associated SNP is often not the causal variant itself but one in linkage disequilibrium with it, because recombination has not fully separated nearby alleles in the population. A overinterprets association as causation, and B is false because associated SNPs frequently lie in introns or intergenic regions. D is backwards: association between the SNP and the disease means the alleles are nonrandomly associated, the opposite of independent assortment, so the region must be narrowed to find the causal change.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** calculation In a family based linkage study, the likelihood of the pedigree data under linkage is computed to be 1000 times the likelihood under no linkage. What is the lod score for this result?
explanation: The lod score is the base 10 logarithm of the odds of linkage versus no linkage, so Z = log10(1000) = 3. A reports the raw odds ratio without taking the logarithm, and C multiplies by 10 instead of applying the log. D gives the reciprocal odds, 1/1000, which would point toward no linkage.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** mapping A female Drosophila heterozygous for two recessive mutations *r* and *s*, with the arrangement *r s* / + +, is test crossed to a male homozygous *r s* / *r s*. Among 1000 progeny, 470 show both recessive traits, 470 are wild type, 30 show only *r*, and 30 show only *s*. What is the map distance between *r* and *s*?

options.text: 3 cM
12 cM
6 cM

explanation: The recombinant classes are the 30 progeny showing only *r* and the 30 showing only *s*, because they differ from both parental arrangements (*r s* and + +). The recombination frequency is (30 + 30)/1000 = 0.06, so the map distance is 0.06 x 100 = 6 cM. A counts only one of the two reciprocal recombinant classes, giving 30/1000 x 100 = 3 cM. B doubles the recombinants to 120/1000 x 100 = 12 cM, and D reports the fraction 0.06 without converting it to map units.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** cross-problem A female Drosophila heterozygous for two recessive mutations *p* and *q*, with the arrangement *p q* / + +, is test crossed to a male homozygous *p q* / *p q*. Assumptions: complete penetrance, no lethality, and equal viability of all classes. The 1000 progeny consist of 450 showing both recessive traits, 450 wild type, 50 showing only *p*, and 50 showing only *q*. Are the genes linked, and if so, how far apart?

options.text: The genes are linked, 5 cM apart.
The genes are linked, 50 cM apart.
The genes are unlinked and assort independently.
The genes are linked, 10 cM apart.

explanation: Under independent assortment a test cross gives a 1:1:1:1 ratio (sums to 4), so the 900 parental versus 100 recombinant progeny are grossly skewed and the genes must be linked. The recombination frequency is (50 + 50)/1000 = 0.10, so the map distance is 0.10 x 100 = 10 cM. A counts only one of the two reciprocal recombinant classes, 50/1000 x 100 = 5 cM, and B mistakes the presence of recombination for the 50% maximum seen between very distant or unlinked genes.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** application A geneticist wants the most accurate map of three linked genes. Why is a single three point test cross preferred over three separate two point test crosses?

options.text: It reveals the gene order directly and corrects for double crossovers that would be missed in two point crosses.
It measures recombination only in the female, removing the need for reciprocal crosses.
It requires no homozygous recessive tester strain.
It produces exactly twice as many progeny per fly as a two point cross.

explanation: A three point test cross provides all three pairwise distances plus the gene order from one set of progeny, and the double crossover class makes the correction for undetected double crossovers possible, so the distances are more accurate than two point estimates that omit double crossovers. B is wrong because the same single sex recombination occurs in either cross design, and C is wrong because a three point test cross still requires a homozygous recessive tester. D is false: progeny number per fly is set by the cross itself, not the number of loci scored.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** concept In a three point cross, fewer double crossovers are observed than expected from the product of the two single crossover frequencies. Which term best describes this outcome, and how is it measured?

options.text: Negative interference, measured as I = 1 - CoC, with I less than 0.
Positive interference, measured as I = 1 - CoC, with I greater than 0.
Linkage disequilibrium, measured as I = 1 - CoC.
Positive interference, measured as I = CoC - 1.

explanation: Fewer double crossovers than expected gives CoC = observed DCO / expected DCO less than 1, so I = 1 - CoC is greater than 0, which is positive interference. A describes negative interference, which requires CoC greater than 1 and I less than 0, the opposite of the observed data. D uses the reversed formula, which would give a negative I here, and C mistakes a cross based quantity for linkage disequilibrium, a population level association.

subject: genetics
question: **Type:** application In a linkage study of a rare autosomal dominant trait, a marker gives a maximum lod score of 3.4 at a recombination fraction of 0.05. What is the most defensible interpretation of this result?

options.text: The result proves the marker itself is the disease causing mutation.
A lod score of 3.4 is below the conventional threshold of 5 and provides no evidence of linkage.
A lod score above 3 means the marker and the trait locus assort independently.
The odds in favor of linkage are 10^3.4, about 2500 to 1, so the trait locus is very likely close to the marker.

explanation: The lod score is the base 10 logarithm of the linkage to no linkage odds, so Z = 3.4 means the data are 10^3.4, about 2500 times, more likely under linkage, and the conventional threshold for declaring linkage is Z = 3. A overstates the finding, because a lod score localizes the trait locus near the marker without identifying the mutation itself.
